Rivenkeep — The Tongues

The First Tongue · The Shoreland speech and its three hands · The Mystaeri thunder-tongue and the grain
· Module of The Legends · Owns the two peoples’ languages, the tongue they both came from, and their writing: Orrowen with its dry cut, its leaf-hand and the Hal; Seilrhass and its grain. The Book’s English is a translation of these, and a leaf the player has not earned stays in its own hand. · Companions: The Legends (canonical), The Legends, in Plain Words, The Legends, in Their Own Hands, The Admiral · Where this doc and the Legends disagree, the Legends win · Version history at the bottom of this doc.

1The Conceit: The Book Is a Translation

Every word the player reads in the Book is English, and none of it was written in English. Seren Two-Inks wrote her leaves in Orrowen, the Shoreland tongue, in the leaf-hand, the running ink of the course-hand. What the Rivenmen cut in stone they cut dry, in word-signs, leaving the small words to the reader. The wood’s knowings were never written at all: they were carved as grain, a writing of meaning that has no sound, and Halyna told them aloud. Under both lies one older tongue, the First Tongue, that neither people remembers. What the player holds is the translation. A leaf the player has not earned stays in its own hand. Earning it translates it.

What Jack asked (2026-09-27, the first notes)

That the line “Untold. Halyna cannot yet hold this deep.” be written in the Shoreland or the Mystaeri tongue, so that the player cannot read it until they have earned the ability through the game’s achievements. The Mystaeri writing should feel like the aliens’ writing in Arrival, and Shoreland like an ancient, Celtic-sounding tongue. Both should be real languages, written the same way throughout. He also asked for a tab that lets the player read either the Book or the Plain Words translation. Version 0.1.0 answered all of it.

1.1 · The first spread, as the player first sees it

The Book opens on I.1, The Torn Cloak. On the facing leaf the Book and the game both show the Stone out of the Grey as the wood gives it before the Epilogue: its own rings, with nothing cut in them. In the grain an unmarked round has no root and so no axis, and it reads, truthfully, nothing is given here. Under it is Seren’s line, written in her ink, in the leaf-hand. The English arrives later, beneath the hand, when the player earns it.

The same line stands under every blank wood leaf in the Book, beneath that leaf’s own round, fully cut and not yet glossed. So from the first minute the player can see both peoples’ writing on one spread, and cannot read either. That is the shape of the whole Book: something they can see and do not yet understand.

1.2 · Two peoples, two tongues, one ancestor

Shoreland (the Rivenmen)Mystaeri (the Naelear)
The spoken tongueOrrowen, “of the Shore” (§3)Seilrhass, “bough-thunder” (§7)
How it soundsstops and clusters, a rolled r, back vowels and a rounded y, stress on the first syllableno stops at all, no o or u, and one knock after the first syllable of every longer word: Ael’thar
How it worksverb first; two initial mutations; a dual number; conjugated prepositions; no verb “to have”. It is Celtic in how it works and in nothing it saysverb last; modifiers before the noun; postpositions; living and mute things are grammatically apart
Its writingthe course-hand (Garl Dhrenn), an alphabet of straight chisel strokes on a mortar line, in three hands: the dry cut for stone, word-signs with the small words left out (§5); the leaf-hand for ink, the whole tongue joined and quick (§6); and the Hal, the first builders’ (§4.8)the grain (Eilseth): the cross-section of a trunk, marks cut across its growth rings, heart to bark. It records meaning and has no sound (§8, §9)
How it is taken inread with the eyes: letters by sound, word-signs by the word they stand forknown by touch, whole, as a memory. Only the Bonded can hold it; the telling is the hard part
Its old formthe Hal, the first builders’ speech. The living can see every sign of it and cannot sound itthe Eldest speech, surviving in the oldest carved names (Esthaer, and the borrowed Mystaeri)
Its ancestorThe First Tongue, Tumaʔ, “what is held in common”: one people, before the grey, who cut 45 marks on whatever stood. The stone kept its sound; the wood kept its meaning. Neither people knows it (§2)
A further handthe Captain’s coal, the Title only; the Last Carver’s, the Epilogue onlythe soft letters (rhelranth), “fine and curling, as beautiful as frost on a window”: sound spelled on stone. A sketch, not yet drawn (§8.9)

One line holds the difference: stone writes what is said; wood writes what is meant. The course-hand can be learned by anyone with eyes, which is why the Last Carver could cut it. The grain can be seen by anyone and known only by the Bonded, which is why Seren can name its roots by eye and must leave the rest to Halyna. And one line holds the kinship: the stone kept the sound of the First Tongue, and the wood kept its meaning, so the Knowing is the nearest living survivor of a tongue no one alive can speak.

1.4 · The four rules the conceit keeps

Truth or nothing

Players decode. So every letter, word-sign and mark the player can see is a true encoding of a real text, drawn by rule. Nothing is ever decorative. Where no text has been written in the tongue yet, the leaf shows nothing, or ruled empty courses, and never invented letters. Empty wood is drawn as rings with no marks, which in the grain means exactly “nothing is cut here”.

The Book only adds

A translation is laid beneath its hand; it never replaces it (Legends law 7). The fragments of a wood leaf stay above its whole telling, and the tabs are views, never edits.

Every unlock is a milestone every player reaches

Translations ride campaign milestones and events the sim has already recorded, each event with a campaign fallback. No skill achievement ever holds back a leaf (Legends laws 1, 4 and 5).

Decoders are rewarded, never required

The course-hand is a real alphabet, and the dry cut’s word-signs are a real list. The Title is shown with its English from the first launch, so it works as a key. A player who studies it can read Seren’s line before earning it, and that is the reward. The grain’s root signs can be read by eye, as Seren reads them. Everything past the root must be known, and waits for Halyna. The kinship of the two tongues is never told; a decoder may find it.

2The First Tongue: The Ancestor of Both

Jack’s note: “Imagine that all languages come from an ultimate base language.” Orrowen and Seilrhass are made to sound like opposites, and they are. Under them lies the First Tongue, Tumaʔ, “what is held in common”: one tongue that both descend from, reverse-engineered as a philologist would build the primitive roots under two daughter languages. It has a sound system, 624 roots, the ordered sound laws that turn them into both living tongues, and 45 first marks from which the course-hand’s letters, the dry cut’s word-signs and the grain’s signs all descend. Every form in this section is computed by a sound-law engine from its ancestral form and checked against both lexicons; nothing in a table of forms is typed by hand.

The check

356 derivations from 253 inherited roots, 0 mismatches. Every one of the 310 Orrowen entries and 215 Seilrhass entries published in v0.1 falls out of the laws, directly or as a formation whose every part does, with a short list of named irregularities (§2.3). Every Hal form the Shoreland spec gave comes out exactly (three are emended first), and so does every Eldest form. The canon Hal texts, the Stonwryt and the proverb, are reproduced word for word. The 371 reserve roots derive in both tongues by the same laws and collide with no existing word. What the check cannot do is judge beauty or originality: the reserve forms passed a blacklist and the whole English dictionary, and a dictionary pass against Welsh, Irish and the Tolkien lexicons is still owed before any of them ships (§13.8).

Notation. An asterisk marks a First Tongue form: *tolm-. In ancestral forms th is /θ/, dh is /ð/, x is /x/ (as in Scots loch), ŋ is the ng of sing, and ʔ is the catch, a stop in the throat, the grandfather of the Mystaeri knock. A hyphen marks a suffix seam and + a compound seam. “O” is Orrowen, “S” is Seilrhass. The name is Jack’s to confirm Jack: Tumaʔ in the First Tongue, Tuma in Orrowen, Theinae in Seilrhass, and in English the First Tongue.

2.1 · What the First Tongue was, and why no one knows it

  • One people, one tongue, one hand. Before there was a grey or a wall, one people spoke Tumaʔ. They cut their marks on whatever stood: a stone set on end, or the trunk of a living tree. Their word for both was *tolm-, “a standing thing”.
  • A mark was a word and a sound at once. Each of the first marks stood for a thing, and it could also be read for the first sound of its name. A line of marks said what was meant and how it was said, both at once. Neither living hand can do that.
  • A word held. The tongue’s name for itself comes from *tum-, “hold, keep, in the hand and in the mind”. In Orrowen the root means “remember” (tum); in Seilrhass, “hold, know by touch” (thein). So the hearth’s yes and the wood’s Knowing are one verb.
  • The parting. No tale tells it, and nothing here needs one Jack. The Book fixes only the two ends: the Mystaeri “were old” before the Shorelanders cut their first stone (II.2), and the first Stonewrights “came up onto the high ridges” in the age before the havens (II.1). The two kinds of standing thing became the two peoples’ matter. Those who stayed with the trees cut their marks into living wood, and every ring the tree grew carried them outward: what grows keeps its meaning and loses its sound. Those who went up to the rock cut their marks in stone, which does not grow: the chisel wore the marks straight, and the builders read them for their sounds.
  • The tongues drifted, as tongues do. The wood’s speech lost every stop and every back vowel, and its catch became the knock. The stone’s speech kept its stops, lost its endings, and turned the lost endings into mutations. By the time the grey sails came, no word of one could be heard in the other.
Stone: the ShorelandersWood: the Mystaeri
the soundkept longest. The Hal still has its endings and three sounds that have since mergedworn down to seven consonants and a knock
the meaning of the markslet go: each mark became a letter for one soundkept: each mark is still read for what it means
the shapesworn straight, stood on a bed, arms kept only to the rightset along a file, bowed and tapered, grown in rings
kept whole by boththe Fore (the cross) and the Door (the gate); the word for "both"; the proverbthe same

Why the Knowing is the nearest survivor. Only the wood kept what the first marks meant, and “a knowing cannot be turned” (the foreword). The stone kept how the First Tongue sounded, and sound is what time changes: the Rivenmen cannot sound their own Hal. So the one part of the First Tongue anyone alive can still take in whole is the wood’s. This doc says so; the Book never does (§2.8).

Why no one knows. The Hal is unreadable even to the Rivenmen (§3.4). The Mystaeri “never once went down to the shore with our hands open, save once” (V.4). The grain has no sound, so the one hand that kept the First Tongue’s meanings cannot tell anyone how it sounded. And the kin words look nothing alike: tresk and thaess, tolm and thael, ol and ael, molt and nael. Only the laws show that they are one word.

2.2 · How it sounded, and its grammar in brief

Stops and back vowels, like the stone’s tongue, with the wood’s breathy clusters (xw-, xr-) and a catch in one root in eight. It sounds heavier than Seilrhass and less worn than Orrowen: *trosk-i, *xreun-aʔ, *waʔr-ai, *swe-reŋ-o-s.

lipstongue-tipbackthroat
stopsp · bt · dk · gʔ (the catch)
nasalsmnŋ
fricativesfth /θ/ · dh /ð/ · sxh
approximantswl · ry
  • Clusters. At the start of a word: stop + r or l; s + stop; xr, xw, xwr, xwl, gw, sw. After a vowel, most sonorant + consonant pairs, st, sk, and doubled ll, nn, mm, rr, ss. Common: t, k, s, n, l, r, m; rarer: b, ŋ, h, y.
  • Vowels. Five short vowels, a e i o u, and the diphthongs ai ei oi au eu ui. The back vowels o and u are frequent, and the wood lost both. There are no long vowels: length in the Hal comes from the catch.
  • Syllables and stress. A syllable is (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C). Stress falls on the first syllable, as in both daughters. A catch carries a falling pitch on its syllable, and that pitch survives in the knock’s “high falling pitch”.

The catch, ʔ, and its three fates. The catch is the First Tongue’s own colour, and it is where the knock began. In the wood’s speech a stop at the head of the second syllable left a catch before it, and the catch then spread to every word of two syllables or more: the Mystaeri knock is the First Tongue’s catch, moved. A root with the catch after its vowel is often the solemn form of a plainer root: *sol- “lie still” beside *soʔl- “the deep rest” (O sollan, peace).

Where it standsIn Orrowen (O1)In Seilrhass (S1)
after a vowel, before l r m n sdoubles the consonant: *waʔl- > vallbreaks the vowel: aʔ > ae, eʔ > ea, oʔ > ae, iʔ > i, uʔ > ei: *waʔl- > vael
after a vowel, before any other consonant, or at the endlengthens the vowel: *gann-aʔ > Hal gannā, *feʔth- > Hal vēth-breaks the vowel, as above
between vowels, or at the startlostlost

Roots and ablaut. Most roots are one syllable, CVC or CVCC (*tolm-, *krask-, *senn-). A root may show e, a or o in different words: *tol-/*tal- gives tolm a stone, tald rise, and the wood’s thal the neck; *krenn-/*krann- gives crenn a captain and rhann heavy; *bro-/*bra-/*bre- gives brod a word, ranth a word, renn a mouth. Extensions make new stems: *-d- “made, brought to” (*tal-d- rise up; *gal-d- build; *xal-d- a wall), *-t-, and *-n- and *-l- (*xwre-n- frost in stone, *xwre-l- frost in wood).

The grammar the daughters inherited.

  • Nouns end in a thematic vowel, *-o- (broad) or *-i- (slender). The nominative adds *-s: *tolm-o-s. Orrowen built on this form, which is why the Hal ends in -os and -is. The bare stem was used for calling and naming, *tolm-o, and Seilrhass built on that, which is why it has no case endings. The broad and slender classes of Orrowen are these two vowels, remembered.
  • Other endings: *-aʔ “a whole of two or more” (O dual -a, and the feminine); *-uʔ “the place of” (O -ow); *-aθi plural (O -Ath); *-en “belonging to” (O -en; S plural -en); *-eʔ “one of” (S -ea); *-aʔr “all of a kind” (S -aer, later -ear); *-el “one, a small one” (O -el).
  • Verbs take the person endings *-om, -iθ, -os, -ana, -aʔ, -ar, -us, -ant. Orrowen kept them. The 3sg *-os fell with the other endings, which is why the living 3sg is the bare stem (Hal STONOS > ston). Tumar, “we remember”, is *tum-ar, “we hold”.
  • Particles could stand before or after the word they governed. Orrowen, which put its verb first, fixed them before the word, and that froze their final -n and final vowels into the mutations. Seilrhass, which put its verb last, fixed them after the word: its verb suffixes -e, -es and -ar are the particles *e “now”, *es “at another time” and *ar “toward”, fused to the verb after the final vowels had fallen. So *es became a future in the stone and a past in the wood: the stone looked forward with it, and the wood looked back.
  • Pronouns and pointing words were many, and each tongue kept a different set: *en “this one here, I”; *θo “you”; *o “he, it”; *ey “she”; *ol “together, we”; *sa/*se “that one by you”; *la/*le “that living one”; *xa/*xe “that mute thing”; *ra “this”; *re “that”. The wood’s split between living and mute pronouns is the First Tongue’s.

2.3 · The sound laws

The laws are few and regular. Each daughter has a first stage, new here, from the First Tongue to its old speech (the Hal; the Eldest speech), and a second stage, the specs’ own laws made exact, from the old speech to the living tongue.

To Orrowen · stage 1: the First Tongue to the Hal

O2 · The old diphthongs closeai, ei, oi > ē; au, ou > ū; eu > iu; ui > y. A long vowel before two consonants is shortened*kail-o-s > Hal kēlos (Kael); *xreun-aʔ > xriunā (> Hal Hriunā); *xui-a > xya (> Hal hya); *weinn-i-s > wēnnis > wennis (> Hal vennis)

The principled irregularities, three emendations and one re-analysis

Every irregular form has a reason, and three small emendations to the v0.1 Hal are adopted (none changes a living word) Jack. The seven harmony slips of v0.1 (vennoth, delvoth, flennath, Kethow Stellath, treskat, ul glennol, Rytom) are untouched by the ancestor, which only shows that flennath and tevath are old ā-stems, so the broad suffix is right for those two.

WordWhat is irregularWhy
flenn (Hal hwlennā)the final -ā fellH2 keeps -ā only where it is still a living ending, the dual or the feminine. In *xwlen-naʔ it was a stem vowel. Its broad plural flennath keeps the old ā-stem's class, as tevath does
arra (Hal arrā)keeps -ā, though "a guest" is neither dual nor feminineit is an old dual: *arr-aʔ, "the two at a threshold, guest and host". A guest is half of a pair
vaerekeeps its final -ethe -e is the long e of the old *-ai (S1), which S7 does not drop. The spec's "final vowels stayed after r" is replaced by this: eir (from *ir-i) loses its -e
varenkeeps the old agent *-aneas the spec says; S3 makes it -en
Esthaer, Mystaerikeep -aeras the spec says: cut, or borrowed, before S8
sei, rei, vei beside si, ri, vione first-tongue word gives twothe stressed twins. *si, *ri, *wi stayed i as unstressed small words and became ei where they carried stress (S2): "if", "to go", "to give" beside "with", "against", "for"
cedh, cemmspelled with c before ea spelling rule, not a sound. The Book writes c before an e that the i-colouring made out of a (*ka-ð-i, *kamm-i-s), and k before an old e (keth, kest)
theldethnot the regular Hal *thaldathithe plural was rebuilt on the singular theld- after the i-colouring (analogy)
nel, newnot *nael, *naewthe Hal's own contractions of na + el, na + ew
-Os, 2pl (Hal -us)living -os / -ys, not the -us the tables givethe harmony law of the Orrowen spec: an unstressed suffix vowel was reduced, then took the stem's colour, as Hal -ola became -ol / -yl. The engine runs the colouring (H6) but not the reduction, so the tables give the Hal's -us; the living 2pl is the harmonic -Os (tumos, kethys)
Seren (was Hal Serenos)emendation: Hal SEREŊOSthe name now carries *reŋ-. The Hal writes it with the dead letter ŋ
re (was Hal rea in v0.1)emendation: Hal rethe Stonwryt itself cuts RE, and re softens because it ends in a vowel
va (was Hal vanan in v0.1)emendation: Hal vanvanan would give *van by H1–H2; *wa-n gives Hal van, living va
thaelre-analysis (not a form change)the mystaeri spec's "thae + old -l" becomes *tolm-i, the standing thing

2.4 · Worked derivations: four sayings, back to the First Tongue

Each word of each line below is derived by the engine; the build fails if any does not come out. Each table runs from the First Tongue form, through the old speech, to the living word, and then to the word as the line says it, mutation and all.

Tumar.

Ve ith naelenn ael raltheine.

First tongueEldestlivingas the line says itgloss

The Title opens Ul dumol ol varn, “In memory of our home”. At the end of the war the green sliver says Ve ith naelenn ael raltheine, “We remember our home too”. Under both lie the same two First Tongue words, *tum- “hold” and *ol “together”. The hearth’s answer, Tumar, is *tum-ar, “we hold”. The canon says the sliver “gave them the answer of this hearth … and it did not stop where we stop”. In the First Tongue it is the same answer.

The saying is older than the parting. The wood’s wording is the older one: its words are the First Tongue’s own. The stone rebuilt all of it except the last word, and that word is still one word in both tongues: vana, vann, “both”.

None of the Stonwryt’s words met a law between the First Tongue and the Hal. The vow under the tale-stone is cut in the First Tongue itself, word for word: it is the oldest sentence anyone can still see. The Rivenmen cannot sound it, and the Mystaeri would not know one word of it. It can be read word for word at all only because a vow is always cut whole, in letters (§5.2).

(d) The Guest’s three words

Hess… Helv… Sennyl…

First tongueHallivingas the line says itgloss
*hess-i-sHESSIShessHess…stop
*half-i-sHELVIShelvHelv…the upper air, sky
*senn-i-sSENNISsennSennyl…go down: die (+ -Ol, dying)

What his own tongue says for the same, and the word at the end of the gift’s sentence:

First tongueEldestlivingas the line says itgloss
*kul-ikeilerheilrheilstop (O kyl, change)
*molt-onaelenaelnaelsky, breath (O molt, heart)
*feʔs-iveaseveasveasedie (O vess, night)
*senn-isennesennsennbeneath (O senn, die)

The Guest reached for “stop, sky, dying” in the shore’s tongue. His third word, Sennyl, is at the root *senn-, “going down”. His own people kept that root as senn, “beneath”, and the gift’s sentence ends with it: ei ve la senn vease, “and we are dying under it”. The last word he said at the door and the last clause of the gift he brought are one word, split by the parting.

2.5 · The kinship: the words that are one word in both tongues

38 words are one word in both tongues, and they fall where the Book already cares most. The meaning in the First Tongue is the one both senses grew from.

First tongueOrrowenSeilrhassWhere it touches the Book
*tol- / tal- rise, stand up talltolm a stone · tald rise, stand up (v.) · taldow a tower, a high placethael a tree · thal the neck, where life goes up into…The one word for the standing thing split between the peoples: the stone-folk kept it for stone, the wood-folk for the tree. The earlier analysis of <em>thael</em> as <em>thae</em> + an old <em>-l</em> is replaced.
*xreun- set hard, hardenrhyn set fast (of mortar), take hold · Rhyna 'she who sets fast'rhen stone, the mute thingRhyna's name and the wood's word for stone are one. The Guest's errand-name Aelrhen, 'bond-to-stone', is at the root *ol-xreun: 'together, set fast'.
*tum- hold, keep (in the hand and in the mind)tum remember · tumol rememberingthein to holdThe hearth's yes, Tumar 'we remember', is in the first tongue 'we hold'. The Knowing (theinas) is the same holding.
*ol together, one with anotherol we · olna we two (+S)ael bond, joiningThe Title says ol five times ('our home, our families...'); the Aelthar and the sliver's 'too' are the same word.
*pa- twopa two (+S) · pana bothvann twoThe proverb's last word is this root in both tongues: grest um vana / vann li thaess.
*trosk- split, cleavetresk a cleft, a splitthaess to splitThe Riven Stone and the Torn Cloak (O tresk) and the wound of the proverb (S thaess) are one word.

Two crossings worth seeing. Death and night trade places across the two tongues. The stone says “die” with *senn- “go down” (O senn, “go out, as a fire in peace”); the wood kept *senn- for “beneath”. The wood says “die” with *feʔ- “fade” (S veas); the stone kept *feʔ- for “night” (O vess). In the same way, the stone’s word for stone is the wood’s word for the tree, and the wood’s word for stone is the stone’s word for mortar setting fast.

2.6 · The first marks: the sign-set both hands came from

The First Tongue wrote with 45 marks, cut on whatever stood. Each was a small picture, and each was named by a First Tongue word. Stone took the marks to the chisel: they were worn straight and set on a bed, then read for the first sounds of their names, and a reform of the first builders laid them out as a system of uprights and laid stones, which is the course-hand. Some marks the chisel kept whole as words, and those are the dry cut’s word-signs (§5). Wood took the same marks into the growing tree: they were set on files and bowed by the knife, read for what they mean, and grown into new signs. That is the grain. Two marks were kept whole by both peoples: the Fore (a stroke crossed near its head: the Latin cross, the Bar Before) and the Door (two posts and a lintel: the gate mark, and DOOR).

Where the table says a mark was lost on stone, read lost from the letters: many of those marks were kept by the chisel whole, as the heads and crowns of the dry cut’s word-signs (the Cup is TUM, the Drop LORR, the Star ORL, the Scar VORR, the Knot TOVV, the Mouth BROD, the Hand GARL, the Eye VESK, the Kneel LUMM, and so on: §5.4). And the stone kept the marks as words, not as meanings: a word-sign is read as one Orrowen word, whose meaning drifts with the word.

The laws of form

On stone: the chisel, the first sound, and the reform. C6 is the “reformed” hand in Jack’s sense: few strokes, laid by rule, one letter to a sound. The first builders then kept cutting word-signs wherever a mark would do (§3.4), and C3 and C4 are laws of the letters; the word-signs obey C1, C2 and their own laws (§5.2).

LawWhat happens
C1The chisel straightens.A curve becomes a straight stroke or a corner; a closed curve opens into strokes; a solid is cut as its outline's base.
C2Everything stands on a bed.A mark is stood on the mortar line; its roots are replaced by the bed; a mark that hung or floated is set down.
C3Stones are laid to the right.An arm on the left of a stem is cut away; what is kept runs to the right, as a mason lays each stone against the last.
C4Three leans.Every upright leans forward, steps, or leans back, and nothing else.
C5The first sound.A mark is read for the first sound of its name (acrophony). Stone writes what is said.
C6The laying of the letters (the reform).The first builders' scribes made the letter of each sound out of two parts: the upright of its place, taken from the three oldest letters p, t and k; and the laid stones of its manner, taken from the mark whose name began with that kind of sound. Everything else about the old marks was let go. Like the reformed Egyptian that note 1 names, it is an economy: few strokes, laid by rule.
C7Small marks become pinnings.The marks read for a vowel become small loose stones set low between the ashlars, in mirrored pairs.
C8Marks of ending and binding stay marks.What closed or bound a line in the old hand stays outside the alphabet as punctuation: the end, the door, the bar, the tally.

In wood: the file, the knife, and the meaning.

LawWhat happens
G1The mark goes on a file.Its stem runs from the heart outward; whatever lay across the stem now lies along the ring; a line laid along the whole ring is a condition or a rule.
G2The knife and the growing.Strokes bow and taper at both ends; corners round; a closed shape stays straight only when it names a thing of stone.
G3Meaning, not sound.A mark is known by what it means. Its soft reading is the living word for that meaning, not the mark's old name. Wood writes what is meant.
G4Signs grow new signs.Marks join on one file (modifier inward) and grow parts: a lens for a thing of wood, a square for a thing of stone, a star for a flash, a wedge for a blow, a check for a hurt.
G5Time and place.What comes first is cut nearer the heart (a ring is an hour); who and where are files; a pause is an empty ring.
G6The mirror.The first tongue's 'not' was a mark turned to face the other way. The grain kept it as negation, and gave every symmetrical sign the entry-nick so that it has a mirror.
G7The two line-qualities.The Square and the Bough became the classifier: straight for what is of stone, curved for what is of wood.

Every course-hand letter, from the marks

The reform’s rule (C6). A letter is the upright of its place + the laid stones of its manner. The three uprights come from the three oldest letters: the Bearer for the lips (p), the Course for the tongue-tip (t) and the Split for the back of the mouth (k). Each manner’s stones come from the mark whose own name began with that kind of sound: the voicing pin from the Post, *gann-; the nasal’s middle stone from the Breath Within, *molt-; the fricative’s low stone from the Breathing, *hoss-; and so on. So the reform is itself an act of reading by first sound: it asked what each mark sounded, and kept only the strokes that told it.

The two marks kept whole

  • The Fore (*re-il, “the one before; first”). In wood it is the Bar Before, the root of the Screen line; its soft reading, reil, is the Fore’s own name, worn. On stone it is the first builders’ mark, “first, before all”, and in the dry cut it is the word-sign hosast, the foremark (§5.5). Its right arm and foot also gave the letter r. It is a Latin cross, and that is fine (note 8): it is older than both peoples, and each kept it for “first”. Whether the Shorelanders also keep it as a holy sign is Jack’s call; the design does not need it, and the Book’s faith needs no emblem Jack.
  • The Door (*gann-aʔ, “the two posts”). On stone it is the gate mark that closes an oath, capped as the coping that closes a tale; it is also the word ganna and the pair-name custom, “a pair is a gate”, and the dry cut’s word-sign GANNA. In wood it is DOOR, its posts battered in. “We were a people of doors” (IV.3). So, it turns out, were both.

They are no one’s alphabet. The first marks are proto-writing, so some are the world’s commonest strokes: the Stem (|), the Bar (—), the Fore (+, by design), the End (T), the Door (Π), the Cut (V), the Three (|||). None is a Futhark rune (no stave with straight branches; the Roots’ three feet are uneven), an Ogham letter (the Tally cuts notches, not strokes), a Cirth letter, a Tengwa, or an Arrival logogram.

2.7 · The roots

624 roots. The 253 inherited roots are the roots behind every existing word of both tongues, with their small words, affixes and names. The 371 reserve roots are First Tongue words that neither living tongue had used, each with its regular form in both tongues, laid by for the whole Book’s translation (§11): a reserve word enters Orrowen as a Hal word (so its Hal form and its mutations are known), and Seilrhass as a root like any other. ★ marks a root that both tongues kept. Where a tongue did not keep a root, the cell gives the form it would have, and says “falls together with” where that form is already another word, and “a lift” where it is on the originality blacklist and must not be used. The reserve roots were drawn from the First Tongue’s own sound pattern, seeded so the list can be remade exactly, and screened: no clash with any existing word, no blacklisted form, and no form in either tongue that is an English word. Any reserve word can be swapped for another draw without touching the laws Jack.

Names are names. The cradle-names (Corlen, Voss, Hale, Marl, Tamm, Aske, Harl, Ulden, Hesk, Lanner, Aldun, Bena, Idlan, Denna) each have a regular First Tongue shape, so the laws account for their sounds, but no meaning is given (Jack’s note 6). Brenn’s shape happens to be the First Tongue’s word for “mouth”; the Book gives him no meaning, and nothing needs to.

2.8 · The lore: letting the kinship show, without editing a tale

Call-out for Jack Jack

The Book should never say that the two tongues are kin. No one at the hearth knows it. It can let the player find it, in the places the Book already keeps for native hands and their translations (Legends map §4).

  1. The mark on the black chest (I.4) is the Fore. The tale says only “a chest of black stone, with the mark of the first builders cut in its lid”, and that surface is still owed. Draw it as the Fore in the Hal’s cut style: a stroke crossed near its head, square-footed on its bed. From One Word (Cam 1) the player has the Bar Before in Seren’s sign-list, so the two are the same sign, and nothing in the Book says so. Its translation, at The Bedrock Hand (Cam 16): The first builders’ mark: “first; before all”.
  2. The head of the lintel column (owed; Read Down the Lintel, Cam 32). Above the topmost Hal name there is one line older than the Hal, cut in the first marks. It stays untranslated until item 4.
  3. Seren’s last line in the Book of Knowings (optional: it adds to the appendix, not to a tale), added with item 4: The Bar Before is the mark on the lid of the chest I carried. I looked at it every night of the war, and did not see it.
  4. A last achievement, The First Tongue (native Tuma), at the launch after The Last Carver, when nothing else is left to earn. It changes no word; it adds three translation lines: under the lintel’s first line, What is held in common.; under the proverb, wherever it is shown in both tongues, In both tongues the last word is one word: both.; under the Stone out of the Grey, Stone writes what is said, and wood what is meant. Here, for the first time since the first tongue, both are cut on one face. It keeps the Legends’ laws: cosmetic, reached by every player, after and never before, and it only adds.
  5. “The Knowing is the nearest survivor” needs no new line. The foreword already says “Words can be turned, and a knowing cannot.” This doc gives the reason (§2.1).
  6. Echoes the tales already hold, for players who dig, and nothing to add: Tumar is “we hold”; the Guest’s last word and the gift’s last clause are one root; Rhyna’s name is the wood’s word for stone, and the Guest’s errand-name Aelrhen, “bond-to-stone”, is at the root “together, set fast”; Halvard’s -vard is the Aelvaren’s -varen.
  7. Never: in a tale, in store art, before the Finale, or as a mechanic.

Faith, reverently. If “an ultimate base language” is, for Jack, the one tongue before the scattering, the design leaves exactly that room and never claims it. The Book names no cause for the parting. The First Tongue’s word for God, *marð- “the Maker, the one knelt to”, survives only in stone (Mardh); the wood kept no name for Him, only the kneeling. The Stone’s grain says “our God” as the one they kneel to.

Recommended: adopt 1 and 4 (the drawing, and one late achievement), with 3 if the Book itself should notice at the very end.

3Orrowen: The Shoreland Tongue

Orrowen, “of the Shore”, is what the Rivenmen speak, what Seren writes, and what the hearth answers in. It is built to feel ancient and Celtic without a Celtic word in it: the likeness lies in how the tongue works (verb first, the mutations, the dual, the conjugated prepositions), never in its vocabulary. It is also built to be the opposite of the thunder-tongue in every way a listener would notice, and yet it descends from the same First Tongue (§2): every word in it is derived by the sound laws, with no mismatches. Version 2 keeps the whole grammar of v0.1 and adds what Jack’s notes asked for: a stone grammar for the economical chisel register (§5), a running ink hand for the whole tongue (§6), the Hal placed as the most economical hand of all (§3.4), and Seren’s name given its meaning (§3.6). The script, Garl Dhrenn, is written three ways, from the most economical to the fullest:

HandOrrowenWhat it writesWhere
the HalGarl Halword-signs and old letters; no endings, no small words, no word-gaps, no bites; right to left, mirroredthe first builders' stones: the slates of the Rite, the old lintels, the black chest's mark
the dry cutryt broc, "dry cutting"word-signs for the common words; letters for names, rare words and endings; the small words left out, as a dry-stone wall leaves out its mortareverything cut in stone now: capstones, lintels, works, the Stonwryt coin, the Book when it is cut in the granite of the hall
the leaf-handGarl Flennthe whole tongue, every small word and every mutation, in letters joined by the penink: the Book, the rolls, every leaf
(the coal)garl brenththe whole tongue in plain unjoined lettersthe Captain's Title only, "as a man writes who has not written much"

A vow is always cut whole, in letters, with every word: “a sign holds what is meant; a vow must hold what was said.” That is why the tale-stone’s Stonwryt can be read word for word.

The names were chosen so that the words for writing are the words for masonry. A scribe of the guild lays a line (cadh trenn) as a mason lays a course, and a letter is a stone. A Stonewright cutting a line dry lays it as a dry-stone waller lays a wall: no mortar, the stones chosen to fit by their shapes alone, and the small words, the mortar words, left for the reader to lay back in.

3.2 · The sound of it

Eighteen consonants. Three more lived in the Hal and have merged: /ŋ/ into n, /ʍ/ (hw) into f, /x/ into h. The glide /j/ exists only as softened g.

lipsteeth / tongue-tipback
stops, voicelessptk (written c or k)
stops, voicedbdg
nasalsmn—
fricatives, voicelessfth /θ/ · sh
fricatives, voicedvdh /ð/—
approximantswl—
rhoticsr (tap or trill) · rh /r̥/ ("the rough r")

Six vowels, and two long nuclei: ae /ɛː/, only from old long ē (as in Kael), and ow /ou/, from old long ū and in the place-suffix -ow. Unstressed e is often /ə/.

frontfront roundedback
highiy /y/u
mideo
lowa
  • Broad and slender. a, o, u, ow are broad; e, i, y, ae are slender. A word’s class is the class of its last full vowel, and its suffixes follow it. Root vowels are free, so Corlen and Pellow are good words.
  • Stress falls on the first syllable of every content word. Particles and pronouns are unstressed and lean on the next word.
  • The music comes from few long vowels, many sonorant codas (-rn, -ld, -lm, -rl, -nn, -mm) and a frequent rolled r. Nothing in it has the thunder-break. To a Shoreland ear the Mystaeri “knock”.
  • Frequency. Common: l, r, n, t, d, s, th, m. Rarer: b, g, dh, v, h. Rare: f, rh, w.

How the Book spells it

The Book spells Orrowen as Seren would hear it, not letter for letter from the course-hand (§4.2 gives the mapping). These rules keep every existing Shoreland name valid.

SpellingSoundRule
c / k/k/k before e, i, y, ae and at the end of a word after them (Kael, Aske, Hesk, keth, kyl); k in -sk and -sk- (hosk, lusk, Treskan); sc- before any vowel (sceth); c everywhere else (Corlen, crenn, covv)
th, dh/θ/, /ð/dh is never written dd
rh/r̥/word-initial, or at a compound seam
y/y/ vowel; /j/ word-initially before a vowel/j/ occurs only as softened g
ae/ɛː/one long vowel, not a + e. (In the thunder-tongue the same letters are a diphthong: same spelling, different sound)
ow/ou/
doubled consonantslong consonant after a short stressed vowelnn, mm, ll, rr, ss: Brenn, Tamm, Pellow, carm, Voss
w/w/a consonant (Aldwena), or the second half of ow
wr/r/the Book keeps the old w only in Stonwryt, which the guild still spells the old way

The Book never uses Welsh ll, dd, ff, ch or Irish bh, mh, gc, dt. Orrowen must not look Welsh or Irish on the page.

Syllables

A syllable is (C)(C)V(C)(C). z, x, q, j never occur, and nor do the endings -ion, -iel, -dor. Where a mutation would make an illegal cluster, a softened g before a consonant drops, a softened rh after a consonant drops, and a nasalised d before r stays d.

PositionAllowed
Onsetsany single consonant except /j/ (which comes only from mutation); stop + r or l (br, bl, dr, tr, cr, cl, gr, gl, pr, pl); s + stop (sp, st, sc/sk); th + r (rare); str only in Stonwryt-type compounds
Codasany single consonant except h, w and /j/; sonorant + stop (rd, rt, ld, lt, nd, nt, rc); sonorant + sonorant (rn, rl, lm, rm); sonorant + fricative (rv, lv, rth, rdh); st, sk
Geminatesonly nn, mm, ll, rr, ss, and only after a short stressed vowel

3.3 · Grammar

Glosses in this doc use S = softening, N = nasalising, VN = verbal noun, DU = dual, PST = past, FUT = future, NEG = negative, Q = question, REL = relative. The romanised line shows the mutated sound; the course-hand writes the base letter and a bite.

Word order: verb first

  • Verb, subject, object, then the rest. Keth et tolm “hold the stone”; Carm et lodh hy et trun “cries the mortar from the ground”.
  • The noun comes first in its phrase. Adjectives, demonstratives and possessors follow it: et gunn sy “the deep this”, that is, “this deep”; hosk et ganna “lintel [of] the gate”.
  • Numerals come before a singular noun: sull carm “three call”; delv vennuld “twelve True Man”.
  • Particles come before the verb and mutate it: re (PST), es (FUT), nath (NEG), ho (Q), sa (REL).
  • Emphasis is a cleft with the copula: El et tolm sa heth “It is the stone that holds”.

Nouns: three numbers, one article, and the construct

There is no grammatical gender; only the pronouns o (he, it) and ey (she) tell sex. That keeps the soft mutation off the article, which is the Welsh and Sindarin habit this tongue avoids.

How it is formedExample
singularthe bare stemtolm (a stone)
dualpa ("two") + S + the singularpa yarl ("two hands", from garl); pa dholm ("two stones")
pluralstem + -Ath (-ath broad, -eth slender)tolmath (stones); theldeth (families)

A few old duals are words of their own ending in -a: ganna “gate”, literally “the two posts”; pana “both”; and every pair-name. Some nouns name a whole kind, and one member takes -el: Stonwrytan “the guild” gives stonwrytel “one Stonewright”.

Harmony. A suffix vowel takes the class of the stem’s last full vowel. The script writes these two vowels with their own harmonic letters, so the class is written once per word, by its stem.

Harmonic vowelbroadslenderIn the suffixes
Aaeplural -Ath, agent -Ard, participle -At, 1du -An, 3du -A, 1pl -Ar, 3pl -Ant, ordinal -Ast
Ooyverbal noun -Ol, abstract -Oth, 1sg -Om, 2pl -Os

The article is et, the same for every number. It never mutates and never causes a mutation. A proper name takes none, and neither does a noun with a possessive. A noun followed by a definite possessor takes no article: this is the construct, and its possessor is softened. Hosk et ganna is “the lintel of the gate”; *Et hosk et ganna is wrong (a star marks a wrong form). Putting an article on the head of a construct is the classic foreigner’s error, and it is exactly the Last Carver’s (§10.18).

OrrowenLiterallyMeaning
garl Dhrennhand S-coursethe course-hand
lest Vardhhouse S-Goda temple
Kethow Dhreskkeep S-cleftRivenkeep
tumol ol varnmemory [of] our homememory of our home

The two mutations

Both change only the first consonant of the next word, and only once. The course-hand always writes the base letter with a bite under it, so the dictionary form can always be found. The outcomes and triggers are Orrowen’s own: neither table is Welsh’s or Irish’s, though both are the same kind of thing.

Softening (S, “the wearing”). In the old tongue these consonants wore soft between vowels. The vowels at the ends of words are gone; the wearing stayed. f, v, w, th, dh, s, h, l, r, n and all vowels are unchanged.

basepbmtdc/kgrh
softenedvwvdhrhy (nothing before a consonant)h (nothing after a consonant)

Nasalising (N, “the bedding”). These words once ended in -n, and the n bedded into the word that followed. f, v, w, th, dh, s, h, l, r, rh, m, n are unchanged.

A verb is a stem and a person ending. Tense is a particle before the verb. There is no second-person dual: a pair is spoken to as many and answers as two.

Pronouns and prepositions

One set of forms is both pronoun and possessive; the mutation after it marks the possessive. The dual pronouns are the plural plus -na. A pronoun after a verb is emphatic (Tumar ol “We remember”); an object pronoun follows the subject (Re hadhan o “we two laid it”).

When the mutation cannot show, nothing marks the possessive. Before a word the softening leaves unchanged (f, v, w, th, dh, s, h, l, r, n, a vowel), o saed after a verb reads “he, half”, not “its half”, and o hosen reads “he … like”, not “his equal”. Say the possessor as a noun (saed et covv, “the half of the cloak”) or recast (uld hosen et Crenn, “a man like the Captain”). The same holds for en, ol, va before a letter the bedding leaves unchanged. back-translation

Prepositions take the person endings directly; there is no “to me” or “on him”. ul (in, +N), hy (from, +S) and dem (until, +N) follow the same pattern.

Hy is also “than” (“greater from X”): hos strom hyo, “one greater than he”. After a verb of going the “from” reading wins (orr hy, “leave”), so a comparison is not set after orr. The most is sost, “self, very”: et strom sost, the greatest. An adverb is the bare quality after the verb. back-translation

Having, being able, feeling, knowing

Orrowen has no verb “to have”, no “can”, and no verb for most feelings. A thing is at you; a feeling is laid upon you, as a course is laid. And the Shoreland word for knowing the wood is the canon’s own: to know it is to hold it.

Negation, questions, relatives

  • Not: nath + N before a verb (nath geth “does not hold”); nel for the copula; the prefix na- + S for “un-”: nawrodhat “untold”, nadhum “forget”, nayald “destroy” (un-build), nalodhat “unbonded” (un-mortared).
  • “Only” of a clause is nath … veth, “not … but”: sa nath re yorrar veth amm ew venn et dask, “who fought only when the cause was just”. Hosel “only, alone” set after a verb reads “alone”. Nath … tul is “not yet” (Seren’s own line), never “no longer”; the tongue has no “no longer”, and says it another way (re vammant so hrenneth, “they had lost their captains”). The negative past is nath re + S (nath re yal, “was not”). back-translation
  • Questions: ho + S. The question words are cedh who, vodh what, ul vodh where (“in what”), hy vodh why (“from what”), amm vodh when.
  • Relatives: sa + S with a gap: et tolm sa heth “the stone that holds”; Voss sa re vess “Voss who asked” (from pess).

The formal and oath register

  1. The dual for pairs. The Bonded speak of themselves as “we two” and are spoken of by their pair-name with 3du verbs: Tuma Halyna “Halyna remember”. Where the Book gives Halyna a plural verb, the Orrowen original is dual. Common speech in the havens let the dual slip; the guild never did.
  2. Swearing. An oath begins Rytom um … “I cut [my word] upon …”, from ryt, a cut vow. It closes with the one-word vow Ston. “It stands.”, followed in writing by the gate mark. Liturgy keeps the Hal form Stonos. A vow is cut whole, in letters, even in stone (§5.2).
  3. Respect. Elders and bonded pairs are addressed in the 2pl. The Captain calls a True Man tho, in the singular, as a comrade.
  4. Antiphony. A line said “one voice to the comma and the other the rest” is split at the wedge mark. In Seren’s two inks, one ink runs to the wedge and the other takes the rest.
  5. The Hal in liturgy. The Rite of the Cornerstone is recited in the Hal. The guild pronounces it by the living tongue’s rules as best it can, and knows the words sound wrong.

Names, and the pair-name

X of the Y is a construct: Rhyna Yanna Ulvenn “Rhyna of the Inner Gate”. X the Y is apposition: Kael Nydherd “Kael the Counter”. A compound epithet is modifier and softened head: Halvard Tolmvard “Halvard Stone-Warden”, which translates his own name. At the sealing (hoskol, “the laying of the lintel”) the guild names a pair as a gate is made:

The three canon pair-names come out of one rule by three different softenings, and every pair-name ends in -a because the lintel is the dual. A pair-name takes a dual verb and, in writing, carries a sealing lintel. The unbonded keep one name. Seren has no lintel and never will; “one name is a mourning”.

The lintel of the western stair shows the whole history in one column, “one beneath another, for as many generations as the quarry was worked”: Hal names at the top, cut right to left; haven spellings in the middle; Halvard’s line at the foot in the living hand. Names are always letters, so the column reads by letter, and a player who has earned the old hand can read it downward and watch the tongue change (§12.2, Read Down the Lintel).

The four hands on the economy scale

Writing on the Shore began with meanings and ended with sounds, and every step toward sound was also a step toward ink.

So the Hal is the most economical hand of all that can still be sounded. The first builders had just made the letters (the reform, §2.6), but they cut with the old marks wherever a mark would do, spelled only names and the words no mark held, and left every ending and every small word to the reader, who spoke the Hal and could not mistake them. The living dry cut is a little fuller: the living tongue has lost the Hal’s endings and turned their loss into mutations and harmonic suffixes, so the endings that still carry meaning are laid on in letters. The leaf-hand writes everything. Two things keep this true to the First Tongue: a word-sign is a word, not a meaning (it is read as one Orrowen word, aloud, and when the word’s meaning drifted, the sign followed the word: the Cup is read tum, “remember”, though the mark meant “hold”), and the tale-stone’s Stonwryt is cut in full, in letters, word for word, because it is a vow. It is the one Hal text anyone can still sound.

The sound changes, in order

The exact laws, stage by stage from the First Tongue, are in §2.3, and they derive every Orrowen word with no mismatches. In brief, from the Hal to the living tongue:

  1. The wearing. Inside the Hal, between vowels, at compound seams and after a word ending in a vowel, a single p b m t d k g hr was said soft: v w v dh r h y h. The Hal hand never wrote it.
  2. The bedding. After a word ending in -n, p t k were voiced and b d g became nasals.
  3. The fall of the endings. Unstressed final syllables were lost: -os, -is, short vowels, the -n of the particles. With the endings gone, the wearing and the bedding were no longer explained by any sound, and they became grammar, which is how real Celtic mutations arose. Old tolmos > tolm; xaldos > hald; ulan > ul, still nasalising.
  4. Long vowels shifted: ā > o, ē > ae, ī > i, ō > u, ū > ow. Old kēlos > Kael; old orrū > orrow “shore”. Final long -ā survived as -a: the dual ending, the lintel of every pair-name.
  5. Three mergers: x into h (xal > hal), ŋ into n (soŋmas > somm), hw into f (hwlennā > flenn “leaf”). The Hal hand still has a letter for each.
  6. Old wr- lost its w (wryta > ryt). The guild still spells its greatest word the old way, Stonwryt, and says it /ˈstonryt/.
  7. Harmony. Unstressed suffix vowels reduced, then took the colour of the stem: old kethola > kethyl, but tumola > tumol.

Where each trigger came from

Every trigger is explained by its old ending, which the First Tongue explains in turn: the particles were fixed before the word, and their final -n and final vowels froze into the mutations (§2.2). Two rows are emended from v0.1: Hal re (not rea), and Hal van (not vanan).

Why a Rivenman cannot read the Hal

He can see every letter of it. What he cannot do is sound it. It runs right to left and every letter faces the way it runs, so an old p leans like a living k. It has no word-gaps. It spells the endings the living tongue has lost (TOLMOS for tolm). It writes no bites, so the pair the Rivenmen call Aldwena is cut ALD · BEN. Three of its letters stand for sounds no one has said in twelve generations. And some of its words are simply gone. This is why “the first fathers of the guild had known better, and we had forgotten them”: the forgetting is written into the stone. Halyna read the slate leaves by lamplight because the Bonded keep the Hal as a liturgy; earning the old hand is learning what they already knew.

And most of it is not in letters at all. Outside the one vow, the Hal is cut in word-signs, mirrored, with no endings and no small words. A Rivenman knows perhaps half of those signs from the living dry cut (the same heads and crowns, turned the other way and cut taller), but he cannot supply the Hal’s endings or its small words, because he does not speak the Hal. So the Bonded keep the slate leaves of the Rite as a liturgy, learned by heart with their Hal readings, and read the signs as reminders of words they already know.

3.7 · The canon lexicon (231 entries)

The fields are built from the Shorelanders’ own metaphors: to tell a tale is to lay a course (cadh trenn); a promise is a cut stone (ryt); a pair is a gate (ganna, the dual of “post”); to know the wood is to hold it (keth); freedom is loosing (lusk, lunn). So one Orrowen word often carries several English ones: trenn is course, line and tale; keth is hold, keep and know; vesk is see and read; tresk is cleft, riven and torn. Columns: the living form; the Hal form where it is known (most nouns are the stem + -os broad or -is slender); the harmony class (B broad, S slender); the sense; notes; and, new in v2, how the dry cut writes it: its word-sign (HEAD+crown, with its number in the inventory, §5.6), its sign with a complement, or letters. The First Tongue derives every entry (§2.4). This is the canon; the whole tier-3 lexicon of 3,015 entries, which contains it, is summarised in §11.3.

Seven forms break the harmony rule Jack

Still open from v0.1, with one new fact: the First Tongue shows that flennath and tevath are old ā-stems, so their broad endings are right; the tier-3 lexicon keeps the canon’s three old broad stems (tresk, flenn, tev) broad.

The renderer’s analyser found seven words whose suffix vowel is broad on a slender stem: vennoth (by rule vennyth), delvoth (delvyth), flennath (flenneth), Kethow Stellath (Stelleth), ul glennol (glennyl), Rytom um (Rytym), and treskat, the Torn Cloak’s own Covv Treskat (tresket). The course-hand is unaffected: lexicon words are spelled in full vowels, so they read correctly either way. Either regularise all seven, or declare them old broad stems that keep their broad endings, as tevath already is. Covv Treskat is the only one a player is likely to see. The spelling rule for c and k also needs one more clause to match the lexicon: “k in -sk and -sk-; sc- before any vowel”.

4The Course-Hand (Garl Dhrenn)

An alphabet of straight chisel strokes that stand on a mortar line. It records sound, and it is cut in stone, so it has no curves. It is Ogham-like in spirit (strokes set on a line, made to be cut) and its own in every shape and rule: its letters stand on one side of the line only, and their shapes say how the sound is made. The letters are unchanged in v2. The dry cut uses them for names, rare words and complements (§5); a vow is cut in them whole; and the leaf-hand is them, written (§6). Every letter descends from a first mark by the first builders’ reform (§2.6).

4.1 · The picture in one paragraph

Every letter stands on the mortar line (lodh), as a stone stands on its bed. Consonants are ashlars: tall, joined, cut whole. Each has an upright rising from the bed and one or more laid stones running to its right. The upright tells where the sound is made: a forward-leaning prop (the lips), a stepped offset (the tongue-tip) or a back-leaning shore (the back of the mouth). The laid stones tell how. Vowels are pinnings: small loose stones set between the ashlars, their parts never touching. A mutation is a bite cut into the mortar under a letter’s foot, so the letter itself stays whole. Each word is a stone with its own bed, parted from the next by a head-joint, and successive lines break the joint as a mason staggers courses. A pair-name carries a sealing lintel. A page of it looks like a wall.

4.2 · From the tongue to the letters

The course-hand writes the underlying form, not the Book’s spelling. Each base consonant is one letter, with its mutation as a bite. Each root vowel is a full vowel letter. Each suffix vowel is a harmonic letter.

Sound or spellingLetter(s)
p b m f v w t d n th dh s l r rh k g hone letter each (th, dh, rh are single letters)
c and kthe one letter k (the split is only a Book spelling rule)
a softened or nasalised consonantits base letter + a bite. dumol is written t+N · u · m · O · l
y /j/ (softened g)g + S bite
a o u e i y in a root; A, O in a suffixthe full vowel letter; the harmonic letters A, O
ae · ow · a doubled consonanta e · o w · the letter twice
a vowel-initial nasalised word (m-, n-)an N bite under the first vowel

So the Book’s spelling cannot be turned back into the hand without the lexicon (the Book writes dumol; only the grammar knows it is tumol with a nasal bite). The other way always works, because the hand shows every base and every mutation. Worked example: Seren’s first word, Nawrodhat “untold”, is the prefix na- (which softens) + brodhat “told”. The hand writes n a bS r o dh A t: the b stands whole with a V-bite under it, and the harmonic A takes its class from the o before it, so it is read a.

4.3 · How a letter is built

The three uprights (place). Coordinates are in cell units, origin at the letter’s left foot on the bed, y up.

UprightPlacePolylineAttach x at height y
proplips (p b m f v w)(0,0) → (1.2,3), leaning forwardx = 0.4·y
offsettongue-tip (t d n th dh s l r rh)(0,0) → (0,1.5) → (0.9,1.5) → (0.9,3), a stepped wallx = 0 if y < 1.5; x = 0.9 if y ≥ 1.5
shoreback (k g h)(1.2,0) → (0,3), leaning backx = 1.2 − 0.4·y

The laid stones (manner). They lie at three heights: top (y = 3), middle (2) and low (1). A joined stone starts on the upright; a free stone stands apart. The pin is a short second upright, a bedded stroke from (3.6, 0) to (3.6, 1.3), and it marks voicing.

The families answer the mutations. p b m share the prop, and so do the soft forms they wear to, v w; t d n th dh share the offset; k g h share the shore. Both mutations keep a sound on its own upright, with two exceptions that history explains: softened rh became h, a bare breath; and nasalised g was once /ŋ/, the shore-nasal the Hal still writes. So the living hand’s one empty slot, the shore nasal, is the gap the merger left.

Vowels (pinnings). The broad vowels carry a capstone over short pins; the slender ones a tall pin with a low stone beside it. y is the leaning pin: e’s tall pin riven from its bed, leaning over its low stone as the riven ridge leans over the Keep.

ShapeReads as

A (harmonic)as a, capstone broken in twoa in a broad word, e in a slender one
O (harmonic)as o, capstone broken in twoo in a broad word, y in a slender one

The harmony mark: once per word. A harmonic letter has no value of its own. It takes the class of the nearest full vowel before it in the same stone. Theldeth and lunnath end in the same two letters, A th, read -eth after e and -ath after u. The Title teaches this in its fourth and eighth words.

The end rule, which gives every stroke its “up”

A stroke end is square where it lies on the bed or on another stroke of the same letter. Otherwise it tapers over 0.4 u, where the chisel lifts. A stroke with no square end at all (a free stone, a capstone, a lintel) is dressed square at both ends. The rule is computed, not stored, and the grain’s knife-cuts, which taper at both ends, can never be mistaken for it.

4.4 · Bites, stones, marks, lintels

A bite is a notch cut down through the bed band, under the letter’s foot.

BiteShape (cell units)Meaning
softeninga V: (fx − 0.45, 0) · (fx, −0.7) · (fx + 0.45, 0)S
nasalisinga square: (fx − 0.38, 0) to (fx + 0.38, −0.7)N
Lettersfx
prop letters0
offset letters0
shore letters1.2
a, u, e, A0.25
o, i, O1.95
y0.25 (the foot of the leaning pin)
  • A bite goes under the first letter of a word, or under the first letter of a root after na-. It is written only where the mutation changes the sound: es ston has none.
  • Names and set compounds are spelled as said, with no bite: Halvard, Lurrvard, gorndholm, vennuld, and pair-names in running text. The bite marks grammar, not etymology.
  • An N bite under a vowel reads m- before a broad vowel and n- before a slender one. A softened rh or g that falls silent keeps its letter and its bite: the hand never drops a letter the tongue has dropped.

Stones. (v0.1 called a word with its own bed a “word-stone”; v2 calls it simply a stone, to keep it apart from the dry cut’s word-signs.) Each word has its own bed band, broken at the head-joint, so a line looks like a course of stones. A word is never split across lines. Breaking the joint: where a head-joint on the lower line falls within 1.0 u of one on the line above, the lower line’s joints widen by 0.25 u until they clear (or, if that would overflow the measure, narrow by 0.2 u steps to a floor of 1.4 u). A joint is a word break whatever its width, so reading is untouched.

Punctuation. Every mark is a stone in the line, in its own cell. Questions and cries have none: the particle ho and the imperative carry them. Direct speech is not marked; the Book’s quotation marks are Seren’s, added in translation.

MarkShapeUse
perpenda short bedded upright, 1.6 uend of a sentence. The "joint closed"
wedgea free laid stone at y = 1a pause (comma). In antiphony it is where the second voice takes the line
gatetwo posts and a lintelend of an oath or vow. It follows Ston.
copingthe gate with a second, wider stone laid over itend of a tale: "This I lay as it was laid for me." A course is capped
(none)—questions (the particle ho carries them) and cries (the imperative carries them)

The sealing lintel. A pair-name in running text is spelled as it is said (h a l y n a), with one unbroken free stone at y = 3.75 over the whole word. That is how a reader knows a pair-name: it has a gate over it. The Stonwryt ligature is how a master-pair signs a vow under a capstone: his post (the first syllable of his cradle-name), a half head-joint, her post (her cradle-name stem, in base letters, with no bite), and one lintel over both on one shared bed. The final -a is not cut, because the lintel is the -a, and the lintel softens the second post. So Halyna’s Stonwryt reads HAL | RHYN and the old capstone’s ALD | BEN. A reader who knows the rule says Halyna and Aldwena. One who does not sees two unknown names.

4.5 · Numerals

Speech counts in twenties; the guild also counts in twelves, “twelvefold, as the old masters counted it”. A number is a run of numeral letters, each capped by its own short laid stone at y = 3.75; the caps break letter by letter, where a sealing lintel is unbroken. The numeral letters are the initials of the number words. Values add, except that a unit letter standing directly before d, m or b multiplies it.

the Twelvea single capped d

4.6 · Reading it back

For each stone, read the letters left to right (right to left and un-mirrored in the Hal):

  1. Classify each letter. Height 3 (or 4 in the Hal) is an ashlar; height 2 (or 2.5) is a pinning. An ashlar’s first stroke gives its upright: a forward lean is the prop, a step is the offset, a back lean is the shore. Its laid stones and pins give the manner. A pinning’s parts give the vowel.
  2. Resolve the harmonic letters from the nearest full vowel before them.
  3. Read any bite under the first letter, apply the mutation to get the spoken form, and keep the base for the lexicon.
  4. Read the marks: perpend, wedge, gate, coping. A sealing lintel means a pair-name; caps mean the letters are numbers.
  5. Undo a Stonwryt ligature: first post + softened second post + a.

Four look-alikes a reader must not trip on

  • A letter’s free low stone is not a wedge. l and w end in a free stone at y = 1 inside their own cell. A wedge is the same stone in a cell of its own, a letter gap after the word.
  • A middle stone meets the offset’s riser partway; a joined top stone leaves from its top corner. On n, r, rh the riser shows above the stone; on t, d, l, dh nothing shows above it. In the coal hand, read this and not the height.
  • Full a against harmonic A. The imperative plural (Talda), the collective -an, the old duals and every pair-name’s -a have an unbroken capstone. The 3du -A (Tuma Halyna) is broken. The capstone tells an order to many from two who do a thing.
  • The Last Carver’s bites are tapered strokes: his N bite is three short strokes, a cup; an S bite would be two, a V.
Proved from the pictures alone

In the blind decode test (2026-09-27) a reader who had only the rules of the Orrowen and course-hand chapters, and screenshots of the drawings with every title and description stripped out, read ten course-hand images back exactly, letter for letter, bite for bite and mark for mark: the cut, coal and Carver forms, both bites, harmony, the sealing lintel, the wedge, the perpend and the gate. The English came out word for word from the lexicon. Nothing in the renderer needed changing; the four look-alikes above are what slowed the reading. The Hal texts and the charts were not part of that test.

Reading a dry-cut line adds one step before step 1: sort each stone’s signs. A sign 4.6 u tall on a footing is a word-sign (look it up by its head and its crown, §5.6); a sign 2 u tall standing before a word-sign, with its one laid stone running left from the head of a pin, is the turned stone (not); everything else is a letter. Letters after a word-sign on its bed are its complement. Then lay the mortar back in (§5.2).

4.7 · Four ways to make the letters and the signs

FormWhere it is usedHow to draw it
The cut (garl tolm): the dry cut, and letters cut wholecapstones, lintels, the tale-stone, works, the coin; the Book "when there is peace enough to cut it"; the EpilogueV-cut facets. The bed band is cut as a shallow channel and the bites go deeper; every word-sign also has its footing
The leaf-hand (Garl Flenn)Seren's leaves and every scribe's before her; the rollsRewritten in v2 as a joined running hand. A flat nib 0.30 u at 25°, hairline joins, a slant of 0.18. Halyna's two inks alternate by paragraph; in antiphony the wedge is where the ink changes
The coal hand (garl brenth)the Title, written by the Captain on the torn cloak and the capstonesUnchanged: blunt strokes 0.5 u wide, square at both ends; each endpoint jittered by up to ±0.12 u and each laid stone tilted by up to ±4°, from a PRNG (mulberry32) seeded by an FNV-1a hash of the text, so the Title is the same drawing for every player; letters at 1.2×; no bed band (cloth has no mortar); bites as short strokes below. The coal is letters, every word: the Captain "was no Stonewright" and "wrote, slowly, as a man writes who has not written much" (I.1), so he wrote as he spoke, in the plain letters every child of the Shore learns first, and knew no word-signs
The Hal (Garl Hal)the first builders' stonesas the cut, mirrored and heightened

Cut rendering. Each stroke is two flat V-cut facets, lit from the top left, in one ink: the drawings in this doc are stroke-only SVG in currentColor under the class stone-ink, with the shade facet, the mortar and the bites at fixed strengths. No filters, no gradients. The Title is 43 letters and five marks; a whole leaf of Seren’s hand fits well inside a page. The leaf-hand is no longer a flat-pen sketch: it is drawn, and built as a font (§6).

The Last Carver’s hand is the fourth, and it is a mistake made four ways. He learned the letters only from the coal Title, so: every letter he cut occurs in the Title; he cut no bed, because cloth has no mortar and he never knew letters stand on one; every stroke tapers at both ends, as a knife-cut in living wood does, because the rule that a stroke is squared where it is bedded is the one thing the Title could not teach him; and the cutting stops with an open joint, no mark, “the chisel’s last stroke still sharp at the end of the line”. He copied the Title’s nasal bite faithfully. So his only error of language is the extra word (§10.18). And a fifth tell, new in v2: he cut the mortar. Every mortar word of the Title’s first line is cut, ul and five times ol, and one more the Title never had. No Stonewright cuts a small word in stone, least of all et. He cut stone as the Captain wrote on cloth: in letters, every word, as it is said.

4.8 · The old register: Garl Hal, the first builders’ hand

The same letters, transformed, and the same word-signs. The top names on the lintel of the western stair, the slate leaves of the Rite, the mark on the black chest and the old capstone’s Stonwryt are all in this hand.

RuleDetail
1. MirrorEvery letter is mirrored in its cell: x′ = cell width − x
2. Right to leftLetters run right to left, facing the way they run. The prop still leans forward in the direction of writing, which is leftward. So to a living eye an old p has the lean of a living k, and an old a looks like a living o
3. Taller coursesConsonants are 4 u tall (y × 4/3) and vowels 2.5 u (y × 1.25). Lintels and caps move up to match
4. Scriptio continuaNo head-joints. One unbroken bed runs the whole line
5. No bitesThe old hand writes the base letter where speech already softened it
6. Full endingsEvery Hal ending is spelled out (TOLMOS, HALDOS). No harmonic letters: every vowel is full
7. Three archaic lettersŋ (shore-nasal; merged into n), hw (merged into f), x (merged into h), from the table above
8. Long vowelsAn old long vowel carries the long-stone, a free laid stone at y = 3.25 over it
9. MarksPerpend, gate and coping are the same, mirrored. There is no wedge

The Hal’s word-signs. The Hal cuts the same heads and crowns as the dry cut (§5), under its own rules 1 to 5: mirrored in their cells, cut at 4/3 of their height (a word-sign stands 6.13 u, a letter 4), on the one continuous bed, with no footing (height alone tells a sign from a letter), no complements and no bites. Only names, the words no mark held, and a vow are cut in letters, and the letters carry their full Hal endings. So the proverb, which the Hal speech spells in 29 letters, the Hal hand cuts in seven signs:

The misreading is designed. Mirrored, the Hal vowels swap: an old a looks like a living o, e like i, A like O; u is symmetric, and an old y mirrors into a shape the living hand does not have. No mirrored Hal consonant looks like any living letter, because every mirrored laid stone runs leftward. So a living reader who ignores the direction reads the consonants as nonsense and the vowels wrong. The hand tells him it is the Hal only by its height, its missing joints and its leftward stones.

5The Dry Cut (Ryt Broc): Orrowen’s Chisel Register

Jack’s note 1: “Because Orrowen is a chisel language, we need an economy of words. It seems like the lettering should be like the reformed Egyptian of the Book of Mormon in its economy.” The dry cut is that economy. The stone is cut; the mortar is the reader’s. It cuts only the stones of a sentence (its nouns, verbs, qualities and numbers), as word-signs where a word has one, and leaves out the small words, the mortar words, for the reader to lay back in. The reason is the chisel’s: a word cut in granite costs a mason an hour, and a small word costs him as much as a large one. Across the eight sample texts the dry cut uses 117 signs where the leaf-hand uses 339 letters and marks: 35 per cent. A granite Book would be about a third as long as the ink one.

5.1 · The picture in one paragraph

A word-sign is one of the First Tongue’s marks, worn straight by the chisel and stood on the bed, and read as one Orrowen word. 27 marks serve as heads: each alone is a root sign, read as the word the stone kept for it (the Cup is tum, “remember”; the Course is trenn; the Door is ganna). Any head may carry a crown: one of 20 other marks, cut small and set over the head like a capstone on a pillar, which turns it into a neighbouring word (the Hearth under the Still is varn, home; the Hearth with the Drop is theld, family). The head gives the field and the crown the word. A word-sign stands 4.6 u tall, half again as tall as a letter, “proud of the course”, and it sits on a footing, a second mortar line under its own, so a reader always knows a sign from a letter. Endings that matter are laid on after the sign in letters; names, rare words and loans are cut in letters; not keeps one mark of its own, the turned stone. There are 328 word-signs: 134 write words of the v0.1 lexicon, and 194 write reserve words of the First Tongue, for the whole Book’s translation.

It is the “reformed” hand in Jack’s sense, and not a copy of one. Logograms with phonetic complements are an idea shared by Egyptian, Maya and Chinese writing, and ideas are free. Nothing in the dry cut copies the characters of any of them. Its signs are the First Tongue’s own marks, and its economy is the First Tongue’s: the first marks wrote no small words, as the grain still writes none.

5.2 · The stone grammar

Eleven rules. The notation below writes [WORD] for the word-sign read word, HEAD+crown for a sign by its parts, and bold letters after a sign, as [THELD]A th, for its complement.

  1. D1 · Only the stones are cut. Nouns, verbs, qualities, numbers, and the few adverbs and conjunctions that carry weight (tul “yet”, somm “while”, amm “when”). A word with a word-sign is cut as its word-sign; any other word in letters.
  2. D2 · The mortar words are left out. They are never cut, except in a vow (D9):
    Left outThe mortar wordHow the reader lays it back in
    the articleetalways: a stone is "the" stone
    the copula and the state verbel, ew; doss, noss, re yal-a line with no verb is a naming (D4); the "at" and "upon" idioms keep their nouns only
    the conjunctionseth "and", ell "or", veth "but"the wedge stands between the things it joins; which of the three is meant is read from the sense
    the relative and the questionsa, ho"a stone does not ask": questions are not cut
    the tense particlesre (past), es (future)stone has no tense: a work's inscription speaks of what stands, a memorial of what was, a vow of what shall be. Where the time must be cut, a time is cut (a day, a year, a count of generations)
    the pronouns and possessivesen, tho, o, ey, olna, ol, va, sona, sothe verb's ending, or the order, or the stone itself: an inscription speaks with the voice of those who cut it, so "our" is the wall's own
    the demonstrativessy, ull"this" is the stone the words are cut on
    the prepositionsul, hy, um, lo, demfrom the verb and the order: "cries mortar ground" is read "the mortar cries from the ground", "lay stone stone" as "stone upon stone"
    the small quantifiersgor "every", sost "very"the plural complement, or nothing
  3. D3 · The one mortar word that keeps a mark is not. Nath, nel, new and the prefix na- are cut as the turned stone, set against the stone they turn, on its bed. A thing cut not-so must never be read as so.
  4. D4 · Order is the order of speech. The verb first, then its subject, its object, the rest, exactly as spoken. A line that begins with a noun has no verb and is a naming: a heading, a memorial, a label, a proverb. Two nouns side by side are a construct, the second the possessor (hosk ganna, “the lintel of the gate”), unless the line is a proverb, when they are predicate and subject.
  5. D5 · Endings are laid on in letters (phonetic complements). A word-sign alone is the bare stem: a singular noun, the 3rd-person or imperative singular of a verb, an adjective. An ending that says something the order cannot is cut after it, in letters, on the same bed. The harmonic letters A and O take their class from the sign’s own word. An irregular ending is cut in full vowels, as a name is. A person ending is cut only when no subject stone follows: Tuma Halyna is [TUM] =Halyna.
    EndingCut asExample
    plural -AthA th[THELD]A th theldeth, families
    verbal noun -OlO l[TUM]O l tumol, memory
    participle -AtA t[BRODH]A t brodhat, told
    agent -ArdA r d[VESK]A r d veskerd, a seer
    abstract -OthO th[VENN]O th vennoth, faith
    singulative, dear -ele l[TEV]e l tevel, young
    collective -ana n[TRESK]a n Treskan, the Rivenmen
    belonging -ene n[ORROW]e n Orrowen, the tongue
    place -owo w[MYST]o w Mystow, the Mystlands
    ordinal -AstA s t(with numeral letters)
    person endingsO m, i th, A n, A, A r, O s, A n t[TUM]A r Tumar, we remember
    imperative plural -aa (a full vowel)[TALD]a Talda, rise
    the dual, the feminine -aa[ODH]a odha, a mother
  6. D6 · No mutations are cut. A mutation belongs to the mortar word that caused it, and the reader lays both back in together.
  7. D7 · Letters, always: the names of persons, and pair-names with their sealing lintel (“a name is said, not meant”); a word with no word-sign; loan words and Mystaeri names, spelled by sound, with the knock as a wedge inside the word; numbers, as capped numeral letters. Place-names that are plain words are cut as their words: Cemm Hyll (Tidesmeet) is [CEMM] [HYLL].
  8. D8 · Compounds are their stones, side by side on one bed: Stonwryt is [STON][RYT]; Stonwrytan is [STON][RYT]a n; vennuld is [VENN][ULD].
  9. D9 · A vow is cut whole. A Stonwryt, an oath (Rytom um …), the Covenant: every word, every mortar word, every ending and every bite, in letters, then the gate. “A sign holds what is meant; a vow must hold what was said”, for a vow is sworn aloud, and whoever raises the stone must be able to say it again word for word. When a vow is only cited (on the Stonwryt coin, on the lintel of a finished work, in the rolls), it is cut dry, and the gate alone is read Ston.
  10. D10 · The marks. The perpend ends a sentence; the wedge is a pause, and stands between the things eth, ell and veth would have joined; the gate ends a vow and is read Ston; the coping ends a tale; the foremark may stand at the head of a work. A cry, a question and direct speech are not marked: “a stone does not ask”.
  11. D11 · Beds and lines. Each word (the turned stone if any, its sign or signs, its complement; or a word in letters) is one stone on its own bed, parted from the next by a head-joint, and lines break the joint as in the letters. Every word-sign also stands on its footing. The line pitch is 6.4 u.

Stone has no tense. A work’s inscription speaks of what stands, a memorial of what was, a vow of what shall be. Where the time must be cut, a time is cut: a day, a year, a count of generations. And the Guest spoke the dry cut: Hess… Helv… Sennyl… are the three stones exactly, for he had already left out every mortar word, “your tongue joins its words with small words that make no sound across water” (§10.8).

5.3 · The word-signs and their laws

The ancestor’s laws of form made the letters out of the marks (§2.6). The word-signs are the marks the chisel kept whole, and they obey the first two of those laws and five of their own.

LawWhat happens
C1The chisel straightens.Curves become straight strokes or corners; a closed curve opens into strokes or is cut as its outline. (Kept from the ancestor.)
C2Everything stands on a bed.Every word-sign has at least one stroke on the mortar line. (Kept.)
W1A word-sign keeps its picture whole.It is not laid to the right as a letter is; it stands on its own centre, and may have parts on either side. The ancestor's C3 (stones laid to the right) and C4 (three leans) are laws of the letters.
W2A word-sign stands proud.4.6 u tall with its crown, 4.2 u as a root; a letter 3.
W3A word-sign has a footing.A second mortar band, y ∈ [−0.62, −0.44], under the sign's cell, from 0.3 u to 4.1 u.
W4A word-sign is a word, not a meaning.It is read as one Orrowen word, aloud, in one way. When the word's meaning drifted from the mark's, the sign went with the word: the Cup, which meant hold, is read tum, remember; the Split, crack, is cresk, break. It is never read for its first sound (that use became the letters).
W5Signs are capped.A second mark, cut small and set over a head as a capstone is set over a pillar, makes a new word from the head's field. The head is pressed to 0.702 of its height to make room. The crown is always free of the head (a 0.45 u joint).
W6Endings are laid on.The complement letters of D5 stand after the sign on its bed.
W7Branches are laid flat.No stroke branches off a stem at a slant as a rune's branch does; a branch is a laid stone, or the stem itself turns. (An originality law, after the runes.)

The geometry. A crowned sign’s strokes are exactly the head’s strokes with every y multiplied by 0.7024, then the crown’s strokes with each point (x, y) moved to (2.2 + 1.2 (x − 2.2), 3.4 + 1.2 (y − 3.4)). Every crown lies wholly above y = 3.4 and every pressed head wholly below 2.95, so a crown can never touch or crowd a head.
