a crowned signthe head pressed, y′ = 0.7024 y (so its top is at 2.95); the crown's 1.0 u box drawn at 1.2× about (2.2, 3.4), so the crown fills y ∈ [3.4, 4.6]

5.5 · The marks of the dry cut

MarkShapeReadingFrom the first marks
the turned stone (NOT)a pin 1.8 u tall with one laid stone running left from its head: strokes [[1.4,0],[1.4,1.8]], [[1.4,1.8],[0.3,1.8]] in a cell 1.8 u widenath, nel, new, the prefix na-: notThe First Tongue's "not" was a mark turned to face the other way (the First Tongue spec G6). A living letter's stones all run right; this is the one stone in the living hand that is laid the wrong way. It stands before the word it turns, on its bed. (The Hal, which is mirrored, cuts it running right.)
the foremarkthe word-sign FORE: a stem crossed near its headhosast, "first"The Fore, kept whole by both peoples. A Latin cross, and "the Latin cross is fine" (note 8). It may stand at the head of a work, on the first stone laid, and on the lid of the black chest
the gatethe punctuationafter a cited vow, Ston "it stands"the Door, kept whole
perpend, wedge, copingthe punctuationas in letters; the wedge also stands for eth, ell, veththe End, the Wedge, the Door and the Bar

The foremark, the word-sign hosast “first”, is the Fore itself: the first builders’ mark, and the grain’s Bar Before. Its look-alike score against the Latin cross is 0.005, the closest of any sign to any character, and it is kept by Jack’s note 8. It may stand at the head of a work, on the first stone laid, and on the lid of the black chest (§2.8).

5.6 · The inventory: 328 word-signs

Grouped by head. Each sign is drawn here from its data as centre-lines on its bed and footing, small, so the list can be searched by eye; the cut form is what the renderer draws (§5.4). Columns: no.; the sign; reads (the word, as the Book spells it); sense; parts (head, and crown if any); cl. (the harmony class its complements take); why (the reading of the picture); src (L a word of the v0.1 lexicon; R a reserve root of the First Tongue, which owes the dictionary pass).

  • Adding a word-sign later. A new word-sign is a head and a crown not yet used together, chosen so that the crown’s sense turns the head’s field toward the word. It is added with its reason, and the checks below are re-run. 239 head-and-crown pairs are still free. No new sign was needed for the whole Book’s lexicon (§11.3).
  • The checks. Every sign is unique (no two of the 328 share a head and a crown, and no reading is used twice). Every sign stands on the bed and keeps its joints (all 328 lie within the 4.4 × 4.6 cell, each has a stroke on y = 0, and no two strokes that do not touch come closer than 0.45 u, in the root form and in the pressed form of every head). Every reading is a real word of the tongue. No sign is a letter (word-signs are 4.2 or 4.6 u tall and stand on a footing; no letter is taller than 3 u). The look-alike screen was run on every head, every sign and the turned stone (§13.3).

5.8 · What the word-signs give the Book

  • Every inscription can now be economical and true. A lintel, a capstone, a marker, the coin: each can carry a real dry-cut line of a few signs.
  • The Stonwryt coin gets a legend at last: the vow’s last clause and its gate, cut dry, round the rim, [SOMM] [TOLM] [TOLM] ⟨gate⟩, “while stone is stone. It stands.” Jack
  • The granite Book that Halyna mean to cut “when there is peace enough” would be cut dry: a third of the ink.
  • The Creed and the guild’s word, as the guild would cut them over the door of its halls: Build, not un-build. Guard, not attack. (nayald is the turned stone and [GALD]; nath before it is a second turned stone) and Not sword, stone. Not killing, keeping. (veth “but” is the wedge).
  • Kinship a decoder can find. The stone’s word-signs are the same first marks as the grain’s signs, worn the other way: the dry cut’s TUM (the Cup, “remember”) is the grain’s HOLD; its SCETH (the Bough, “a hull”) is the grain’s HULL; its LUNN (the Gap) is the grain’s BREATH. Nothing in the Book says so (§2.8), and the grain’s forms of those marks stay exactly as they are.

6The Leaf-Hand (Garl Flenn): The Running Ink

Jack’s note 1, its second half: “The later written language would have to be able to be written quickly like English if the smaller words were included in the language.” The leaf-hand is that later hand. It is the course-hand written, not cut: the same letters, each made in one movement of the pen, the whole hand slanted and joined. It writes the whole tongue, every mortar word and every mutation, as fast as a hand can move. Seren writes the Book in it, and it is built as a working font, Garl Flenn, embedded in this page.

ul t̺umOl ol varn, ol theldAth, ol mardh, ol lunnAth, ol sollan.

The Title of Liberty in the leaf-hand: 48 letters and marks in 20 movements of the pen.

6.1 · The picture in one paragraph

The pen goes up the letter’s upright from the line and lays its stones rightward. The voicing pin, which the chisel cut as a separate short post, becomes a second leg that brings the pen back to the line. A free stone is a quick touch set after. A hairline carries the pen along the line from each letter to the next. A reader of the course-hand can read the leaf-hand at sight: every letter keeps its upright (forward, stepped, back), its stones at their heights, its pin. The bites hang small under the line, the sealing lintel rides over a pair-name, and the harmonic letters dip their capstones where the cut breaks them.

6.2 · The pen’s laws

LawWhat happens
F1One movement to a letter.Each letter begins on the line at its upright's foot, goes up the upright, and lays its joined stones rightward in order. A stone that sits below the top is reached by coming back down the upright (a retrace, which the nib leaves as one thick line).
F2The pin becomes a leg.A voiced letter's last stone turns down at its end (0.12 u on, 0.2 u down) and runs to the line: voiced letters stand on two feet. The ink voices every stop and every breath this one way, so v is f with a leg and dh is th with a leg (the reform's short top stone of the cut v and dh is not written).
F3The step is taken at speed.The offset's step becomes a short jog: (0, 1.35) → (0.5, 1.65).
F4The stones are shortened.An ink letter is the cut letter at 0.55 of its width: a full stone ends at 2.2 u, a short one at 1.32, a free one runs 1.595 → 2.2.
F5A free stone is a touch, set after, or the pen travels to it.The top stones of s, rh and Hal hw are ticks laid after the letter; the low stone of w, l and Hal x is reached by a hairline from the short top stone, and laid thick.
F6A pinning is made in one touch.Each vowel's pin and stone are joined; the harmonic letters' broken capstone becomes a dip in the capstone.
F7The pen runs on.Every letter leaves the line at its advance, and a hairline takes the pen from its last stroke to that point, so the next letter begins where this one ends. No contextual forms are needed: the joins are in the letters.
F8The hand leans.Every point (x, y) is drawn at (x + 0.18 y, y). The prop then leans hard forward, the offset a little forward with its jog, and the shore a little back, so the three places stay three.
F9Corners soften.Each interior corner of a nib stroke is rounded (radius 0.32 u, or 0.45 of the shorter arm) before the nib is swept along it.

Every letter can be told from every other. Place is the upright’s lean (after the slant: hard forward, gently forward with a jog, a little back); manner is the height of the stone and whether it is full, short or a touch; voicing is the second leg. The closest pairs on the look-alike screen are a/A and o/O, told apart by the dip, and b/d, told apart by the lean and the jog. The two inks: Halyna’s tellings alternate their two inks by paragraph, and in antiphony (the Cry, the guild’s word) the ink changes at the wedge. Seren’s own notes, and every leaf that is not Halyna’s, are in her one ink.

6.4 · How fast it is

Speed is how often the pen is lifted: one movement for every stroke that does not begin where the pen already is, and one for every bite, lintel and mark.

A word whose letters all end on the line is written without lifting the pen at all: Tumar is one movement, t-u-m-A-r, and the perpend is the second. Written whole, small words and all, the ink runs about as long as English: the I.1 pilot is 1,020 words of Orrowen against about 1,080 of the Book’s English for the same text (§11.7).

6.5 · The font, Garl Flenn

7Seilrhass: The Thunder-Tongue

Seilrhass, “bough-thunder” (spoken Seil’rhass), is the spoken tongue of the Naelear. “We speak as the storm speaks in the high boughs, in cracks and breaks” (II.2). It is loud, knocking and dialectal, and it is the moment’s tongue: “the thunder is for the moment, the softness for always”. The softness is the grain, which is the same words with the knock taken out, and no sound at all. The tongue is built out of the names Jack already has. Every one of the coined Mystaeri names stays valid, with its meaning. And it descends, with Orrowen, from the First Tongue (§2): it is built on the ancestral stem, without the case ending, and every Seilrhass word falls out of the laws S1 to S8 with no mismatches. The two tongues share 38 words that look nothing alike (§2.5).

7.2 · Sounds

Every Mystaeri name the Book prints uses only these sounds, and the list is closed: nothing may be added without a canon reason.

LetterSound (IPA)Near EnglishNotes

  • There are no oral stops: no p, t, k, b, d, g. There are no m, f, h (except inside rh and th), w or y, and no o or u. Those sounds belong to Shoreland.
  • Frequency. Common: n, l, r, th, s, e, a, ae. Middling: v, ei, ea. Rare: rh and bare i. z, x, q and the endings -ion, -iel, -dor never occur.
  • A syllable is (C)V(C). No onset clusters (rh and th are single sounds). A coda is l, n, r, s, th, ss, nn or nth; sth occurs in one worn root only, esth “fire”. No more than two consonants meet across syllables; where a compound would make three, a linking -e- goes in. Vowel-final roots take -n- before a suffix vowel: rei “go”, reine “goes”.

7.3 · The knock

The rule, from every spoken form in the Book: every word of two or more syllables breaks once, after its first syllable, even inside a root: Ra’lensaen, Ra’lenthae. One-syllable words and the small words never knock. A compound is one word and takes one knock (Nael’saen), and so is a suffixed verb (Ral’theine “remembers”).

What it is: a glottal catch, with a high falling pitch on the syllable before it and the rest of the word said level and soft. Speech comes out in beats of one hard syllable and a soft run, which is why the wall calls the ghost fleet’s knocking “the drums”. The carved soft reading drops the catch: Ael’thar is spoken, Aelthar is carved “whole and soft”.

Why shore ears hear stops. The Story Bible says the spoken tongue has hard stops, yet no word has one. After the catch the next consonant is released hard, and a Rivenman hears a stop that is not there:

Next soundHeard asExampleRivenman's ear
th[t̪θ]Ael'thar [ˈaɛlʔ.t̪θar]"Ail-tar"
s[ts]Nael'saen [ˈnaɛlʔ.tsaɛn]"Nail-tsain"
n[ⁿd]Sen'neir [ˈsɛnʔ.ⁿdeir]"Sen-deir"
v, r, rh, la plain catchRhen'vaela cough in the word

Dialects. “Each deep of the forest speaks it its own way.” Edge speech, nearest the grey’s edge, is the Guest’s, and the one described here. In Grove speech, the council’s, the knock is only a pitch-fall and th is voiced between vowels. In Deep speech the catch is velar and heard as a k: “Aelk-thar”. The dialects differ in a handful of words too, but never in the grain, which is why the canon calls the grain the one thing “bridging even the many dialects”.

7.4 · History in brief

Seilrhass had an older stage, the Eldest speech, which survives in the oldest carved names and in one borrowing. The exact laws, from the First Tongue through the Eldest speech to the living tongue, are in §2.3 (S1 to S8). In brief, four changes lead from the Eldest speech to the living tongue, and they account for every irregularity in the canon names.

  1. The old stops were lost. *t and *k after the first syllable became the knock; elsewhere *t became th and *k became rh. The knock is the ghost of a stop, which is why the drums sound like stone struck.
  2. Final vowels fell in words of two syllables or more (*thaele > thael “tree”). vaere keeps its -e because that -e is the long e of the First Tongue’s *-ai, which did not fall; so does Neivaere. (v0.1 said the vowel stayed after r; the ancestor replaces that rule.)
  3. The collective -aer was reshaped to -ear by analogy with the singular -ea “one of”. Naelear and Rhenear are living forms. Esthaer, the eldest Throne-name, was cut before the change and keeps -aer, and so does the Rivenmen’s early borrowing Mystaeri, which took the old ending and added a Shoreland plural.
  4. The old agent ending *-ane merged with the plural -en. It survives frozen in varen “bearer”. The living agent ending is -ea.
  5. The tense suffixes were once particles. -e, -es and -ar are the First Tongue’s *e “now”, *es “at another time” and *ar “toward”, fused to the verb after the final vowels had fallen. So the wood’s past -es is the stone’s future es: the stone looked forward with it, and the wood looked back.

7.5 · Word-building

Compounds are modifier + head, one word with one knock: Nael·saen “mist-heart”, Rhen·vael “stone-grain”, Seth·varen “carving-bearer”. The English glosses may run either way; the Seilrhass order never does. Names may be who-is compounds: Aelrhen, “bond-stone”, is one who binds himself to stone.

SuffixMeaningExamples

-eaone of; one who; on a number, the n-thnaelea a Mystaeri; sethea a carver; aelea a guest; vannea the second
-ear (relic -aer)those of: a whole people or kindNaelear, Rhenear, tharear kin, ralear forebears

Zero derivation. A root is a noun or a verb by its place: seth a carving, to carve; thae a tide, to grow; thael a tree, to rise, to stand; seil a bough, to bend as a bough bends; nael the mist, to veil. A tree is a standing, and a bough is a bending.

7.6 · Grammar: verb last

Order. Subject, then object, then verb, and nothing after the verb except the small words that close a clause. Time and place come before the object. Modifiers, possessors and relative clauses come before their noun, and postpositions after it. It is the mirror of verb-first Shoreland.

Veweithownnaelennhomeaeltooraltheine.remember-PRESENT

“We remember our home too.”

  • There are no articles. The demonstrative ra “this; the held one” marks a thing known or held: ra vei “this gift, the gift held out”; ra raltheinas “the memory”. This is the definite of knowing, and it is why a Mystaeri hand cutting the Shoreland Title reaches for one word too many: In the memory of…
  • Pronouns never knock, and the third person splits by animacy: living things answer; mute things do not. The late, angry wood speaks of shore-men with rhe, the mute plural. The green sliver speaks of them with le.

Possession is a pronoun before its noun: ve naelenn “our home”; ith “own” strengthens it. Postpositions are small clitic words, all but one on the vowel i:

WordMeaningWordMeaning
liin, at, onthithrough, past
nato, towardsiwith
rhifrom, out ofriagainst, upon
vifor, for the sake ofvaerelike, as ("in the face of")
sennbeneathlaesabove, over

Comparison is reflection: ral thenn na vaere, “as a root to water”.

  • Verbs. The bare root is the order, the mood of every carving: Rei! “Go!” Tense suffixes follow; nothing agrees with the subject. Negation is ni before the verb. The copula is eiss “be so”: Ve se rhesear ni eisse “We are not your enemies”; li eisse “there is”.
  • Clauses close with a small word and stand before the main clause:
WordMeaningExample
seiifneas thaesse sei, aven ves thi rei "if the eye is struck, go by the other road"
anthwhen (literally "at the hour")rhen lanthe anth, sae "when the stone is still, come"
eiruntil (literally "long, to the last")rhen aenne eir, thass "strike until the stone opens"
rhibecause (literally "from")nael vease rhi "because the sky is dying"
viso that
  • Questions close with lae, which is also the verb “to ask”: Rha ressveir eisse lae? Lanthe lae? “Is it worthless wood? Is it waiting?”
  • Relatives use the participle -ea before the noun: renn-ea rhen “the stone that speaks”, lexicalised as rennrhen, “a gun”.
  • Adverbs stand before the verb: ael together, too; eir still, long; eilen always (“all the rings”); reil first; thes then.
  • Numbers are counted in hands, base five, with vinn “hand” meaning five:
1234510firstsecondlastthree times
ithvannraesnalvinnvann vinnreil (irregular)vanneaeirraes eil ("three rings")

Irregular, as frequent words are, each with its history: varen keeps the old agent ending; reil “first” is suppletive (once the noun “the fore”); esth keeps the only sth coda; Esthaer keeps -aer; vaere keeps its final -e.

The audit so far

The whole lexicon was run through a checker for phonotactics, duplicate forms, and a blacklist of Tolkien, franchise and Celtic forms. Five draft forms collided while designing and were replaced: nae (Scots “no”) became lae; leith (a place-name) became rhel; thil (a Tolkien root) became raes; thei “live” clashed with theine “holds” and became ilae; Ennael (a fan character) became Naelenn. The originality pass then replaced two more (§13.5). Kept: lanth “knot, wait” shares a form with a piece of Sindarin Lanthir but not a word or a meaning, which Jack’s note 4 settles (a form-only echo stays); nael is Jack’s word and stays. Still owed before anything ships: an exact-string search of every new root against the Elvish dictionaries, the Celtic dictionaries and the franchise wikis. Only the headline words have been searched so far.

8The Grain (Eilseth)

This section is the grain as v0.1 built it, and all of it stands. Version 2 (§9) keeps the anchor at the heart and adds the intricate, intertwined outer rings Jack asked for; where it replaces a rule here, it says so, and this section marks the place. A carving is the cross-section of a trunk. The heart is the beginning and the bark is the end, because the knowing grows outward as a tree does. Meaning is carried by marks cut across the growth rings: one ring is one step in time, and the angle a mark stands at says who or where. It records meaning, not sound. It is taken in whole. It is grown, not written, and a later carving literally contains its earlier form. The Book’s own image for it is exact: “the eldest carvings are the youngest ones grown old.”

8.1 · What it is

  • A writing of meaning. A carving records what is meant, not what is said, which is why the canon calls it the writing “bridging even the many dialects” of the thunder-tongue: “whoever lays a hand on the carving knows what the carver meant, whatever tongue the carver spoke”.
  • Taken whole. The Bonded take a round in at once, as a memory. The reading order in §8.8 exists only for eyes and programs.
  • Grown, not written. Rings are growings (thae). The knife-cut is a V with two flat facets, one lit and one in shadow: visually the opposite of an ink stroke.
  • Every sign has a soft reading (eisranth), the Seilrhass word for its meaning spoken without the knock. The ten root signs also keep Seren’s English names, which she gives them by the look of the stroke (“the root, as I name it”).
  • Truth or nothing. Every round the player sees is a real encoding of a real knowing. No round ever carries decorative marks.

8.2 · How a knowing is carved, and how it is known

The carver cuts; the wood grows. An order is cut into a living heart, and the wood grows on around it. Each mark in a round is the cross-section of a ribbon grown along the trunk’s fibres, so every cross-cut shows the same round, and on a plank the carving “ran with the grain, fine and shallow” (V.1). Seren draws every knowing as its round, the end-face, because that shows all of it at once. The Book’s drawings are hers.

The knower touches, and it is given whole. There are no words in a round to turn. A spoken sentence can be reordered, misheard or punned on, and its small words can be lost across water, as the Guest lost Shoreland’s. A round has no word order, no homophones and no small words. Every relation is laid out in space: who is the file, when is the ring, “the same one” is a ray, “because” is a tie, “not” is a mirror. One drawing has exactly one reading, so “no word could be twisted and no promise misheard” is literally true of the grain.

Why only the Bonded. A round is “a forest’s thought”, too large for one shore-mind: Seren “felt something come into her too great to hold, and let go”. The Aetherbond’s shared mind can hold it, because “what the one knows, the other knows”. It needs no special mechanism. It is the same act as the knowing of a wall.

The telling is the hard part. Halyna “set each word down like a marking-stone where the knowing lies”. In grain terms, every English word they choose is a gloss laid on one mark. That is exactly what the Book shows: the round, with Seren’s words set beside the marks they belong to. The telling grows more faithful because more classes of mark can be glossed (§8.6), not because the wood changes.

Deceit without lies. A carving of the Tide that Learned Deceit cuts its decoys hollow. Read whole, the round says plainly: show this; do not mean it. It is the enemy’s eye on the water that is fooled, never the knower of the wood. “The wood does not lie. It was told to make us believe a lie, and it obeyed.” The lie is a hollow cut, and the hollowness is itself carved.

8.3 · The round

PartReal anatomyRule
Piththe centre of the stemradius 4.5. Round for wood grown in peace. Square (side 9, turned to the axis) for every heart and hull grown since the council's vote: this is the war-pith, Grow until the shore is silent "beneath all the other carvings", which the wood "cannot unlearn" (V.4). A round never has more than one pith, except in the Joined Tide
Heart ring (ring 1)juvenile wood: the fast first growth, widewidth 72 in a sapling round. Otherwise clamp(0.22 × the sum of the other ring widths, 56, 96). The root sign is cut here, from the pith outward, and is the largest mark
Growth rings (rings 2…K)growth rings, each an earlywood/latewood pairmarked ring width 46 × seeded(0.84…1.20); empty ring width 18 × seeded(0.90…1.15). K ≤ 24. V.6, the longest leaf, has 24 paragraphs. Above 13 rings, marked rings shrink toward a minimum width of 26. Each ring is a latewood line (weight 2.2) with a paler earlywood band inside it. Two or three year-hairlines per ring (weight 0.5, 35% opacity) show the years and carry nothing
Band-rulea false ring: a growth stop in mid-seasonthe ring line is doubled (a second line 5 units outside it). There are two per round, and they part the three bands. They are the Book's two RING markers made visible
Included barkbark overgrown by later wooda dark, rough line 4.5 wide on a ring. It marks where an older carving ended and a later Tide grew over it
Barkthe barka rough band 12 + 4 × min(K, 6) wide outside ring K. Its outer contour is noise made of harmonics 5, 7, 11, 17, 29 and 41 (amplitudes 1–4). It is crossed by radial fissure hairlines. No mark ever crosses the outer contour. Marks in the bark are limited to names, the seal and pale rings
Heartwood / sapwood tintthe colour of old woodthe rings inside band-rule 1 are tinted heartwood. A sapling (Hasty wood, the green sliver) has no heartwood and is tinted green-wood. Myststone is overlaid in stone-grey

All rings of a round share one shape around the pith, with a little seeded wobble, so they never cross; a knot bends the ring lines near it outward, so the grain visibly flows round it. Every free parameter is seeded from the round’s id (mulberry32 over an FNV-1a hash), so the same round is the same drawing for every reader, which is the Book’s law of determinism. Adding or removing a mark never moves a ring: the Stone’s unmarked stage and its marked stage share every ring exactly.

8.4 · The ring grammar: how a round is read

The axis. The root sign is cut from the pith outward in the heart ring, and its direction is the axis. Everything is read relative to it; the page may turn the round, and the reader finds the root first. The Book draws the axis near the top, turned by a seeded ±12° so no two rounds line up mechanically.

Files: angle is who and where. A round has 16 files, radii at 22.5° steps clockwise from the axis, numbered 0–15. Everything cut on one file within a band is about one referent: one hull-group, one road, one stone, one people. Even files are bearings, relative to the carving’s main road, facing the shore; odd files are placeless, for referents with no road. Real compass names belong to Halyna’s telling; the Knowing generator fills them from the board.

FileBearing
0ahead, toward the shore on the main road
4the right hand
8behind: home, the grey, the other side
12the left hand
2, 6, 10, 14the diagonals

Rings: radius is when. One ring is one step. Marks in the same ring happen together, at one hour: “three roads, one hour” is three marks in one ring. Outer rings come after inner ones. A thin empty ring means a morrow passes. A mark stretched across rings holds through those steps: until.

The three bands: beginning, middle, end. Two band-rules, doubled ring lines, part the round into three. They are the Book’s two grain-rules made visible, and they mean different things in an order and in a telling:

BandIn an order (a seth: the 46 carvings, Burn, the council's carving)In a telling (a theinas: the wood leaves, the gift, the sliver, the Stone)
I, the heartthe root: what kind of order this is (its line), plus any older carving it grew fromthe first movement. One ring per paragraph
II, the sapthe parts: who, where, what each group is told, who waits on whomthe second movement, one ring per paragraph
III, the bark ringsthe turnings: if and else, the home clause, and the aim (Cut against)the third movement, one ring per paragraph
the bark itselfthe name of whoever grew it (a Tide or a Throne)the seal: This is held in the grain … and the grain holds it still

A sapling (Hasty wood, Burn, the green sliver) is too young for heartwood: it is all heart, one ring and no rules. Every wood leaf’s round has exactly as many rings as the leaf has paragraphs, and its band-rules fall where the leaf’s two grain-rules fall. In a joined round (several piths inside shared rings), the shared rings are measured about the round’s centre, and every pith’s root points along the one axis.

Line quality classifies. The line of a closed shape tells which world a thing belongs to. Straight-edged (the square and its kin) means of stone: the wall, the gun, the house behind the stone, the shore-men’s home, the door. Curved (lens, drop, loop) means of wood: bough, hull, seed, heart, home, one of us. The same person-figure with a square crown is one of stone, and with a lens crown one of us. Open strokes (acts) are not classified.

Weight carries nothing. The stroke width is fixed per round. A thicker cut never means louder or more urgent (that device belongs to Arrival).

Not is a mirror. Negation is the sign’s mirror image across its own file. So every sign must look different from its mirror: the chiral ones already do, and every other sign carries the entry-nick, a short cut entering beside its head from the clockwise side, where the knife went in. Mirrored, the nick is on the other side.

8.5 · The signs

The inventory is 70 signs, 6 condition bands and 34 grammar devices, and v2 adds 47 signs to it (§9.9). Every sign grows from the First Tongue’s marks by the wood’s laws of form (§2.6). Each sign is a parametric V-cut mark defined once in a local frame and placed on its file and ring, so a program can draw any sentence by rule and read it back by rule.

The sign chart: every sign alone on a chip of end-grain, pith toward the foot, with its soft reading and its meaning. On a narrow screen it scrolls sideways inside its frame.

The eleven that open a carving: the ten roots and Burn

Each root keeps Seren’s name and is drawn from her exact words in the Book of Knowings, where she reads the root by eye and “never more than the root, for the rest the wood gives only to the Bonded, and it must be known, not read.” Each root maps to one of the fleet’s growth lines (Admiral §16b): the Wave is Flood, the Lone Stroke Sounding, the Bar Before Screen, the Spark Hunt, the Mute Square Siege, the Two Mouths Feint, the Turned Stern Lure, the Breath Bleed, the Knot Patience, the Smoothed Cut Mask.

A root alone in a sapling. The meaning above is the root’s lasting signature, what it says when it opens an older carving. Condition bands: what lies along the ring

A condition is not cut across the ring. It lies along it, like a real ring feature (a frost ring, a ring shake), over files s0…s1 or the whole ring, and gives the surroundings of whatever is cut in that ring on those files. A gap in a band is itself meaning: a MIST band with files 3–5 left open reads “the sky comes open there”.

How a tie’s ends are read. By the marks it touches, not by the file its end happens to fall on. Each end stops one knife-width (3 units) from its mark and nearer to it than to any other. A tie across rings leaves its source’s head and lands on its target’s foot. The thick end is the source, the fine end the target. A tie that ends on a file where nothing is cut in that ring ties to that file’s bearing, a place.

Composition rules

  1. One root per round, cut first, in ring 1, from the pith, along the axis. It owns files 15, 0 and 1 of ring 1.
  2. At most two signs on one file in one ring, as a ligature, modifier inward and head outward, exactly as a Seilrhass compound. Reading heart to bark is reading left to right in Seilrhass. v2 In a telling, at most one mark per cell (§9.10).
  3. At most eight marked files per ring, and every mark keeps at least 3 units from its ring lines and its neighbours. v2 The eight-file limit is withdrawn; the gate rule keeps the air instead.
  4. Conditions lie along the ring; acts and things cut across it. A mark cut inside a condition band takes that condition (“wait in the grey”).
  5. Rays join marks on one file; ties join marks on different files. Only the memory ray runs inward. v2 Ties become carved runners of role to or then (§9.6).
  6. The seal and the name stay in the bark. Nothing is ever cut beyond the bark’s outer contour.
  7. The canonical order: band I, II, III, then the bark; within a band ring by ring outward; within a ring file by file clockwise from 0; then bands, rays, memory rays and ties.

8.6 · How a carving grows across the Tides

The Law of the Rings, made literal. What a carving can hold is how old its wood is.

WoodIts ageDrawn ringsWhat it can holdWhere it appears
green (a sapling)one season1, the heart ring only; no heartwoodone signthe Hasty Tide; Burn (the Fall); the green sliver
forty summersa generation2 marked rings, plus empty rings for timea phrase: the root plus one sign, and one tie ("waits for its brother")the Second Tide
a shore-man's lifea long human life3–6a sentence, and a memory in it: memory rays, the first forkthe Tide of Remembering
a long lifeseveral human lives4–9; several pithsthe morrow: ties between hulls, joined piths, hollow and smoothed marks, forks and chainsthe Joined Tide, Deceit, the Last Tide; every Standard-Bearer's heart (Saenvael)
the eldestages; the pillars; Myststoneup to 24, plus a full barka judgement; names; groansthe Thrones; the gift; the Stone out of the Grey

The growth rules

  • The same root. Every carving of a line cuts that line’s root in ring 1, on the axis. That is what Seren reads by eye.
  • Containment. A carving that grows from a parent reproduces the parent’s rings exactly as its own innermost rings. The parent’s bark becomes included bark, and the new Tide’s rings grow outside it. The inner rings are never re-cut, because the wood “cannot unlearn what is carved in it”. Where a child changes what its parent said, it does so with a later mark on the same file: the outer ring speaks last.
  • Old bark and rules. Band-rule 1 of any grown carving lies on the ring where the root’s sapling bark was, so it is drawn as both a double line and included bark.
  • Borrowing, dress, chains, reach-back. A primitive borrowed from another line enters as a graft, a V of included bark around the marks that carry it. Early forms worn as a disguise are cut hollow. A hinge that carves an older stratagem ends in that stratagem’s root cut half size. A carving that reaches back contains the far ancestor’s rings, not the middle one’s.
  • Joined piths. From the Joined Tide on, each formation of an order has its own pith, inside shared rings. The piths’ own rings never touch: separate hearts, then one trunk, as stems that grow together really look. It is the dark mirror of the Aetherbond.
  • Thrones. A Throne’s Judgement is an order in eldest wood, its true name in the bark. In battle its bark closes one pale ring per groan.
  • The war-pith. Grow until the shore is silent was cut on the last round pith of the war (§10.17). Every heart grown under that council since has a square pith, “beneath all the other carvings, as the first ring lies beneath all the rings”. The square is the Mute Square, the sign for stone: the war’s wood grew the mute thing into its own heart.

The Knowing ladder, in the grain

The fleet’s Knowing of the Wood (Admiral §9b) rises with the war, “the Ender’s Game ordering turned on the tellers”: at first a shore-mind receives only the shape of a knowing, and over the Tides Halyna learn to hold more of it and to tell it. In the grain that ladder is exact. The Book draws every round in full from the moment it exists, and glosses only what is held. Each band of the Legends’ knowing depth (Legends map §4) unlocks a class of marks for glossing, and §12.2 names each one as an achievement. v2 adds its devices to the same bands (§9.15).

The blank wood leaves: what each round is

Every blank facing leaf shows the round of the wood it will be told from, its ring count the leaf’s paragraph count by movement. For each paragraph its ring carries the paragraph’s core knowings (its subject, its act, its condition or bearing), one to six marks: a truthful skeleton of the telling, not a word-for-word copy. 8.7 · Names in the bark

A name is “the last thing in a knowing that will go into words”, so it is cut last: in the bark, on file 0. A name is a ligature of the signs of its compound, modifier inward, exactly as the Seilrhass word is built. The grain itself (vael) is written as a free grain-arc, a short hairline along the ring: the only hairline that is not a ray or a tie, and it occurs only in names.

8.8 · Reading by rule, and the proof

Grain Notation (GN) is the canonical linear form of a round, and every sample in §10 gives it. v2’s notation is a strict superset of this one (§9.14). The literal reading replaces each token with its gloss in the canonical order. The telling is Halyna’s English: a translation, not a gloss. Both are given for every sample.

round <id> {wood: green|forty|life|long|eldest|stone; pith: round|war[ ×n]; rings: K; rules after: [b1, b2]}
  I
    r1     0: WAVE*                  (* = the root)
  II
    r2   p0·4: EDGE+BREAKER          (pN· = on pith N's own rings)
    r3     3: !LIVE+SAPLING×3        (! = not: the mirror)
  III
    r5    12: GO
  bark
    bark   0: BOND+TIDE              (a name)
  band MIST r4 files 0–15 · ray 3: r2–r4 · mem 8: r8 → pith · tie 0.r5 → 3.r5
  1. Find the pith or piths, round or square.
  2. Trace the ring lines and classify each: single, doubled (a band-rule), dark and rough (included bark), or pale (a groan, in the bark).
  3. Find the root, the mark that touches the pith in ring 1. Its direction is the axis.
  4. For every mark take its angle (the file, measured about its own pith, or in the shared rings of a joined round about the round’s centre), its inner and outer radius (the ring span), its element signature (the sign), its mirror test (negation), and its bites, hollowness, smoothness and scale (the other devices).
  5. Classify the hairlines: radial between marks is a ray; radial to a pith ending in three root-hairs is a memory ray; along a ring is a tie within the ring; curving outward is a tie across rings. A hairline along a ring that opens into a knocked-out split with a bright upper rim is the DREAD band, not a tie.
  6. Write the GN in the canonical order.
The decode test: 1 of 6 first time, 6 of 6 after the fixes

A reader with only the rules and the pictures (every title, description and data attribute stripped) read six rounds: E1-03, VI-1, E2-01, GROW, the Aelthar and E4-01. One passed first time. Every miss was traced to its cause and removed by a rule or a check, so it cannot recur: a root alone in a sapling now has its own table (it says its whole young-wood order); “held at the root” is now a device (remembered); KNEEL and AXE were overlaid at root size and KNEEL’s fold recut; the lean now means “brow to brow”; tie ends now land on their own marks, and a validator checks every one (8 of 28 ends used to sit over an empty neighbouring file); and a joined round’s shared rings are measured about its centre. All six now read as their samples give them. That second reading was not blind, so the honest claim is narrower: each cause has been removed, and the tie check is mechanical. A fresh blind reader on the new drawings is the real re-test, and is worth running.

8.9 · A third hand: the soft letters (a sketch) Jack

The canon gives the Mystaeri a third writing: “letters no one could read, fine and curling, as beautiful as frost on a window”, cut on stone, where “here and there among the letters they had tried to cut our own words by their sound … the sounds were close, and the symbols wrong” (IV.1, IV.2, IV.5). These letters, rhelranth “frost-words”, spell sound. Stone carries no knowing, which is why “stone does not translate”: to anyone without Seilrhass they are mute. By the truth rule they may only be drawn if they are real, so this sketch makes them real. It is not drawn yet.

Consonants: a stem whose head curlsVowels: a rime-drop hanging under the letter before
v curl right · th curl right + 1 barb · s curl right + 2 barbsa one round drop · e a drop drawn out to the right · i a bead (a dot)
l curl left · r curl left + 1 barb · rh curl left + 2 barbsae the drop and a bead beside it · ea the drawn drop and a bead · ei two beads
n a double curl, both waysthe knock: a short hook between syllables · doubling: a second head on the stem
  • How it is written. Left to right along a gentle curve, as on the face of a standing stone; a word ends with a space. Each curl is at most 270°, single and never nested. The strokes are fine and even, and every stem is upright: never thick-and-thin, never a Z or a 2 for a skeleton (§13).
  • Shoreland by sound. The letters have no stops and no back vowels, so a Shoreland word takes the nearest sounds: p b m f w are written v, t d th, k g h rh, o a, u e, a Shoreland y i. “The sounds were close, and the symbols wrong.”
  • The mute stones’ warning (proposed): Nael enth li naelsaenen ni rhith. Le rhithveir ni eisse. Ve nael sath li eisse. At the edge of the grey, do not fell the pillars. They are not timber. We are behind the grey. The Guest’s three Shoreland words are spelled among the letters by sound, and the obvious plea in Orrowen, Hess. Doss et helv ul sennyl. “Stop. The sky is in dying.”, is built from them. A player who has learned Orrowen can then read the sound-spelled words inside the frost-letters; the rest of the stone stays mute.
  • They never translate by reading, because stone does not translate. Their meaning is added beside them from the wood: at IV.2 (“so we cut our plea on the mute thing”) or at IV.4; the three grey stones of Eldhythe’s harbour-house get theirs when Thaesaen falls.

9The Grain, Version 2: Intricate and Intertwined

Jack’s note 7: “I like that Seilrhass has an anchor in the middle of the tree and the details are added in the outer rings. This keeps it separate from The Arrival. But the same flavor. I would like to see it more intricate and more intertwined.” Version 2 keeps the anchor exactly: the pith, the root sign cut from it along the axis, the rings as steps, the sixteen files as who-and-where, the three bands, the seal in the bark. Everything new is cut outside the heart ring, and it grows denser ring by ring, because each outer ring has more wood in it and older wood holds more. More intricate: a ring’s knowings stack in years, outer rings split each file into cells, and a fringe of finer marks, parts and pockets say what v1 could not. More intertwined: every relation between signs is a runner, a narrow living cut that grows through the wood from the sign that governs to the sign it governs, crossing the others over and under, and every crossing means something.

9.1 · What Jack asked, and what the prototypes showed

Jack's wordsAs a rule of v2
"an anchor in the middle of the tree"The pith and the root sign are untouched. The heart ring carries the root and nothing fine: no fringe, no braid, no bind, no pocket
"the details are added in the outer rings"Intricacy is gated by age and ring: the fine devices appear only beyond band-rule 1, and outer rings get more cells
"This keeps it separate from The Arrival. But the same flavor"The flavour kept: a script of meaning, taken whole, in circles. The look refused: one inked ring, tendrils, smoke, weight
"more intricate"years and cells, the fringe, parts and the kind-arc, pockets, 47 more signs. The "sub-rings and ring-splits for clauses" are the years (sub-rings that wedge in where a referent's story grows) and the pockets (ring-splits holding a knowing within a knowing)
"more intertwined"runners grown through the wood; passes, breaks, braids and binds
(note 8) "all languages come from an ultimate base language"every new sign and device is derived from the First Tongue's 45 marks by the laws of form G1–G7
(note 5) "tier 3 on how far to take the translation"a whole wood leaf can be carved: the inventory, the layout and the worked leaf, IV.6
(note 4) "Nothing obvious. Nothing we could get sued for."every new sign was checked against its v1 neighbours and the letter and rune look-alikes, and recut where it read as one

Two layouts were built and drawn with the whole of IV.6 before the rules were written.

  • Full-circle sub-rings, one per knowing, failed. Each sentence became a thin ring right round the round, holding one to three marks. IV.6 became 68 concentric lines with specks on them: a vinyl record, sparse and mechanical, and its runners, confined to channels and gates, read as a circuit board.
  • Years packed by referent, cells in the outer rings, and runners grown through the wood is what v2 adopts. The same leaf is 29 years and 915 units in radius, against about 1,950 for the rejected layout. The marks cluster where the story is, and the runners flow along the grain between them. The heart stays plain.
  • A lattice router alone draws 45° jogs and parallel bundles, which again read as a circuit board. String-pulling in polar coordinates removed the look: a straight run there is a gentle drift across the grain, never a chord.

9.2 · What stays, and what changes

Unchanged from v1: what the grain is (meaning, not sound; taken whole; grown, not written; a soft reading for every sign; truth or nothing); the round (pith, heart ring, growth rings, band-rules, included bark, the bark and its seed); the axis and the sixteen files; the rings (outer after inner; an empty ring a morrow; a span until; three bands, three movements); the local frame, the entry-nick, the classifier (straight means of stone, curved means of wood) and the rule that weight carries nothing; the 70 signs, six bands and every v1 device, among them the ten roots, Burn, and BARB, the Bar Before, a Latin cross, kept; names in the bark; and the tie-end reading rule, which now applies to runner ends.

"marks in the same ring happen together, at one hour"still true of the ring. Inside it, marks on one file are ordered outward (years, then cells clockwise). Marks on different files are ordered only by runners
"Everything cut on one file within a band is about one referent"in a telling, within a ring, and a file keeps its referent from ring to ring until a new thing-sign stands first on it; orders keep the band rule

Every Admiral carving and every v1 sample keeps its Grain Notation, and its meaning, exactly. Only the drawing changes: ties become carved runners, marks take v2’s breadth, the ring lines yield a little round every mark, and the meaningless year-hairlines of one-year rings are no longer drawn, because in v2 a year-line always means a year (§9.13).

9.3 · The Law of the Rings, made visible: intricacy grows outward and with age

The canon’s law is that “a hull of one season holds one sign; of forty summers, a phrase; of a shore-man’s life, a sentence, and a memory in it. The eldest pillars hold a judgement.” v1 made it literal in ring counts. v2 makes it literal in the knife as well. Each age of wood may carry only the devices it has grown into, and within any round the heart is plain and the fine work is outward. This is Jack’s “anchor in the middle … details added in the outer rings”, enforced by rule.

  • Ring 1, the heart ring, holds the root and, in a telling, the first knowings. It takes no fringe, braid, bind or pocket, and has one cell per slot.
  • Band I takes runners and the fringe, and at most two cells. It takes no pocket, braid, bind or break.
  • Beyond band-rule 1 everything is allowed, and cells grow with the girth.
  • Where a leaf’s opening words want a fine device, the heart cuts them plainly instead, and the fine devices stay outward: “though you took us for it” in IV.4’s heart is a runner to a likeness, not a pocket. The tier-3 pass found seven leaves whose openings want one, and every one resolves this way without moving a word Jack.

So the carving is quiet at the heart and busy in the sapwood, as a real tree’s figure is.

9.4 · Years and cells

LevelIn a telling (a wood leaf)In an order (an Admiral carving)Drawn as
the roundthe whole telling (theinas)the carving (seth)one heart v1

  • Years. A ring of a telling is cut in years of about 32 units (seeded). Each year holds one step of each referent’s story. Under every mark that is not in its ring’s first year, the grain shows a faint year-line: a partial ring, real wood’s wedging ring, a year that grew only where something grew in it. Years are never drawn as full circles (that was the rejected vinyl look). A ring of one year, every Admiral order and every v1 sample, keeps v1’s width.
  • The packing rule. Knowings are placed in the order the telling gives them, and each mark takes the next free cell of its own file: cell by cell clockwise across the slot, then the next year outward. So within a referent, later is outward; across referents in one ring the grain does not order, and where order across referents matters, a then runner says so. Adding or removing a runner never moves a mark.
  • Cells: more rays as the girth grows. Ring k has c = clamp(⌊(r·SLOT − 6) / 58⌋, 1, 4) cells per file’s slot. Every cell lies inside its slot, so a cell never changes the referent. Trees add rays as their circumference grows; the cells are that. On IV.6 the cells (1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4 by ring) cut the leaf from 53 years to 29.
  • Breadth and room. A mark’s breadth shrinks with its cell, and the root may be up to 56 units broad in a heart ring of at least 72, so the root is always the largest mark. Every half-file and half-cell line keeps 3 units clear, and the top 5.5 units of every year are free: that is the runners’ room.
  • The grain’s flow. Round every mark the nearest ring lines bow away by up to 1.2 units, and where a runner crosses a ring line, the line dips: the wood yields round what is cut in it, as grain yields round a passing root. It is anatomy, and carries nothing.

The part device. A sign cut with some of its elements whole and the rest hollow names that part of the thing. It is v1’s hollow (“shown, not meant”) turned to use: the rest of the thing is shown, so that the part is meant. It gives the body and the made thing their parts without new signs.

The kind-arc, ‿, a fine ring-arc cut under the three feet of a ×3, means those of that kind: a whole people (Seilrhass -ear), where ×3 alone is a plural (-en). US×3‿ is Naelear; STONEFOLK×3‿ the shore-folk as a people; ROOT×3‿ ralear, forebears. It comes from the Bed, *loð-: those set in one bed.

The fringe, written SIGN{f,…}, is eleven tiny cuts at three stations round a sign: how many, which and how much, and how it went. It is the Tally (*kail-) grown round the sign: only is the Lone Mark small, still the Bed small, at last the End reduced to its point, gently the Cup, slowly the Curl drawn out. It is never Ogham: it sits beside or under one sign, never along a stem-line, never as a run of parallel strokes, and counts stop at four.

9.6 · Runners: the living branch-lines

A runner is a narrow living cut that springs from the head of the sign that governs, and grows through the wood to the sign, file or pocket it governs. It is the Course (*trenn-, “a running line”) grown from a Stem’s head: like the wood’s roots, it runs with the grain and crosses the rings where it must. It is cut, not drawn: a V-cut with two facets, 1.35 units half-wide at its node, where it swells into a small bud, tapering to 0.45 at its end. The thick end is the source; the taper gives the direction, and is not weight. A runner may be cut smoothed (a hidden relation) or hollow (a seeming one), as a mark may. Its end says its role, confirmed by where it lands:

  • The file is the pronoun. A runner of role to or in whose target is written @f ends in the empty cell of file f: “to that file’s one”. The grain needs no sign for us in every knowing; it points at our file.
  • Split runners. A runner may fork once, into two or three shoots of the same role: “what one pillar felt, all the ranks felt”. A shoot never forks again.
  • The blind is what “Fear leaves no mark on wood” means. The grain has no sign for a shore-man’s fear. Where the host’s fear stood, the wood cuts only an empty cup, a because that lands on nothing, and Halyna glosses it: “We do not know why.” Jack
  • How a runner is grown. By a seeded, grain-following search on a polar lattice, which walls off every mark and never crosses a ring line inward (only memory runs inward), prefers to run along a ring and climb late, keeps runners apart so they cross when they must instead of running in bundles, and is then smoothed and given a slow meander. The meaning is in the endpoints, the terminal and the crossings, never in the path’s shape. A decoder only traces a route.
  • Composition. Prefer the file referent to a runner that crosses years to a repeated sign. A runner stays within its ring when it can, and across rings runs only outward. Two runners of the same role from one mark to one target are one runner. No runner passes through a pocket. At most one fork, three shoots and 300° of turning, and no loop.

Where the small words went. Seilrhass joins its words with small words, and the grain never cut one. v1 had two relation-lines; v2’s runners, crossings and knots give the grain its whole grammar of relation, as the chisel’s economy asks of the stone, without a single small word. 9.7 · Crossings: pass, break, braid, bind

At every crossing of two runners, one is cut through (over) and the other is broken on both sides (under). The kind of crossing is read from the under-strand’s ends and from what the strands are doing. This is the Upon (*um-, “upon; seen from below, beneath”), the one first mark that was already about over and under; the wood kept it as BENEATH, and v2 makes it the grammar of every crossing.

KindDrawnMeansOver is
passclean endsthe two relations both hold. The later lies upon the earlier, as later growth lies upon earlier wood: "the outer ring speaks last" [v1 G2]the runner later in canonical order: its source's ring, then year, then file clockwise, then cell, then GN order. A decoder can check it, and must
breakeach cut end of the under-strand splinters into two tines, 2.8 long at −40° and +36°the over-strand thwarts the under-strand: prevails over it, cuts it off, turns it backthe thwarting runner, earlier or later

A break is declared in the notation (lap e1 ⊳ f1) and crosses square, exactly once. A pass is never declared; it happens wherever two routes cross, and it carries its fixed reading. Every crossing is at 15° or more. In the tellings: IV.6’s “we turned against the current” is our turning breaking the current’s taking; V.4’s “the vote was carried by the weight of anger and grief” is the young’s runner breaking the elders’ plea; IV.4’s “the host drew back … the blade … went deep” is the drawing-back breaking the rite’s shallow cut.

Braids. Two or three runners that share a stretch of one cord and plait along it hold one relation by turns, and the over-strand at each crossing is whose turn it is. A braid has exactly as many crossings as its pattern is long, and it is short, open at both ends, and runs along one ring.

PatternMeansIn the tellings
abab… (2 strands, alternating)by turns; each to the other; the one and then the otherII.2: "we tended the wood, and the wood kept us"; IV.2: "The iron came back for the young ones. We put up more. It came again."
aaaa…the one prevails at every turnV.4: the elders' counsel of patience against the young's grief, turn after turn ("and counselled patience still"), until the young break it
abcabc… (3 strands, the standard plait)these three, each holding the othersII.2: "The wood needed the breath, the breath needed the wood, and we needed both"
…!the last crossing is a break: at the last turn, the one over thwarts the otherIV.6: "the fire went out of us slowly as the grey closed over" is abab!: fire and grey by turns, until the grey. IV.2: "At the last the stumps put up nothing"

Binds: knots where meanings bind. Two runners meet head-on, and each hooks through the other: the two relations are bound into one, and each holds only with the other. “Harm to one is harm to both.” “One life, in two kinds.” A promise; a rite’s joining. A bind may send out one runner of role then or to, what the bound pair together does. Three strands chain as two locks, never a three-fold rotational figure. A bind is grammar and never a sign: BOND (ael) is the word, two cuts that grow into one, and AELTHAR is the rite’s name-sign. The Aelthar’s last ring, “harm to one is harm to both”, may cut its two WOUND runners as a bind, with its out-runner to BOND Jack:

9.8 · Pockets: a knowing inside a knowing

A pocket is a lens-shaped hollow in a year, whose lines part round it, holding a knowing that another knowing contains: words said, sung, asked or believed, or a carving cited whole. It is real anatomy, a resin pocket or a bark pocket between the rings, round which the grain splits and rejoins. It is the grain’s ring-split.

KindGNBorderHoldsIn the tellings
said (resin pocket)pocket P said s0–s1 { … }a smooth double line: 0.9 wide at 62%, and 0.7 at 34% set 1.25 inside itwords said, sung, asked, believed, named: the content of MOUTH, HEAR, SING, NAME, HOLD, TRUE+HOLD (believe)V.4: the elders' "Send another. Learn their words." and the young's answer; IV.4: Stop. Sky. Dying.; II.2: "You called it the fog…"; V.6: the Song of the Years
cut (bark pocket)pocket P cut s0–s1 { … }a jagged line (±0.9), included bark's own texture v1a carving: an order, a judgement, an older knowing, cited whole, or by its root cut half size (v1's chain)III.2: each Throne's "Our judgement was …"; V.3: "Then an older carving woke in us … Home when wounded" is { STERN½ }; V.4: "Grow until the shore is silent"; IV.6: what the keel held of IV.4

A pocket spans at most six files, takes its year’s whole mark band, and is 8 units deeper; the year’s lines bow away from it. It has one mouth, a small gap at the tip facing its governing runner, and exactly one that runner ends just inside it. It holds up to eight items, cut with the finer knife in its own reading order, and it may hold one pocket more. No runner passes through a pocket. When the cited knowing is itself a whole round (IV.4’s ring 15 cites the gift’s sentence), the pocket holds that round’s root at half size, and the Book draws the cited round beside it.

9.9 · The 47 new signs

A new sign was added only where a concept of the eight wood leaves needed a Seilrhass root. Everything else is a ligature, exactly as Seilrhass builds its compounds: timber is AXE+WOOD, the council SILVERBARK×3, to learn NEW+HOLD, to believe TRUE+HOLD (“hold true”), to hope MORROW+HOLD, a guest BOND+US, a host DOOR+STONEFOLK, a lie SQUARE+CARVE (“a cut that carries nothing”), war STRIKE×3. Parts come from the part device. Every new sign grows from the First Tongue’s marks by the wood’s laws (§2.6), and most belong to a family grown from a v1 sign, so a reader who knows the head of the family can guess its members: the MOUTH family (MOUTH, HEAR, SING, CRY, LAUGH, EAT); the EYE family (EYE, WEEP, FIND); the HAND family (HAND, TAKE, LOSE); the Cup family (HOLD, NAME, TEND, HOLY); the HEART family (HEART, ANGER, SHAME, GLAD); the Bed family (DEEP, EARTH, SAND, MOSS); the Star family (FLASH, SOFTLIGHT, MORNING, DUSK, SUMMER). Every soft reading is a Seilrhass word that already exists: 21 are in the lexicon, and 26 are reserve roots whose forms the sound laws computed. None is coined. In the tables, L is a lexicon word and R a reserve root; Chiral says whether the sign already differs from its mirror (one that does not carries the entry-nick).

The look check. Each new sign was drawn alone on a chip of end-grain and beside the v1 signs it is nearest to, and checked against Latin letters, digits, Greek and Hebrew letters, runes and interface icons. Every first drawing that read as something else was recut, and one, COME, was withdrawn:

SignFirst drawing read asRecut to
WOODa Latin E (a stem with three arcs off it)a billet: a lens sawn at both tips
FOLLOW, TRUE! and ¡: two colinear cuts, or a drop under a stemFOLLOW: the short cut set well aside. TRUE: a plumb between a floor-bar and a small square
MORROWHebrew kaf/bet, katakana コ (a square C)a closed rounded band along the ring
HEARfirst a Latin C, then a ? (a stem with a sideways hook)MOUTH turned toward the heart
BRIDGEGreek Ω (an arch on out-turned feet)a shallow span over a low arc, with no feet
CARRYa T (a stem under a crosswise lens)the stem leans, as the Bearer's prop leans
LOSEan emoticon, "(:"HAND with one finger gone, the thing fallen beside it
TAKEGreek Ψ, then a yen signan asymmetric grasp: only the clockwise finger closes
BEASTthe same silhouette as EARTH (a bar on legs)a thing with teeth: a half-lens with a toothed edge
WINDa nested crescent, ☽an S-gust and its eddy
EARTHa comb, or a table on legsthree uneven, splayed root-hairs
COMEthe mirror of FALLwithdrawn

Left, and watched: LEAF and BEARER are near φ (a lens with a line through it); CHEST is near ō; CHOOSE is near ♀ without its cross. As in v1: never show one of these alone at large size out of its round. Pairs that must never collapse, checked at mark size and at the pocket’s 0.6 scale:

PairWhat tells them apart
OVER / DEEP / BENEATHthe gap: OVER's cut does not touch its floor-bar; DEEP's does; BENEATH's bar is at the head
HEAR / MOUTH / CARVEwhich end is joined: the head (HEAR) or the foot (MOUTH). HEAR and MOUTH are bulging lenses; CARVE is a straight V
NAME / HOLY / TEND / HOLDwhat the cup holds: a groove lens, a solid lens, a shoot, or nothing
FIND / WEEP / EYEa punch in the lens; a drop below the foot; nothing
MORNING / DUSK / SHORE / EDGEthe star beyond the arc; within it; a curl at the bar's end; the arc alone
SUMMER / TIDE / SPARKTIDE with a star; TIDE; a star with no arc
LIE / SHOREa lens at the arc's end; a curl
CARRY / STOP / KNOTa leaning bowed stem and a pointed lens; a straight stem against a bar; a round knot with a dark heart that the rings bow round
TAKE / LOSE / HANDa finger closed over a solid lens; one finger gone with the lens outside; the open palm
SILVERBARK / TREEthe star-notches at the bough tips
BONE / EYEknobs at the ends of a cut; tails at the ends of a lens

9.10 · Composition rules v2

  1. One root per round, cut first, from the pith, along the axis, spanning the whole heart ring. In a telling, the root names what the telling is of: the Stone’s root is STONEFOLK, “it is of one of the stone-folk”, and the gift’s is STOP, the plea.
  2. One mark per cell, and a mark is one sign or a ligature of two, modifier inward, head outward. Ligature parts are cut at 0.7 breadth with the finer knife.
  3. Where things stand. An act is cut on the file of its doer; a thing on the file of the one it is, or belongs to. A runner goes from the act to what it governs. A belonging (a part, a person’s mind, word, name, breath, hand, eye, bones or blood) never introduces a new referent on its file; it belongs to the one already there.
  4. Conditions lie along the ring over files, in one year, and a mark inside a condition’s files and year takes the condition.
  5. Line quality classifies closed shapes only. Runners, fringe marks and terminals never classify.
  6. Runners follow their composition rules; a break must be declared; a pass is never declared.
  7. The root sets the axis. The seal and names stay in the bark. No runner enters the bark band.
  8. Properties of one mark combine: negation, hollow, smoothed, count, ordinal, question, half, span, part and the fringe (~!STRIKE, WOOD+!SMOOTH{all}, BEARER:keel{only}).
  9. Likeness. An as runner goes to its likeness; a likeness that is only an image, not present in the knowing, is cut hollow: “the trees breathed out the grey as sleepers breathe” is TREE×3+LIVE →as ~LIE.
  10. No small words are cut.
  11. Economy for tier 3. Every knowing of a wood leaf is carved, but only once: one mark per content word; a referent repeated in a knowing is pointed at, not re-cut; a clause shared by two knowings is carved in the first and reached from the second by a runner.
  12. Age gating and the canonical order bind every round.

9.11 · Carving a whole wood leaf

One great round per leaf. A wood leaf is one telling, known from one heart, so it is one round: its three movements are its three bands, parted by band-rules where the Book’s two RING markers stand; its paragraphs are its rings; inside each ring the paragraph’s knowings fill the years and cells, and runners knit them together; the formula “This is held in the grain” is the seal in the bark Jack.

LayoutWhy not
one great round per movement (three rounds a leaf)A movement is not a heart. It would lose the band-rules, which are the Book's own RING markers made visible, and the heartwood inside band-rule 1. It is no more legible: V.6's second movement alone is 42 sentences. The legibility problem is solved by plates, not by cutting the heart in three
one small round per knowing, arranged inside a leaf-roundThat is circles within a circle: Circular Gallifreyan's signature, and exactly what v1 forbids. Several piths in one round already means something in the grain: the Joined Tide, "several formations under one order" [v1 G8]
full-circle sub-rings, one per knowingtried, and rejected on the evidence: sparse, mechanical, a vinyl record

From a leaf’s text to its round: split the leaf at its two RING markers into three bands, one ring per paragraph; give places and bearings the even files relative to the telling’s road (the shore ahead on 0, home and the grey behind on 8, the right hand on 4, the left on 12), and persons and things with no road the odd files; the teller takes its bearing’s file, or 12 by custom; for each sentence cut its content words on their referents’ files and join them with runners by role; pack; declare the breaks, braids and binds the knowings mean; validate. A router failure means the notation must change, never the rule. The sentence’s framing is Halyna’s, not the wood’s: “We do not know why” is the blind, and “for fear leaves no mark on wood” is its gloss.

III.2 is ten hearts, one round per Throne, war-pith, its line’s root. Its band I (six rings, “We came late … at the third cry it was cut, and it fell”) is identical in all ten, and glossable from the first Throne on. Its band II is that Throne’s own entry, with its name as a said-pocket and its judgement as a cut-pocket. The recommended band III is each heart’s own fall, cut by the wood as it fell, so Halyna’s closing paragraph is the ten band-IIIs told together, glossable only when all ten have fallen Jack.

Showing it in the Book: the whole round, and the ring plates

  • The blank leaf shows the whole v2 round, fully and truthfully cut, with no glosses. At page width it is a texture to take in whole: the plain heart, and the intertwined sapwood. The Stone’s facing leaf still shows rings only until the Epilogue.
  • Ring plates are Seren’s reading of the round, set on the facing page, one per paragraph: that ring alone, re-laid at reading scale, drawn as an annulus with no pith (so it can never be mistaken for “nothing is given here”). Runners to or from other rings are drawn to the plate’s edge as stubs, and the margin carries a small pencil tag, “→ r8” or “from r4”, in Seren’s course-hand numerals: the tags are her apparatus, not the grain. At 600 px a plate’s marks are 18 to 26 px: legible. The pilot’s ring 9 is drawn as a plate in §11.9.
  • The three tabs. The grain is language-free, so it is identical under all three: The Book shows Halyna’s telling; Plain Words the modern telling with plain glosses; Original the whole round, then the ring plates in order, each with its literal reading under it once the ladder allows (§12.3).

Three rings, read by rule.

Ring 5 · literal

On the water’s file: not holding. On the current’s: taking. On the road’s: the road. On home’s: home. On ours, in cells clockwise: burning, turning; the keel; holding. On the wood’s: the dying wood; holding. The current’s taking goes to us. Our turning goes to home, and breaks the current’s taking. We turn because the water does not hold the keel. We hold, to the road; the road, to home; the dying wood holds, to the road. In our next year we go, to home.

Ring 5 · telling

We turned against the current, burning, for no water holds a keel that knows its way; and we sailed ourselves home. Even charred, even dying, the wood knows the way home.

Ring 7 · literal

We, in cells clockwise: find (to the old hidden ways) in the thinnest grey; burning, all; the keel, only; bones, few. The old ways are among roots; to them the shore does not go. The fire, not burning, slowly, and the grey, closing, are braided abab!: by turns, and at the last the grey thwarts the fire. The Guest’s bones are in ours.

Ring 7 · telling

Under the thinnest of the grey we found the old channels, the secret waters that run among the roots where no shore-man’s keel has gone. All that way we burned, and the fire went out of us slowly as the grey closed over, until nothing was left of us but the keel, a few ribs, and the Guest’s bones in them.

Ring 9 · literal

The council, in cells: those of us; going, to us; holding, to us, because sending, to us. In its next year: joined hands, to our keel; holding all, that: [a cut-pocket: the gift; the foot, and dust; the neck; the brow leaning; the axe turning; struck and falling; burning; the sending]. Then, on the wood’s file: wood, not hiding, at all.

Ring 9 · telling

The council of the long-lived came down to us, and knew us, for they had sent us. They laid their hands on our keel, many hands together, and knew the whole of it: the gift set down, and the foot that put it in the dust; the neck held gently, the foreheads meeting, the blade that slipped; the Guest struck down, the fire, the shove into the current. Wood can hide nothing.

What the prototype still does badly, for the production renderer: three runners of the crowded ring 7 found no way and are not drawn (a wider search window is needed before failing); the declared break crosses twice (the one-crossing rule must also forbid re-crossing); and long runners near the bark can read, at page size, as extra rings. Recommended remedy: cut runners in the mid tone, so the marks stay the brightest thing in the round, which is how the round above is drawn Jack.

9.13 · Version 1 and version 2, side by side

Every v1 drawing keeps its notation; v2 redraws it. A green sapling changes least (one sign from the pith, and only the flow); a carving with ties changes most, because its ties become carved runners. The GIFT and E4-01 pairs are set in their samples (§10.14, §10.16).

The later Tides may be carved richer: the Joined Tide’s “one hull waits upon another” as then runners with binds; Deceit’s decoys as hollow marks and hollow runners, and its aim as a break; the Last Tide’s forks drawn. Recommended: no. The carvings’ notation is settled, and v2’s richer drawing alone already shows the Tides’ growth Jack.

9.14 · Notation, decoding, and the proof

Grain Notation v2 is the canonical linear form of a round, written in the order a round is read, and a strict superset of v1: every v1 text is a v2 text with the same meaning (a v1 tie is a v2 runner of role to or then), and one drawing has exactly one canonical notation, which draws that drawing up to seeded noise.

WrittenIs
SIGNone of the 117 signs
! ~ _ >not (the mirror) · hollow (a seeming) · smoothed (hidden) · causative
:partthe part device
×3 ‿many; and a whole kind
½ ? #n @n ^r… * \half size; question; count; ordinal; span; the root; lean
{…}the fringe
run …a runner, by role
@fa file referent
∅the blind
lap a ⊳ ba break
braid …: abab!a braid
bind …a bind
pocket P said|cut s0–s1 {…}a pocket
  • Decoding a v2 drawing adds three steps to v1’s: count years by the year-lines and the mark feet, and cells clockwise within a slot; trace each runner from its node, through its crossings (the continuous strand is over), to its terminal, and read its role from the terminal; read each pocket’s items in its own order. The drawing then gives back its notation.
  • The literal reading replaces each token with its gloss in the canonical order. It is a gloss, not the telling; Halyna’s English is the telling.
  • A validator is run before any export: signs and ligatures known, parts legal, age gating, one mark per cell, every runner’s terminal on its own target, breaks crossing exactly once, braids with exactly as many crossings as their pattern, pockets closed, the heart plain. It found and fixed the drafts’ own slips, and it is what the blind back-translation of IV.4 read from (§11.9).
  • Readings a decoder needs from the register. A few readings are not a sign’s own gloss, and a decoder given only the spec would read them wrongly. The blind back-translation found them, and they are now rules:

9.15 · The ladder v2

Each v2 device becomes glossable at one of the canon’s Knowing bands. The Book draws every round whole from the start, and glosses only what is held.

Band (campaigns)What becomes glossable in v2 (in addition to v1's column)
K1 · one shape (1–6)the root, by one word v1
K2 · two shapes (7–14; the Night of the Naming, 13)every sign, including the 47 new ones; the part device; the kind-arc; conditions; the quantity fringe (all, few, half; count)
K3 · sentences and the memory (15–22)then runners (v1's cross-ring ties); memory; the question; the ordinal; cut-pockets ("an older carving woke in us"); the time fringe (again, still, at last); the blind, printed as Seren's [ ] until K3 and then as we do not know why
K4 · ties (23–26)the other runner roles (to, in, with, for, because, as, through); file referents; joined piths v1; braids; binds; passes
K5 · aim (27–31)hollow and smoothed marks and runners; breaks ("The wood … was told to make us believe a lie, and it obeyed": a thwarting is a kind of aim); the aim place, half size and the twin v1
K6 · a whole morrow (32)forks and chains v1; said-pockets (a plan's words, a council's words); the manner and degree fringe (slowly, gently; only, more, most)

K7★ · all tenthe sliver v1; III.2's closing ring

Tier 3. By the Finale every device is glossable, so every wood leaf reads whole under Original, with its literal reading. The translation achievements are unchanged: they ride these bands (§12.2) Jack.

9.16 · Coverage: every concept of the wood leaves, in the grain

The eight wood leaves (II.2, III.2, IV.2, IV.4, IV.6, V.3, V.4, V.6) and the 47 carvings of the Book of Knowings hold 670 content lemmas once the small words are set aside. Every one is mapped to a grain form, and every form passes the validator’s sign and ligature checks. Proof rings of the seven uncarved leaves were written at their true ring positions, with Thaesaen’s whole heart for III.2, and so were all 47 carvings as orders in wood of their own Tide’s age: all pass clean. No new sign was needed beyond the 47: the 117 signs, with 29 new compounds and the notation rules, carry every concept. The one real tension, between tier 3 and the plain heart, resolves without moving a word (§9.3).

The concepts that needed thought, leaf by leaf (A = II.2, T = III.2, X = IV.2, G = IV.4, V = IV.6, W = V.3, C = V.4, S = V.6):

The additions to the rules, each found by the coverage pass or the back-translation: a band on an item, and a band alone as a thing (the sky, the sea); addresses and doers inside a pocket; numbers above five as hands (ten is X+HAND#2, and bites still stop at four); the file referent with a ring, and the self (a runner to its own file reads “themselves”); the blind of place (“we did not know where they went”); idioms of the mirror, the fringe and the hollow; the canonical order completed; knowing form for authors; the plain heart’s substitutes; the kind of round, and names; DOOR:post; body sides by placement, never files; young wood’s substitutes; “remember” inside a pocket as ROOT+HOLD; the readings above; and a belonging does not introduce a referent, which the back-translation found when a reader without the file legend lost track of who stood on a file.

9.18 · The page cut, v3: the same carving, cut to be seen

Jack’s note 7 asked for the grain to be “more intricate and more intertwined”, with the anchor kept. The v2 rules made the carving so. But at page size, about 700 px wide, a whole leaf still read as sparse and faint: small scattered marks and pale lines, not a carving. v2 cut every round with one knife, sized for reading scale. On IV.6, whose radius is about 1,000 units, one unit is about a third of a pixel on the page, so a runner 2.7 units wide became a sub-pixel hairline, and its crossings, gaps of about 3 units, disappeared. The structure was all there. It was drawn too finely to see.

The v3 renderer changes only how a whole round is cut for the page. The Grain Notation, every rule of the grain v2 spec, the packing, the router and the signs are unchanged. Checked by code on IV.6, IV.4, the gift’s sentence and E4-01, the v2 and v3 drawings have the same marks, the same runner courses, the same crossings (over, under and kind), the same runner ends and the same validator warnings. A whole round is cut at a page weight, pw = R / 400, between 1 and 2.8, where R is the radius of its outermost ring. At that weight the runners are heavier and lie in dark grooves, and the gaps where one passes under another are wider. A dark knot-eye surrounds every mark. The ring lines yield further round the marks and are dragged where runners cross, with a wake of grain along every runner. The ring lines split into finer strands where the carving disturbs them, and a flecked figure of grain runs between the rings. All of it follows the Law of the Rings: nothing in the heart ring, a little in band I, and the most outward. So the anchor stays plain and the detail is outward, as Jack asked.

At reading scale

What does not change

  • Young and small carvings, the ring plates and the chips render byte-identical to v2. That includes the Hasty seven (E1-01 to E1-07), Burn, VI.1, Naelear and E4-01 (pw 1), the chip, and every ring plate: IV.6’s plates 5, 7 and 9, IV.4’s plates 5 and 12 and the gift’s plate 2. So E1-01 and Burn in §9.13, E4-01 in §10.16 and IV.4’s ring 9 in §11.9 are already the v3 drawings. The plates are the reading surface (§9.11), and they keep v2’s exact cut.
  • Rounds of three rings or fewer, and stage-0 rounds, are never page-weighted. Young carvings stay simple, as the Law of the Rings wants.
  • Nothing leaves the rim, and nothing is ink that was not. The wake, the figure and the splits are masked to rings 2 and beyond. The knot-eye is a knock-out, darker wood. There is no spiral, no tendril, no smoke, no closed circle besides the growth rings and no interlace off a crossing, so none of the looks the grain v2 bans comes back.
  • The runners’ tone. At page weight, runners are cut in one tone at 88%, and the marks stay the brightest thing in the round at 97%. That keeps the intent of the recommended call on the runners’ tone (§9.17, call 2).
  • The Texts’ drawings (§10) are unchanged in this version. Their young and small rounds are already the v3 drawings, byte for byte; the larger ones, the gift’s sentence among them (pw 1.46), would be cut somewhat heavier by v3.

The decode check

Both whole rounds were re-rendered by v3 with their titles, descriptions and labels stripped, cut into v2 and v3 crop pairs at reading scale (IV.6 51 crops, IV.4 70) and read by eye against the grain’s reading rules, then compared with the model’s own list of what each crop holds.
