Renderer notes v3 v3.0–v3.12, whole
v3.0 What was wrong

At page size (about 700 px wide) a whole leaf read as sparse and faint: small scattered marks and pale lines, not a carving.

The v2 renderer cut every round with one knife, sized for reading scale. On IV.6 (radius about 1,000 units) one unit is about 0.35 px on the page, and on IV.4 (about 1,280 units) about 0.27 px. So the v2 runner, 2.7 units at its node, becomes a sub-pixel hairline, and its crossings (gaps of about 3 units) disappear.

The structure (runners, braids, binds, years, cells) was all there; it was simply drawn too finely to see.

v3.1 The page weight
  • A whole round is cut at a page weight pw = clamp(R_K / 400, 1, 2.8), where R_K is the nominal radius of its outermost ring.
    • IV.6: pw = 2.34.
    • IV.4: pw = 2.80.
    • The gift’s sentence: pw = 1.46.
  • Every v3 device scales with pw. At pw = 1 nothing in v3 applies.
  • Byte-identical to v2 (checked): the Hasty seven, Burn, VI.1, Naelear, E4-01 (pw 1), the chip, and every ring plate (IV.6 plates 5, 7 and 9, IV.4 plates 5 and 12, the gift’s plate 2).
    • The plates are the reading surface (§9.11), so they keep v2’s exact cut.
  • Rounds of three rings or fewer, stage-0 rounds and plates are never page-weighted. Young carvings stay simple.
v3.2 The Law of the Rings, carried into the figure

Each ring k gets a figure strength tex(k), which sets how much of v3’s secondary texture it shows:

Wheretex(k)
the heart ring, or a joined round’s own pith rings0
band I0.45
band II0.80
band III1.0
a round of six rings or fewerthe band’s value × 0.6

So the anchor stays plain and the detail is outward, as Jack asked. The heart ring gets:

  • no figure, wake, knot-eye or ring-split;
  • runners at v2’s own knife. A runner is kept at v2 width wherever it runs inside the heart ring.
  • The one v3 change the heart shares with the rest of the round is the wider dark knock-out margin round every cut, the root’s included (v3.4). It adds no ink.
v3.3 Runners: bolder, and visibly over and under
  1. The knife. A runner is cut at pwr = 1 + 0.5 (pw − 1) of its v2 width at the node and along its body (IV.6 ×1.67, IV.4 ×1.90).
    • Its terminal point stays v2’s 0.45, so it still stops a knife-width short of the head it lands on.
    • The bud keeps v2’s node-to-body ratio.
    • A braid’s strands take half the extra weight, which keeps the plait open.
    • A pocket’s runners keep the pocket’s finer knife.
  2. Clearance caps. The heavier knife narrows wherever it would crowd something (legibility fixes 1 and 3, below):
    • it keeps 1.9 units from any other mark’s ink, as v2’s cut did;
    • it keeps 1.0 unit from its own two marks’ ink, as v2’s bud did;
    • a runner running within 25° of another takes at most half the wood between them, less a dark margin, so two runners never merge;
    • it keeps 8.3 units from another runner’s end, which is the reach of a terminal (cup, tines, root-hairs, bars, bud).
    • Narrowings are held over ±8 units and eased at 0.12 per unit. They are never thinner than v2’s own cut.
  3. Stroked, in steps of the taper. On a heavy round (more than 40,000 units of runner, the same test as v2’s silhouette mode), the runners are drawn as stroked centre-lines:
    • one path per width step, five steps along the taper;
    • round joins, and a square end at the node;
    • bud, terminals and splinters are cut as before.
    • This is more compact than v2’s silhouettes, and the wake (v3.5) reuses the same paths.
  4. Tone. Runners are one tone at 0.88. The marks stay the brightest thing in the round at 0.97, which keeps the intent of the recommended call on the runners’ tone (§9.17, call 2).
  5. The groove. The wood’s knock-out margin round a runner widens from 2.2 to 2.2 + 3 (pw − 1): IV.6 6.2, IV.4 7.6. Each runner lies in a dark groove, so where two cross the over-strand is visibly lifted.
  6. The gap. The under-strand’s gap at a crossing widens to:
    • H_RUN·pwr + 1.5·(1 + 0.9 (pw − 1)) each side;
    • at half that extra for a braid’s or a bind’s close strands.

The under-strand’s cut ends are round (clean: a pass). A break’s ends still splinter (two tines, 2.8 × (1 + 0.5 (pwr − 1)) long, at −40° and +36°), so pass and break read at page size.

v3.4 Round every mark: the knot-eye and the yield
  • Knot-eye. Round every mark outside the heart ring, the wood’s mask knocks out a lens at 62%, pointed along the grain.
    • It reaches 3 + 2.2 (pw − 1) along the ring and 2 + 1.2 (pw − 1) across it, both scaled by 0.6 + 0.4·tex.
    • It is a knot’s darker wood. It adds no ink, so it can never be a band, a pocket or a sign.
    • The knock-out margin round every sign widens from 3.4 to 3.4 + 2.4 (pw − 1).
  • Yield. The ring lines’ yield round a mark deepens to 1.2 × (1 + 2.5 (pw − 1)) outside the heart ring.
    • The spec’s check that no two ring lines come within 4 units still passes on both rounds.
  • Latewood. Latewood bands are up to 1 + 0.6 (pw − 1) wider, and 1 + 0.1 (pw − 1) stronger, outside the heart ring.
v3.5 Where runners pass: the bark-flow
  • The dip. Where a runner crosses a ring line, the line dips further and wider:
    • 1.3 + 3.5 (pw − 1)·t over 3.6 + 6 (pw − 1)·t units, where t = min(1, tex / 0.45);
    • the grain is dragged along a passing root.
  • The wake. Six faint contour lines lie at even, widening distances from every runner’s course:
    • opacity 0.28 falling to 0.07, line width 0.55 pw^1.5;
    • where runners lie close their wakes merge, and where they cross the wakes turn with them;
    • the grain swirls round the runners, which is the “intertwined” look at page size;
    • drawn as the runners’ own stroke paths in a mask, and gated by tex band by band.
  • Where the wake is never drawn:
    • in the heart ring;
    • in a pocket (± 4 units) or a lined condition band (STILL, WATER, WHITE, DREAD);
    • within 2.5 + 0.75 (pw − 1) units of a year-line.
v3.6 Ring-splits
  • Where the carving disturbs a ring line (a mark’s yield, or a runner’s dip), the line’s latewood splits into 1 to 3 finer strands on its inner side. They follow its bow and rejoin it in open wood, like the grain crowding round a knot.
  • The number of strands grows with tex: 1 in band I, 2 in band II, 3 beyond.
  • Guards, so a split never reads as a line that carries meaning:
    • pieces are at most 150 units, so never a whole ring and never a band-rule;
    • opacity 0.30 / 0.24 / 0.18, width 0.6 (1 + 0.55 (pw − 1));
    • a split is always attached to a ring line at both ends, whereas a pocket border is a closed lens with tips on half-file lines, a mouth and items (see v3.9).
v3.7 The figure
  • Seeded grain lines run between the ring lines at spacing (9.5 − 3.5·tex)(1 + 0.3 (pw − 1)). They are broken into runs of 90 to 320 units, each flecked by one of three seeded dash patterns (5 to 20 units on, 9 to 34 off, × pw^0.6).
  • Knot-halo. Each line parts round every mark: above a mark’s head it crowds over, below its foot it crowds under, and beside the mark it rejoins. The line drops out where it would cross the mark.
  • Bark-flow. Each line is dragged along every runner that crosses it.
  • Guards:
    • never within 4 units of a year’s floor, where year-lines are read;
    • never in a pocket or a lined condition band;
    • opacity 0.15 to 0.29 in four tiers, width 0.6 pw^1.3.
  • A figure line is always fainter than a year-line or a pocket border, and it is flecked, never a full circle. Drawn as continuous lines, the figure read as the rejected vinyl look (§9.1).
v3.8 Year-lines
  • At page weight a year-line is cut as what it is: a wedging ring. It is a sliver that swells in its middle and pinches out at both ends, 0.8 (1 + 0.9 (pw − 1)) wide at 40%.
  • It is laid above the wood’s knock-out, so a mark’s wider margin never eats the year-line under its foot (legibility fix 5, below).
  • It spans exactly the v2 year-line’s arc (±0.62 of a cell), at the year’s floor.
v3.9 Legibility regressions found by the decode check, and fixed
  1. Heavy strokes crowded other marks and terminals.
    • What happened: IV.4’s c7 ran over c3’s through-tines, and a4’s as-runner bled onto the heads beside it.
    • Fix: the clearance caps of v3.3 (2).
  2. The node’s round cap read as a bud-knot or a cup.
    • What happened: IV.6’s a2 at its source looked like a terminal.
    • Fix: the run from the node is cut square, and the bud keeps v2’s shape.
  3. Width steps, cut square, made ladder-notches that read as crossing gaps.
    • Fix: round joins, width hysteresis, and eased plateaus.
  4. The wake had seams. Butt joins in its mask left light squares at every width step.
    • Fix: round caps and group opacity.
  5. Year-lines were eaten by the wider knock-out margins.
    • Fix: the slivers of v3.8, drawn above the mask, with the wake and the figure kept clear of them.
  6. The anchor was no longer plain. Runners inside the heart ring were cut heavy.
    • Fix: they keep v2’s knife.
  7. Wood figure could rival the read lines. Wake lines at 0.34 and ring-splits at 0.40, some 1.7 units wide, could be mistaken for pocket borders (said: 0.62 and 0.34).
    • Fix: the wake is capped at 0.28 and ring-splits at 0.30, and the splits are finer.
v3.10 Not Arrival, and the other near-looks (the grain v2 bans), re-checked
  • Nothing leaves the rim: the wake, figure and splits are masked to rings 2 to K.
  • There is no ink blot and no smoke. The knot-eye is a knock-out: darker wood, not ink.
  • There are no tendrils and no single brushed ring. The wake follows the runners along the grain, and the figure follows the rings.
  • There is no spiral, no closed circle besides the growth rings, and no interlace off a crossing.
  • Colour is currentColor under class="wood-ink". The masks use luminance only.
v3.11 What v3 does not change, checked by code

On IV.6, IV.4, the gift’s sentence and E4-01, the v2 and v3 renders have identical:

  • marks (placement, span and breadth);
  • runner courses;
  • crossings (over, under, kind): IV.6 has 109 passes, 1 break, 3 braid crossings and 1 braid-break; IV.4 has 231 passes, 9 break crossings and 2 bind locks;
  • runner ends;
  • validator warnings.

The router, the packing and the signs are not touched. The whole-round check is deterministic (two runs byte-identical).

v3.12 Size
Roundv2v3Budget for a leaf
IV.6 whole306.8 KB344.7 KB350 KB (within)
IV.4 whole429.1 KB479.2 KB350 KB (v2 was already over)
the gift’s sentence74.8 KB113.6 KB—
  • Everything is still symbol-based: every sign is one <symbol> placed with <use>.
  • The new cost is:
    • the figure, in four opacity tiers × three dash patterns, each one path, at whole-unit precision;
    • the stroked runner steps, which the wake reuses;
    • the knot-eyes, one path;
    • the year-line slivers, one path.
  • IV.4’s size is mostly v2’s own: 145 KB of symbols and 46 KB of placements.

The call is Jack’s: cut whole rounds for the page by v3, or keep v2’s one knife. The notation, the rules and every reading are the same either way Jack.

10The Texts

Every sample written so far, each given the same way: the drawing in its own hand, the tongue as the Book spells it, word by word, the translation, and the exact letter string (for the course-hand) or the Grain Notation (for the grain). New in v0.2: each Shoreland text is also given in the leaf-hand, as Seren’s ink writes it, and cut dry, as a Stonewright would cut it, with the dry cut’s own reading (the mortar words the reader lays back in are in brackets); and the wood texts are drawn by the v2 renderer, beside their v1 drawings where they differ. Every drawing here is generated by rule from the text beneath it, and every text reads back from its drawing by rule.

How to read the pieces. Word by word puts each word over its gloss (the abbreviations are in §3.3). The hand is the letter string the course-hand writes: letters are separated by .; ^S and ^N are the bites; A and O are the harmonic letters; , is the wedge, | the perpend and #gate the end of an oath; = puts the sealing lintel over a word. GN is Grain Notation (§8.8): * the root, ! not, ×3 many, + a ligature, ^rj a span, ‖ a band-rule, ¦ included bark. The dry cut string (§5.2): @word is the word-sign read word, +A.th its complement letters, ! the turned stone, %h a capped numeral letter.

In the course-hand Orrowen

10.1 · The Title of Liberty Hosk Lunn

Written by the Captain in coal on the torn cloak (I.1). Shown from the first launch, on the prologue art and the store art, with its English, because Kael reads it out. It is the player’s key to the letters.

Orrowen

Ul dumol ol varn, ol theldeth, ol Mardh, ol lunnath, ol sollan.

Word by word
Ulin (+N)dumolN·memoryolour (+N)varn,homeolourtheldeth,family-PLolourMardh,Godolourlunnath,freedom-PLoloursollan.peace
Translation

In memory of our home, our families, our God, our freedoms, our peace.

The hand
u.l t^N.u.m.O.l o.l v.a.r.n , o.l th.e.l.d.A.th , o.l m.a.r.dh , o.l l.u.n.n.A.th , o.l s.o.l.l.a.n |
Leaf-hand

ul t̺umOl ol varn, ol theldAth, ol mardh, ol lunnAth, ol sollan.

Seren’s leaf-hand writes the same token string as the Captain’s coal, every word: 48 letters and marks, joined in 20 movements of the pen. The coal is unjoined.

Cut dry
@tum+O.l @varn , @theld+A.th , @mardh , @lunn+A.th , @sollan |

Memory: home, families, God, freedoms, peace. The five things stand; the six mortar words are the reader’s.

17 signs, 35% of the written line.

  • dumol has no article. It is the head of a construct whose possessors are definite, so “in memory of” is article-less by grammar. That is what makes the Last Carver’s extra word an error.
  • The nasal bite under the t is the Title’s only visible mutation: ul “in” beds the t of tumol into a d.
  • theldeth and lunnath end in the same two letters, read two ways by harmony.
  • Five possessed nouns, five ol: “five things a man might die for”.
  • The Title uses sixteen distinct letters (u l t m o v a r n th e d dh s and the harmonic A O) and the N bite. Everything the Last Carver cut comes from these.

  • The answer is built on the Title’s second word. dumol is tumol with a nasal bite, and Tumar is the same t standing bare: “the answer comes from the first words of the Captain’s Title”.
  • It is also Orrowen’s “yes”. A question is answered by repeating its verb. Every stone leaf asks, and the hearth says yes (Jack’s note 2: “I like that yes means we remember”).
  • In the First Tongue it is *tum-ar, “we hold” (§2.4): the same verb as the wood’s Knowing, theinas. The green sliver’s Ve … raltheine is the same answer in the other tongue.

[This] wall stands. We two laid [it], we two answer [for it], while stone [is] stone. It stands. The vow cited, as it would be cut on the lintel of a finished work or in the rolls; the gate is read Ston. As sworn under a capstone it is cut whole, in letters: (a) and (b) above.

16 signs, 29% of the written line.

What changed between (a) and (b) is the history of §3.4 in one vow. The endings fell (STONOS > ston, XALDOS > hald); old x became h; old ŋ went into somm; the Hal’s unwritten softening of cadhana became the written bite of hadhan; and the fixed suffix vowels turned harmonic (TESSANA > tessen). Why (a) and (b) are whole: a vow is cut whole (§5.2). That is why the first builders’ Stonwryt, alone of all their cuttings, can be read word for word, and why the First Tongue shows it cut in its own words, unchanged (§2.4).

IV.3–IV.4. The only Shoreland the Guest ever learned, said at the warden’s door.

Word by word

Translation

The hand
h.e.s.s , h.e.l.v , s.e.n.n.O.l
Leaf-hand

hess, helv, sennOl

Written, with the wedges where he paused.

Cut dry

Not cut. They were spoken once, at a door, by a Mystaeri mouth; no one would cut them. Cut dry they would be [HESS] , [HELV] , [SENN]O l: the three stones exactly, for the Guest had already left out every mortar word. He spoke the dry cut.

  • Three content words and no small words, as canon says: “your tongue joins its words with small words that make no sound across water”.
  • None of the three needs a stop consonant, so a mouth that has only the thunder-knock can carry them. That may be why these were the three he learned.
  • Sennyl’s rounded y is the one sound he would miss. A Mystaeri mouth has no rounded vowel, so he would have said sennel. Brenn would not have noticed. In his own tongue the three would be rheil, nael, vease.
  • His last word and the gift’s last clause are one root, *senn-, “going down”, split by the parting: the stone’s senn “die”, the wood’s senn “beneath” (§2.4).

10.11 · We remember our home too (VI.1, the green sliver)

The living green sliver grown “in the dark of the dead Throne’s heart, out of sight, as a seedling grows in the crack of a wall”. Its pith is round: it is the only living wood in the Book grown after the war with no war in its heart. A sapling holds one sign, “and the word was home”, but that one sign is a ligature, and the rest of the knowing is folded into it. It must never appear in store art or screenshots.

10.14 · The gift’s sentence (IV.4)

The gift is eldest wood that “time has forgotten”, petrified: Myststone. Its pith is round because it is older than the war. It holds this sentence nearest the surface. Eleven rings: three for the plea, four for the reason, four for who they are and the plea again. Files: 0 is the hearer, the shore-men; 3 is the pillars and their breath (odd, placeless: the pillars have no road); 8 is us, behind the grey; 13 is our children, also placeless.

The sky over us is their breath, and ours, and when you cut them it comes open, and our children cannot live in the open sun. 10.15 · The Hasty seven, and Burn

The Hasty Tide’s wood. Each is a green sapling round, one season old: one ring, no heartwood, a square war-pith, and one sign cut from the pith along the axis. A Hasty sign carries its whole young-wood order in its own anatomy. That is why Halyna could tell one word at first and the whole order at the Night of the Naming: they learned to hold the rest of the same one sign. E1-01, To the shore, is drawn in §8.6, split along its axis into the two planks of V.2, and beside its v2 drawing in §9.13. The seven here are drawn by the v2 renderer: green wood is “drawn exactly as v1” but for the grain’s flow.

10.18 · The Stone out of the Grey (the leaf facing I.1)

The Epilogue. A stone that had been wood came in on the tide in a small grey boat: Myststone, “the one stone his people had that would carry a meaning”. It was cut with a chisel “in our own letters, so that anyone might read it”, and Seren read it with her eyes and did not lay her palms on it. So the grain in the Stone was never known by anyone at the hearth. The Last Carver cut letters for eyes and grain for hands, and only the letters were read. This leaf is the first the player sees and the last to be filled.

The letters

Orrowen

Ul et dumol ol varn, ol theldeth…

Word by word

In the memory of our home, our families…

  • et is the one word too many: an article on the head of a construct. A Mystaeri mind marks any held or remembered thing with ra, “the held one”, so a Mystaeri hand cutting memory reaches for a definite word, and Shoreland has none there. Its two letters are both in the Title, so the inscription uses nothing the Title did not teach.
  • The five tells (§4.7): no bed; every stroke tapered at both ends; the Title’s nasal bite copied faithfully; no mark at the end, where the cutting stops; and, new in v2, he cut the mortar: every small word, in letters, as the coal Title had them, and one more. No Stonewright cuts a small word in stone. “The right thing, said truly, by one who did not yet know how we say it.”

The grain Jack

The Stone’s grain is the wood’s half of The Torn Cloak: what every hull saw on the last whole stone, and what went home through the roots to the groves, where “he knew it … as the wood knows a wall”. It holds all five things of the Title, as the wood names them; the letters stop after two, and the grain does not stop. Eldest wood, petrified, round pith; nine rings, 4 / 3 / 2 by movement, and the seal. The axis points right, so the top stays clear for the letters. Files: in band I, 0 is the stone-man; through bands I–II, 4 is the stone, the sail on it and the marks on the sail, one referent held by the ray; 6 is the stone-folk coming; 8 is us, the other side; in band III, files 0–4 are the five.

11Tier 3: The Whole Book in Its Own Tongues

Jack’s note 5: “I’d like tier 3 on how far to take the translation.” Tier 3 is the furthest: the whole Book in its own tongues. Every stone leaf is written whole in Orrowen, in the leaf-hand, as Seren wrote it; every wood leaf is carved whole in the grain, with Seren’s frame (her title, her headnote and her closing line) in Orrowen, because those are hers and not the wood’s. This section gives the vocabulary that makes it possible, a lexicon now of 3,015 entries; the whole Book, done (§11.4), read back into English blind to test whether the tongues say what the Book says (§11.5), and made one voice by the merge (§11.6); and the two pilots, one leaf of each kind, that set the house style and the formulas every leaf reuses (§11.7, §11.9). The native text lives in the Original tab’s own document, The Legends, in Their Own Hands.

11.1 · What tier 3 means

  • A stone leaf is written in the leaf-hand, whole, because the Book is Seren’s ink (“This Book is ink”). Every mortar word, every ending, every mutation. An inscription quoted in a leaf (the Title, a Stonwryt, a lintel) is drawn in its own hand beside it: coal, cut letters, the Hal, or the dry cut.
  • A wood leaf is carved whole, one great round per leaf, every knowing cut once (§9.11), and Seren reads it in ring plates on the facing page.
  • The translator keeps three habits of the tongue: verb first; the dual for pairs (Halyna are always two, and take a dual verb); and the “at” and “upon” idioms for having, being able and feeling.
  • Nothing is coined. Every word rests on the First Tongue’s roots, and every grain sign on its marks. Every reserve word still owes the Welsh, Irish and Tolkien dictionary pass before it ships (§13.8).

The surfaces, as the Orrowen v2 spec sets them, with two changes from v0.1: Seren’s note is drawn in the leaf-hand, and the black chest’s lid carries the foremark.

11.2 · The lexicon: how it was made, and what it found

3,015 entries (2,880 when the pilots were done; translating the whole Book added 135, below), every one resting on the First Tongue’s roots (the inherited words, the suffixes and the 371 reserve roots), made into the rest by Orrowen’s own suffixes, its prefix na-, its compounds and its constructs. No new root was coined, and no root that only the wood kept was revived in the stone, so the ancestor’s 38 kin words stay exactly 38 (where the Book needs such a word, Orrowen builds it from its own material: eye is veskow, “the seeing-place”).

  • The Book is covered. All 1,202 English lemmas of the stone text, its 62 names and its 62 hyphenated words have an Orrowen rendering: 1,189 lemmas by an entry, and 13 (of, a, have, can, could, belong, ago, either, neither, without, whoever, whichever, wherever) by the grammar itself. By running word count, three-quarters of the stone text lands on canon words.
  • The whole Book is written in it. Every word of the translation, 19,281 in the eighteen units and 1,187 in the pilots, parses against the merged lexicon, with 0 unknown and 0 ill-formed (§11.4).
  • The canon survives whole. Every canon word, name and sense is in the lexicon with its canon gloss verbatim; the audit finds 0 missing and 0 changed.
  • 1,892 entries carry a dry-cut word-sign (1,767 before the merge): 328 are the word-signs themselves, about 1,030 are a word-sign with its complement letters, 198 are compounds cut as two signs, and the rest are phrases whose stones have signs. With the 328 signs, the turned stone and a few complement letters, a mason can cut more than half of the lexicon without spelling a stem. No new word-sign was needed.
  • The analyzer reads romanised Orrowen and the Hal, undoes both mutations and the endings, checks harmony and every mutation against the word before it, and reports unknown or ill-formed words with suggestions; it passes all 87 samples of the spec, finds all 11 of 11 crafted faults, and finds both of the Last Carver’s tells.

The spelling rules every pattern obeys: a harmonic suffix vowel takes the stem’s class; a stem-final c/k is respelled by the vowel after it; an old ā-stem drops its -a before a vowel suffix and goes broad; the canon’s three old broad stems keep their broad endings (treskat, flennath, tevath). Where a suffix’s sense is regular, the derivation is systematic (every verb root has its verbal noun, participle and agent); where it is not (a place, a folk, an un-doing, an “-ish”), only the words a speaker would use are made. A form that would collide with an existing word is not made.

The compound’s seam is the canon’s: the modifier, then the head softened (gorndholm, Halvard, sirrvell). Two seam rules are new, and both are proposals: a softened dr- gives r- (moltrunn, a heartbeat), and a seam that would make a letter pair the Book reads as one sound (t+h, d+h, r+h, a+e, o+w) is not allowed: myst + cless would spell mysthless, so “a fog-bank” is the construct cless vyst instead. Zero derivation adds a sense and never a form: tev “a child” is also “grow”, its root being *taw- “sprout”; lunn “freedom” is also “open”.

EnglishHow Orrowen says it

a, annothing: a bare noun

either … or, neither … norhos … ell; nath … ell nath
whoever, whichever, wherevergor + the relative sa
withoutna- on the verbal noun, or nath … lo
agothe past particle re with a count of time
to (before a verb)the verbal noun
feelingsDoss X um Y, "X is upon Y": the lexicon lists the idiom for grief, fear, shame, gladness, hope, hatred, pride, sickness, fever, patience and courage

The lexicon also gives the Orrowen of the Book’s titles, the Tides (Hyll Pynt the Hasty Tide, Hyll Dhumol the Tide of Remembering), the Captain’s three calls, the hearth’s formulas (Cadhom o hosen re yal cadhat lom, “This I lay as it was laid for me”; Eth re dhess nahos, “And no one answered”), and the wall’s names (scethan dhenn the ghost fleet, wemmeth myst the grey sails, tolmath nawrodh the mute stones). These are tier-3 proposals, not canon.

Counted over the 2,857 entries the lexicon builder made. The 158 added in translation (the pilots’ 23 and the merge’s 135) are cut by the same rules: 119 by their stones, the mortar words left out and a signless word in letters; 20 by a single sign; 10 in letters (names, and words with no sign); 5 in numeral letters (hos, pa); 2 by the turned stone alone (nath re, ho nath); and 2 not at all, because a stone does not ask.

At the merge: the lexicon of the whole Book

The eighteen units wrote 180 rows of additions. The merge read each one against the lexicon and against the other units’ rows, by form and by sense, and let the lexicon’s own rules decide. One form, one row: a new sense of an existing word goes into that word’s meanings, after its canon sense, never into a second row. A phrase takes the class of its last word. Of the 180 rows:

  • 159 became 135 new entries, O2881–O3015. Of those 159 rows, 39 had been reached independently by two to seven units, and they agreed on their form; they collapsed into 15 entries. Halyna’s close in the dual, Cadhan o hosen re yal cadhat lona, “This we lay as it was laid for us”, was written by seven units in the same words.
  • 15 are new senses of 10 existing words. The siege day’s hours are among them: et cadhol the laying, et caldol the hauling, et kethyl the holding. So are the Fall, Ommol, and the shore’s names for two Thrones, Vorrol the Burning and Lennet the Silvered.
  • 2 are regular plurals the analyzer already parses (Mymmyleth the Homecomings, drunnatath drums).
  • 4 were withdrawn for a form that another unit, or the lexicon, already had.
#KindFormsChosen, and why
L1one sense, two formstrenn um dhrenn (S02) · trenn eth trenn (S04)trenn eth trenn. “A paragraph each” is distributive, and the distributive is the X eth X of pilot I.1’s hos eth hos (O2862), used by S03, S04, S06, S07, S08 and W02; X um X is “X upon X”, piling (bystir um wystir, brod um wrod). S01’s third form, trenn gor hos, goes the same way
L2one sense, two formshosk et carm (S01) · cadh et hosk um (S09)cadh et hosk um, “lay the lintel upon”: the exact counterpart of the pilots’ cadh et tolm hosast, “begin” (O2859), one verb for both ends. S01’s noun use (hos lo o dholm hosast eth ullen lo o hosk) was already the pair’s
L3one sense, two forms (with the shared lexicon)kylyl uldath (S06) · kylyth (O1134)kylyth: the shared lexicon made it for the Book’s own lemma “fickleness”, and it keeps the sentence’s two abstracts in -Oth side by side (nel hy voduloth, veth hy hylyth uldath)
L4one sense, two forms (with the shared lexicon)hinnar Dhavow (W02) · tavowhinnar (O2494)tavowhinnar: the shared lexicon’s compound for the Book’s hyphenated “harbour-city”; a definite construct reads “the city of the harbour”, one city. The headnote reads gor dhavowhinnar Orrow
L5one form, two sensesmeskel (O1385): “the root-men” and “treelings”split, as S08 found it must be (V.5: “the wall calls them treelings”): the root-men are uldath veskrivull, “the men of the root” (S08, O2974); meskel keeps “a treeling”
L6near-synonymsul hos hoss (S09, W02) · ul hos fedh (S05), both glossed “at once”both kept, glosses narrowed: ul hos hoss “in one breath” (quickness, the same instant); ul hos fedh “at one time” (things together)
L7near-synonymsfedh lyss (S04) · fedhfedh lyss narrowed to “a short while”; fedh keeps “a time, a season”
L8near-synonymscadh nycul (S09) · nyculcadh nycul narrowed to “deceive: lay a lie in a mind”; nycul keeps “lie, tell a lie”

Screened. Every new row, and every old row the merge touched (146 in all), parses word by word in context against the merged lexicon, with 0 problems; the whole lexicon parses entry by entry as before, and the analyzer’s test passes all 87 samples. No new word is on the Tolkien and franchise blacklist, the reserve screen’s rejected forms or the common-English list. None uses a banned letter (z, x, q, j) or ending (-ion, -iel, -dor). None equals an existing form or its softened or nasalised form, and none reads as na- + another word. No new root: every root a new row names is one the lexicon already used, so no root that only the wood kept is revived, and the kin words stay 38. The three new single words are regular derivations of existing roots: seryl, carrying on (ser + -Ol); bithlernen, southern (bithlern + -en); and desirel, latish (desir + -el).

Findings for Jack

  1. Three reserve roots end in -dor, which both tongues ban: stidor “a herald” (word-sign 246), stendor “a crane”, vundor “measure”. The lexicon keeps them flagged and never uses them. Recommend redrawing all three before the reserve ships, and re-reading sign 246 Jack.
  2. Reserve roots that sound like a mutated canon word. The ancestor’s screen checked base forms only. The ones that meet canon text or the siege’s own words are below. The rest are the ordinary homophony every mutating tongue lives with, and context settles them. But the Creed is the guild’s most-cut line, and nath mosk reading “do not begin” is a trap. Recommend redrawing mosk, heth, cald and dath; any reserve word can be swapped without touching the laws, and the lexicon rebuilds in a second Jack.
    Reserve wordSounds likeWhere it meets the canon
    mosk "begin"N of bosk "attack" (and of osk "trust")the Creed, Par; nath mosk
    heth "spring"S of keth "hold"et tolm sa heth; re heth; ho heth?
    cald "haul"its S is hald "wall", its N is gald "build"the siege's hauling (caldol)
    dhess "dawn"S of tess "answer"re dhess, "answered"
    nask "eat"N of dask "end""until the end" with no article would be dem nask; the Cry says dem et dask
    dath "evil"its N is nath "not"ul nath, "in evil", looks like the negative
    humm "husband"S of cumm "haven"
  3. Grammar the spec left open, settled reversibly: comparison with hy “than” and sost for the most; adverbs as the bare quality after the verb; the negative past as nath re + S (proposed by the I.1 pilot); and nasalised br-, gr- and softened cl-, cr-, which have no repair rule and are applied mechanically.
  4. The size. The brief asked for about 3,000. The lexicon had 2,880 when the pilots were done, and the whole Book’s translation took it to 3,015 with words the Book itself needed. It did not get there by deriving every suffix onto every root, which would make words a speaker would not use (a little dusk, a place of noons).

11.3 · The lexicon: 3,015 entries by field, and a selection

Grouped by the field of the First Tongue root each entry rests on: a compound goes with its head, and names, places, the Book’s terms and the Mystaeri loans go together at the end. Canon 379 · reserve 371 · made for the Book 720 · made by rule 1,545. The whole lexicon, 3,015 rows in 14 tab-separated columns (an id, the form, its Hal, part of speech, class, senses, canon gloss, derivation, root, formation, word-sign, dry cut, source and the Book’s English lemmas it renders), lives beside this doc at Docs/Research/Rivenkeep_Orrowen_Lexicon.tsv. Printed whole here it would take this page past about 4 MB, beside the grain’s drawings, so each field below is a selection: about one entry in twelve, and at least twelve a field, spread evenly through the alphabet and across the four sources, with words the Book uses chosen first among the made ones. Every entry added in translation, the pilots’ 23 and the merge’s 135, is given whole at the end.

lern hoselphr,n · Sthe shape only; the shape alone: a knowing's shape, held before it could be told (the Book's frame for a wood leaf's first fragments, 'As first known, the shape only'); of a knowing, lern is its shape, not a facea phrase: et the + lern 'a shape' (O1184, whose first sense is 'the face') + hosel 'alone, only' (O0990; set after a noun it is 'only' of the noun, the Orrowen spec). Made for Seren's two lines to IV.2 that use it (the headnote's 'Halyna could hold only its shape', kethyl et lern hosel; the label 'the shape only'), so that a reader, and the analyzer's set-phrase hint, take lern as the shape of a knowing and not its face (the blind back-translation of W03 read 'the face alone') (unit W03)VESK+rim (230)T

11.4 · The whole Book

Tier 3 is done. Every leaf of the Book is in its own tongue. The stone leaves, the Rivenmen’s tellings, are written whole in Orrowen, in the leaf-hand, small words and all, as Seren writes the Book in ink; so are Seren’s headnotes, the foreword, the Invocation and the Epilogue. The wood leaves, the Mystwood’s knowings, are carved whole in the grain, one round to a leaf, with Seren’s frame (her title, her headnote and her closing line) in Orrowen. The whole of it, leaf by leaf and facing the Book’s English, is The Legends, in Their Own Hands.

It was made in eighteen units at once: S01–S11 the stone leaves, W01–W07 the wood leaves. Every unit built on the two pilots (§11.7, §11.9) and reused their formulas word for word. Each unit put every word and sign it needed into its own additions, derived from the First Tongue’s roots by the lexicon’s own rules, and had its leaves read back blind. A merge then made the eighteen into one Book: one lexicon, one grain and one rendering of every line the Book repeats (§11.6).

11.5 · The whole Book read back blind

Every unit’s native lines were read back into English blind, by the pilots’ method (§11.8): the reader had the Orrowen or the Grain Notation, the specs, the lexicon and the tools, and no English. Each line was scored on the pilots’ scale: exact; close, where a nuance shifts; drift, where a proposition is lost or changed; wrong, where something is contradicted or invented. Each unit then fixed what the reading found and re-read the fixed lines by rule.

The result: 633 units scored. Before: 575 exact or close (91%), 51 drift, 7 wrong. After: 627 exact or close (99%), 6 drift, no wrong.

The six drifts left are not translation errors. Five are reader slips where the text stands: two in S04 and three in S10. The sixth is the Stone’s DEEP+SQUARE in the Epilogue, a collision in the grain spec, left open for Jack’s call Jack.

11.6 · One Book, one voice: the merge

Eighteen translators working at once will render one English line eighteen ways. The merge read the units against each other and made the Book say each thing once. It found the Book’s recurring phrases by their shared five-word runs across leaves, and checked them paragraph by paragraph. Where units differed, one form was kept: the pilots’ form if there was one, else the majority’s, else the better derivation. The others were changed, and each change is marked in its unit.

11.7 · The stone pilot: I.1, The Torn Cloak, whole in Orrowen

The first stone leaf of tier 3, and the first of the two pilots on which the eighteen units built: I.1 whole, as Seren writes it in her ink. Seren’s headnote, Kael’s telling, the Title, the True Men’s verse, the hearth’s answer and the facing leaf. 1,020 words of Orrowen, against about 1,080 in the Book’s English for the same text: written whole, small words and all, the ink runs about as long as English, which is what note 1 asks of the later hand. Of the 1,020, 827 land on canon words, 96 on reserve roots and 97 on tier-3 words. The analyzer reads every line (72 lines) and reports 0 unknown and 0 ill-formed words. The leaf needed 21 lexicon additions, every one built from existing entries by the lexicon’s rules; no new root. Canon Orrowen (the Title, Tumar, Seren’s line, Covv Treskat, Kael Nydherd, Rytom um …, Ston.) is used exactly as the spec gives it.

Title

kovv treskat

Covv Treskat

I.1 · The Torn Cloak

The riven cloak. treskat is canon: one word for torn, riven, cleft; the canon keeps its broad ending.

Seren’s headnote

re k̬adh krennel kael, kael nydhArd, rytvard et vennuldAth, ul et vess hosAst sa re p̬ess et odh sy trenn. nath re lusk o lom kylOl b̬rod hyo, eth nath re k̬ylOm.

Re hadh Crennel Kael, Kael Nydherd, rytvard et vennuldath, ul et vess hosast sa re vess et odh sy trenn. Nath re lusk o lom kylyl wrod hyo, eth nath re hylym.

Laid by Sergeant Kael, Kael the Counter, oath-keeper of the True Men, on the first night this hearth asked for a tale. He would not let me change a word of it, and I have not.

Word for word: Laid Sergeant Kael, Kael the Counter, oath-keeper of the True Men, on the first night that this hearth asked a tale. He did not allow me a changing of a word of it, and I did not change. “And I have not” is Orrowen’s yes-and-no rule: the verb said again.

Kael’s telling

hebb et tolm lom. nath reskOm, es stonOm. re reskOm loskAt grem sy.

Hebb et tolm lom. Nath reskym; es stonom. Re reskym loskat grem sy.

Give me the stone. No, I will stand. I have sat enough this winter.

Orrowen has no “no”: a man offered a seat refuses it by saying the verb back, Nath reskym, “I do not sit”.

His oath

rytOm um hosk et bystir rerdsennen, sa re rytAnt et pardAth hemm so vollAth umo, es k̺adhOm sy venn, hy vodh nath d̺oss kadhOl ullen lom. ston. # re g̬alOm um et ganna orl ull. el nydhArd g̬alAtAth en, nel vellArd, eth galAt sa nath re nydhOm, nath k̺adhOm o los.

Rytom um hosk et bystir rerdsennen, sa re rytent et pardath hemm so vollath umo: es gadhom sy venn, hy vodh nath noss cadhol ullen lom. Ston. Re yalom um et ganna orl ull. El nydherd yalatath en, nel vellerd; eth galat sa nath re nydhym, nath gadhom o los.

I swear on the lintel of the western stair, where the old wardens cut their names, that I will tell this plain, for I have no other way of telling. I was on the gate that day. I am a counter of things and not a singer, and what I did not count I will not tell you.

The oath is the canon’s Rytom um hosk…, and it closes with Ston., “It stands”, as every oath does: the one word of the leaf the English does not carry Jack. es gadhom sy venn, “I will lay this plumb”: to tell a tale is to lay a course, and a plain telling is a true course. The wardens cut their names and Kael cuts his oath: one verb.

The True Men’s verse

Ganna cresket, pithulath driget,
ul gemmyl lo orrow, wemmeth myst;
re yyst hosel um dholmath luskat,
eth re dhresk et covv um o sest.
Re ryt o lesk galat dem sennyl,
eth re vaver nahos hyor vranast.

The gate was broken, the lords were scattered,
the grey sails gathered along the shore;
one man climbed where the stones lay loosened
and tore the cloak his shoulders wore.
He wrote five things a man might die for,
and none of us has needed more.

First-syllable stress; the odd lines four beats, falling away on a two-syllable ending (DRI-get, LUS-kat, SEN-nyl); the even lines close on the same consonants, not the same vowels, myst · sest · vranast, a rhyme of the ear a mason would call a true joint. “None of us has needed more” is nahos hyor vranast, “none of us a sixth”: the True Men count Jack.

The hearth

Eth re vysk et odh: Tumar.

And the hearth said: We remember.

The whole leaf, every paragraph in the leaf-hand facing the Book’s English, is in the Original’s I.1. Its facing leaf is the Stone’s bare rings, and Seren’s line under them, unchanged.

Grammar the leaf had to settle

#PointWhat the leaf doesWhy
G1The negative past (the lexicon left it open)nath re + S: nath re yal, nath re hylym, nath re vysknath beds the next word, which is re and cannot change; re softens the verb. The tense particle sits next to the verb, as in the canon's sa re vess. Added to the lexicon as a phrase row
G2Verb agreementa plural noun subject takes the plural ending (re yalant et crenneth, re veskent et vennuldath); a collective takes the 3sg (re resk et Stonwrytan, sa re lymm of lunt); the existential doss stays 3sgthe canon's Tuma Halyna agrees with its noun subject; the canon's Re yald et Stonwrytan is 3sg with a collective
G3The object of a verbal nouna possessor, softened: kylyl wrod "changing a word"a verbal noun is a noun; the canon's rellor wrod has the same shape
G4"where" as a relativeul vodh (Lo wisk, ul vodh re ston et hald)the lexicon already gives ul vodh for "where"; the question word serves as the relative, as in many tongues
G5Relatives with a prepositionthe conjugated preposition stays behind: sa re rytent … umo "on which they cut", sa reskys lo "that you sit at", sa re yal et neskyl lo "whose was the leading"the Celtic-type resumptive, which the conjugated prepositions make natural
G6A fronted objectleft out and taken up again: galat sa nath re nydhym, nath gadhom o losOrrowen is verb-first; a thing brought forward is picked up by o
G7The softened cr-hr-: so Hrenn, so hrenneth, Aske Hrisur Lurrthe canon gives Crenn, S Hrenn, so the onset is the canon's own
G8"Only" of a clause (back-translation)nath … veth, "not … but": sa nath re yorrar veth amm ew venn et daskhosel after a verb reads "alone"; nath … veth is already the leaf's lo nayalat veth osk
G9A possessive before a letter that does not soften (back-translation)the possessor said as a noun (saed et covv), or the sentence recast (uld hosen et Crenn)after a verb, o + a word in h, s, l, r, n, f, v, w, th, dh or a vowel shows no bite, so it reads as the subject "he"
G10"Not yet" and "no longer" (back-translation)nath … tul is "not yet" only; "no longer" is said another way (re vammant, "had lost")the canon's Nath noss tul kethyl fixes nath … tul

Collisions the leaf steps around

  • N + br- gives mr-, an onset the tongue does not allow, so no nasalised brodh anywhere: Kael’s tell after es and nath is cadh, “lay”, the tongue’s own idiom for telling.
  • mysk “say” after a nasalising word reads as nasalised bysk “tie”, so the leaf never puts mysk after es or nath. And re vysk is both “said” and “bound”: “bound” is given as the participle.
  • darr “come” softens to rarr, so mellor “come in” is used; the reserve mosk “begin” is the Creed trap, so “the crying began” is re dhald et carmol, “the crying rose”.

11.8 · I.1 read back blind

The test: could the Orrowen be read back into the Book’s English using only the specs, the lexicon and the tools? A reader was given only the Orrowen lines and the two notation lines of the leaf (the Title’s dry cut and Seren’s leaf-hand string), with no English, no word-for-word lines and no notes; wrote the back-translation; froze it (hashed and timestamped) before the pilot’s English was opened; and only then compared.

The result: 12 exact, 6 close, 4 drift, 2 wrong, of 24 paragraphs

All six drifts and wrongs traced to nine clauses. The two wrong paragraphs both held a statement of character: what the True Men are, and that there was no greater man than the Captain. Both failed on the same weakness, a small word with two readings (hosel alone/only; hy from/than) in a position where the wrong one is the natural one. The True Men’s creed, “who fought only when the cause was just”, came back as a last stand, “who fought alone when the end was sure”. Fixed: 8 clauses in 7 lines of the leaf; 3 lexicon rows; 4 lines of the spec made explicit (the unmarked possessive, hy as “than”, “only” as nath … veth, nath … tul as “not yet” only: all now in §3.3); 2 defects in the analyzer. After the fixes the analyzer reports 0 unknown and 0 ill-formed across the leaf, and still passes all 87 samples. The Title, in the leaf-hand and cut dry, and Seren’s line both came back exactly.

11.9 · The wood pilot: IV.4, The Gift Held an Hour, whole in the grain

The whole of IV.4 carved in the grain, with Seren’s frame in Orrowen, in her one ink. The shape of it: Myststone (“wood that time has forgotten”), a round pith, 16 rings in three bands (2 / 11 / 3), the band-rules at the Book’s two RING markers, the seal in the bark. 63 knowings; 156 marks in the rings and 16 more in 8 pockets (6 said, 2 cut); 110 runners (4 split, 2 hollow); 2 breaks, 1 bind, 1 blind, 2 memory rays. Packed, it is 35 years, and its radius is about 1,290 units, inside the estimate for IV.4. No new sign was needed; three compounds were added. The validator reports 0 errors and 0 warnings, and every word of Seren’s frame passes the analyzer.

Seren’s frame, in Orrowen

The title

hebbAt sa re g̬al kethAt hos klem

Hebbet sa re yal kethet hos clem

The Gift Held an Hour.

“The gift that was held one hour.”

The headnote

hosen tum mesk myst, kethAt hy et hebbAt sost, et tolm domm sa re g̬rik brenn hy et tuss, ul hyll t̬umOl, doss o ul lern g̬ebb et pard.

Hosen tum Mesk Myst: kethet hy et hebbet sost, et tolm domm sa re rik Brenn hy et tuss, ul Hyll Dhumol; doss o ul lern Yebb et Pard.

As the Mystwood remembers: known from the gift itself, the dark stone that Brenn picked out of the dust, in the Tide of Remembering; it faces the Warden’s Door.

re k̬eth rhyna o hos klem lo et odh, eth re d̬arr o uloy niss, hosen nynth um t̬olm, hy vodh hebb et mesk hemm sost nag̬alAt pynt.

Re heth Rhyna o hos clem lo et odh, eth re rarr o uloy niss, hosen nynth um dholm, hy vodh hebb et mesk hemm sost nayalat pynt.

Rhyna held it an hour at the hearth, and it came into her slowly, like water over stone, for the eldest wood gives nothing quickly.

re femm halvard o nafedh.

Re femm Halvard o nafedh.

Halvard never touched it.

re g̬al o lo et lodh um et parow, eth re k̬eth o o hosen re k̬eth ey o, eth ew o sa re k̬adh et tolm hosAst ul et brodhOl.

Re yal o lo et lodh um et parow, eth re heth o o hosen re heth ey o, eth ew o sa re hadh et tolm hosast ul et brodhol.

He was at the mortar across the ward, and he knew it as she knew it, and it was he who began the telling.

ew duss sost brodhOl et trenn ul o d̬ask, hy vodh re g̬al maver o b̬rodhOl um =halyna hosen es k̺adh et arra o, ul et brodAth orrowen sa re g̬al lo nafedh.

Ew duss sost brodhol et trenn ul o rask, hy vodh re yal maver o wrodhol um Halyna hosen es gadh et arra o, ul et brodath orrowen sa re yal lo nafedh.

The sentence at its end was the hardest to tell, for it had to be told as the Guest would have said it, in words of ours he never had.

re b̬rodhA =halyna o, hos eth ullen, ul p̺a luth, re k̬adh seren o.

Re wrodha Halyna o, hos eth ullen, ul ba luth; re hadh Seren o.

Told by Halyna, by turns, in two inks; set down by Seren.

amm re g̬al et mesk kreskAt, ell re omm et brodhOl, doss o rellorAt eth nak̬lennAt.

Amm re yal et mesk cresket, ell re omm et brodhol, doss o rellorat eth nahlennet.

Where the wood was broken, or the telling failed, it is marked, and not mended.

The close

eth re t̬ess nahos ¶

Eth re dhess nahos.

And no one answered.

  • “Began” is “laid the first stone”, cadh et tolm hosast: to tell a tale is to lay a course, so to begin a telling is to lay its first stone. The reserve mosk “begin” is the Creed trap, avoided.
  • “Known” is kethet, “held”, the canon’s own verb for knowing wood. Halyna are two, and take the dual (wrodha, 3du); “by turns” is hos eth ullen, “the one and the other”: the pair’s antiphony in three small words. Seren writes her own name in letters, with no lintel.
  • “It had to be told” is the “upon” idiom, doss maver um, “need is upon”, in the past; the pronoun object of the verbal noun is written as its possessor, o wrodhol, “its telling” Jack.
  • “As the Guest would have said it” is es gadh et arra o, “as the Guest would lay it”, with the tongue’s own verb for telling, as Kael’s es gadhom sy venn: after es, mysk “say” would be heard as bysk, and brodh would begin mr-, the onset I.1 avoids. “Words of ours” is et brodath orrowen, “the words of the Shore”, the article keeping brodath out of the nasal after ul. (Revised after the blind reading, which had es mrodh … ul ol mrodath.)

The wood’s telling, in the grain

One ring per paragraph, one or more knowings per sentence, files as the pronouns: we is file 12, you file 0, the Guest file 1, and “whoever held us” is simply file 7 with nothing cut on it. The root is GIFT, “We were given once”.

We are the eldest wood. We were a tree when the world was green to its edges. We fell, and the ages lay down on us as leaves lie down on leaves, until time forgot us and we grew dark and hard. We are not stone, though you took us for it.

Ring 9: the rite as he meant it, and the first bind carved in a whole leaf. Ring 9 is cut in the wood’s own voice, so the grain must not cut as done what was never done. What was made is cut whole (the shallow cut on the host’s arm was opened); what was never made is cut hollow, “shown, not meant”: letting go of the neck, the Guest’s own cut, and the pressing of the arms, whose two bind strands are hollow runners. The bind is the rite’s meaning, harm to one is harm to both, and its out-runner is the promise. Left and right are placement: the host on file 4 stands clockwise of the Guest on file 1, so the host’s right arm and the Guest’s left meet in the bind.

With his left hand he would open a shallow cut on the host’s right arm, and let go the neck, and cut his own left arm, for he would ask no blood he did not give. Then the two would press their bleeding arms together, shoulder to shoulder: a promise of united front, that harm to one was harm to both.

Ring 12: the break. The ring’s centre is the arm’s runner crossing the blade’s shallow runner square and splintering it, lap l2 ⊳ l1: the grain’s own grammar says what the English says with “for”. “Half made” is {half} on the rite; “heard all of it” is HEAR{all}; “no one picked us up” is the shore’s file not taking.

The blade that was meant to go a little way went deep, for the arm was moving. The host’s blood came, and he cried out, and his men came. The Guest did not lift his hand against them, and the cut he would have made on his own arm was never made. They struck him down on the stones of the door, and he died there with the rite half made. We lay in the dust and heard all of it, and no one picked us up.

What the translation did

  • Every sentence is carved, once. One mark to a content word; a referent already cut in a knowing is pointed at, never cut again. Thirteen runners end on a file referent.
  • The heart stays plain, and the fine work is outward: the first pocket is in ring 3, the first break in ring 12. Jack’s “anchor in the middle … details in the outer rings” holds in this leaf exactly.
  • Truth or nothing, in the conditional. IV.4 is full of would. The grain has one device for it, the hollow, and uses it strictly: what was done is cut whole, what was never done is cut hollow.
  • Two breaks, both the leaf’s own turning points: the moving arm thwarting the shallow cut (ring 12), and the foot’s finding thwarting our could-have-spoken (ring 13): “the one that could have spoken to him; and it was the one his foot found”.
  • Two rounds cited, not re-carved. Ring 8 cites the rite as he meant it by the Aelthar’s own round; ring 15 cites the gift’s sentence by its round, root STOP. Each is a cut-pocket holding the root half size, with the cited round drawn beside it.
  • The blind stands alone in ring 11: one mark, one empty cup, “We do not know why. Fear leaves no mark on wood.” The barest ring of the round is the one the whole leaf turns on.

The whole leaf, round and plates facing the Book’s English, is in the Original’s IV.4.

11.10 · IV.4 read back blind

The pilot’s Orrowen and its grain notation were read back into English using only the specs, the lexicon, the analyzer and the validator, then compared paragraph by paragraph. Reported honestly: the test was blind to the pilot but not to the spec, which quotes about 35 fragments of IV.4’s English; and a search for the pilot’s headings also printed its file legend, so the referents in the reading are not a blind result. The uncontaminated baseline for referents is the validator’s own reading of the comment-free notation, and it lost them: that finding became a rule (a belonging does not introduce a referent, §9.10).

11.11 · What the pilots and the whole Book teach, and what is still open

  • The small words are where meaning slips. Both wrong paragraphs of I.1 turned on a small word with two readings; the IV.4 frame’s one drift was an idiom a glosser did not show as one. Write the clause so only one reading is natural, and let the analyzer show set phrases.
  • The stone and the wood fail differently. Orrowen fails on homophony and small words; the grain fails where a reading lives outside the spec. Both now have rules for what was found.
  • Truth or nothing reaches into the grammar: the grain’s hollow for what was never done, the stone’s Ston. for an oath the English does not close.
  • A fresh blind reader for every leaf, before it ships, with the notation and the Orrowen only, and the file legend stripped by a parser before anything is printed.
  • The lexicon is generated, and rows appended by hand are lost on a rebuild unless their recipes go into the builder’s sources: the tooling note every pilot carries.

Still open, for Jack

  1. “What the one knows, the other knows” is now keth in all three leaves: the Bonded’s own verb, “hold; know the wood”. S09 had argued for sesk, “know a fact”, in V.7, where the bond shares a mind and no wood is touched. If that distinction is wanted, it belongs in all three places, so it is one word, chosen once Jack.
  2. “Part One” (III.1) and “Part I” (V.7) stay different. Saed Hosast, “the first half”, is for a catalogue laid in two. Trenn Hosast, “the first course”, is for V.7’s three parts, each laid on its own night: saed means “half”, and three parts cannot be halves. The English differs too. Say if one word should serve both Jack.
  3. !TURN+HOLD and !TURN+HEAR are legal ligatures that the validator reads part by part (“not turning aside, and holding”). A glossed compound could make the reading “a holding not turned”. This is left to the validator.
  4. The grain rules marked proposed or for Jack (A16b referents, A18 the untold ring, A24 the Last Tide’s root, A25 the Epilogue’s v1 sample) wait on a spec pass. Every unit reads right without them Jack.
  5. Owed from before: the Welsh, Irish and Tolkien dictionary pass on every reserve word the text uses (§13.8), and the lexicon’s own findings (the three -dor reserve roots; mosk, heth, cald, dath: §11.2). The units stepped round them throughout, and the merge added nothing that meets them.
  6. For the builder: the merged lexicon, grain spec and concept register replace the shared ones as they stand, and the recipes of the 135 new rows go into the lexicon builder’s sources before any rebuild, or a rebuild loses them.

12.2 · The unlock ladder: achievements that translate

Jack asked that the player be unable to read the native hands: “The human can’t read it because they have not achieved the ability to yet. Only by unlocking the achievements in the game.” The Legends’ laws allow that only on milestones every player reaches. So the translations ride the Legends’ delivery map (map §3, §4): each rung fires at a campaign milestone, or at an event the sim has recorded with a campaign fallback, and each wood rung is one band of the Knowing (§8.6) given a name.   • Every rung is reachable by any way of holding a battle. Each event rung has a campaign fallback; the rest are campaign-keyed. Sinking a fleet and routing it both yield wood.
  • A translation is a ripening, not a new leaf, so it never counts toward the one-leaf-per-debrief law. The debrief shows one line and no more: “A leaf in the course-hand is read.” for a stone rung; the Legends’ own “Halyna have told more of the wood.” for a wood rung.
  • Skill achievements (Pacifist and the rest) may add one gloss line at most, never a leaf and never a translation.
  • After, never before. No rung fires before the player has met what it glosses, and none hints at what comes next. By the Finale every grain device is glossable, so every wood leaf reads whole under Original.

12.3 · The three tabs: The Book | Plain Words | Original

Jack’s note 3: “I like that there are 3 tabs for the book.” Every tale carries three tabs, and so do the foreword, the Invocation and the Book of Knowings (Legends map §8). The Book is the canonical text (The Legends); Plain Words is the modern translation (The Legends, in Plain Words); Original is the native text itself (The Legends, in Their Own Hands). The three files are built to be parallel: the same leaves under the same ids, in the same order, so the tab can swap one for another in place.

  • The native hand is drawn above The Book and Plain Words; the tabs change only the English beneath it. The grain has no language, so it is identical under every tab; only its glosses change: The Book uses the Book’s words (shore, thin wood, the dread), Plain Words plain ones (the coast, cheap ships, the edge of our guns’ range).
  • Original shows the native text for decoders. For a stone leaf: the leaf-hand, whole, facing the Book’s translation, and any inscription the leaf quotes in its own hand (the dry cut, the Hal, the coal) beside its leaf-hand transcription. For a wood leaf: the whole round, then Seren’s ring plates in order, each with its literal reading under it once the ladder allows.
  • A locked leaf shows its own hand under all three tabs, because there is nothing yet to translate. The tab bar still shows, so the player learns where the translation will appear.
  • The tabs are views, not edits. Switching never changes, removes or reorders a word, so the Book-only-adds law holds. The choice is remembered with the settings, not the save, and opens on The Book the first time. The Book wins where they differ.

12.4 · For the builder

  • No leaks. A locked stone surface’s accessible title is “A leaf in the course-hand, not yet read” (a Hal surface’s, “A Stonwryt in the first builders’ hand, not yet read”; a dry-cut stone’s, “A stone in the course-hand, not yet read”); a locked grain round’s is “A carving in the grain, not yet known”, and a single locked mark’s or name’s “A mark in the grain, not yet told” or “A name in the grain, not yet told”; the unmarked Stone’s is “Nothing is given here”. None carries the English, the Orrowen, or an id that names what it tells. A leaf-hand line set in the font carries the same accessible name, not its text. The drawings in this doc are the earned forms.
  • One ink per hand. Every drawing paints only in currentColor, under stone-ink or wood-ink; the page sets the ink, and the ids of every drawing are prefixed so any number can share a page.
  • The leaf-hand is a font. Garl Flenn (15 KB as woff2) sets any leaf from its true-encoding markup; the converter reads the tier-3 lexicon through the analyzer, so every bite and harmonic letter is right. A release build should merge the font’s overlapping contours and draw the sealing lintel as a contextual mark.
  • The dry cut is drawn by rule and read back by rule: every dry-cut drawing in this doc was read back to its token string before the page was written.
  • Weight. A whole-leaf grain round is budgeted at 350 KB, a ring plate at 60 KB; all eight wood leaves whole, with plates, come to about 3.5 MB. Load a leaf’s round and plates when the leaf opens.
  • Size is meaning. A round is drawn at the scale of its wood, so a Hasty sapling is small and a Throne’s heart fills the leaf. Rounds of nine rings or more need a tap-to-enlarge below about 900 px; a course-hand line in body text is legible at 1.55 em.
  • Reduced motion. Any “rings growing”, “runners growing” or “marks growing in” reveal honours prefers-reduced-motion and shows the result at once.
  • Truth or nothing. A stone leaf with no authored Orrowen shows its first paragraph in the hand and the rest as ruled empty courses, never faked. The validators run before export: the round trip for the course-hand and the dry cut, the grain validator for every round, the analyzer for every line of Orrowen.
  • The generators stay out of Docs/. The renderers, the sound-law engine, the analyzer, the validator, the font builder, the sign tables and the lexicon data live with the build tooling. This doc carries the rules and the data needed to redraw any of it.

13Originality

Jack’s note 4: “It’s not that nothing is traceable to others’ works. Just nothing obvious. Nothing we could get sued for.” So the rule is no longer nothing that resembles anything. Two works were invited in as influence, Arrival for the grain and Ogham for the course-hand, and a third, Jack’s reformed Egyptian, for the dry cut’s economy. Everything else was checked against and kept out, by the standard below.

13.1 · The standard

WhatWhy
Must goa trademark, a logo, a franchise's named thingactionable
Must goa letter or sign that is, or is plainly taken from, a letter of a script a player would recognise: Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, the Elder Futhark, the basic CJK characters and the Kangxi radicals, kana, hangul; or of a famous invented script: Tengwar, Cirth, Aurebesh, Dovahzul, D'ni, Kryptonian, Sheikah, the Hylian scripts, Arrival's logogramsobvious
Must goa word of a published invented language (Sindarin, Quenya, D'ni, Klingon, Dothraki, Valyrian, Na'vi) with the same or a related meaning; a real-language word with its own meaning (Welsh seren "star" is kept only as a coincidence of sound, with its own etymology)obvious
May stayform-only echoes: a word whose shape happens to match a word of another tongue, with a different meaning. trenn, rhass, gorn, luth, tum, el, vess, gor, sell, gell, nell, sirr, hal, varn, mesk, gann, pell, crenn, brod, delv, sull, hebb, neth, lanth, na and the rest of v0.1’s near-call list all staynot obvious; every language shares shapes
May staythe world's commonest strokes, where the design needs them: the Door (Π-like) as the gate and GANNA, both peoples' door; the Fore, a Latin cross, as the Bar Before and the foremark ("The Latin cross is fine", note 8); the Stem, the Bar, the Cutgeneric, and kept whole on purpose
May staya resemblance to a letter of an ancient alphabet no player would know (Carian, Lycian, Old Turkic, Old Hungarian, Old Italic, Phoenician)not obvious
May stayan idea taken from a real or an invented system: logograms with phonetic complements (Egyptian, Maya, Chinese), a running hand made from an inscriptional one (Roman cursive), the grain's reading of meaning (Arrival, as Jack wants)ideas are free

The v0.1 near-call list is therefore closed: every item on it is a form-only echo and stays (§13.6). The trenn / Sindarin trenarn call, which v0.1 left for Jack, is resolved by note 4: trenn stays.

13.2 · What we took in spirit, and what we did not

From Arrival (the heptapods’ writing, from Ted Chiang’s story and the film’s design) the grain takes three ideas: a writing of meaning with no sound behind it; a sentence taken in whole rather than read in order; and a form drawn in circles, where the writer must hold the whole before making the first mark. Our version of that last one is the canon’s: a knowing is known whole, as memory, and in Arrival the medium is the writing’s shape where ours is touch. The grain takes none of the look:

Arrival's logogramsEilseth
one ring per sentencemany concentric growth rings; one ring is one step
ink, smoke, soft gradients, blotscrisp V-cut facets on wood, flat fills, no gradients or filters
meaning off the rim (tendrils, hooks)marks cut inside the bark and across the rings; nothing crosses the bark
no start and no enddirectional: the pith is the beginning, the bark the end, and the root sets the axis
stroke weight = tone and urgencyweight carries nothing
a hook makes a questiona question is an unfinished head at a ring line
twelve sectorssixteen files, set by the root and not by the frame
made in one gesture, timelessgrown over years; a later carving contains its earlier form
black on pale fogged glasswood tones, bark, growth rings

Version 2 moves the grain toward three looks v1 had banned outright (branching vines, interlocking, knots), so the boundaries are restated by their signatures, not by broad words. v2 is intricate without borrowing anyone’s look:

Look to avoidIts signatureWhere v2 stands
Arrival (the heptapods' logograms, in the film)one inked ring per sentence; tendrils and hooks off the rim; smoke and blots; thicker means more urgent; no start and no end; made in one gestureMany growth rings, with runners inside them and nothing off the rim v1. Every cut is faceted, with no smoke. A runner's taper gives its direction, not its tone; weight carries nothing v1. The round reads heart to bark, and a later ring grows over an earlier one v1. Jack's "same flavour" is kept as an idea: a writing of meaning, taken whole, in circles
Nomai (Outer Wilds)text written along a spiral; each spiral is one speaker; replies branch off as new spirals, and a conversation is a tree of spirals on a wallRunners carry no text along them: the signs stand apart, and the runners only join them. Runners follow the grain and never spiral: at most 300° of turning, no curl tighter than 5 units (terminals and locks apart), no loop. They fork once at most, and a shoot never forks. Everything is enclosed in growth rings
Circular Gallifreyanword-circles inside a sentence-circle; dots and arcs on the circles; straight lines joining circles; read anticlockwise from the bottomNo circle anywhere but the growth rings. Year-lines are partial arcs, never closed. No dot sits on a line: punches are inside signs. Runners join signs, never circles, and they drift; they are never chords. No small rounds inside a leaf-round. The grain reads clockwise from the root v1
The Elden Ring emblemoverlapping, interlocking ring arcs; a golden glow; a staff line through the ringsRings never interlock. Only runners, which are open cuts, cross, and a bind is two open hooks, never two closed curves linked. No glow. No straight staff: the only straight radial line is a ray, within one file v1
Celtic and Norse interlace: knot panels and borders, the triquetra, the triskele, Solomon's knot, the endless knot, Borromean rings, and the valknut, which has a modern extremist use as wellinterlace as ornament: closed, symmetric, periodic panels; rotational three-fold knotsInterlace appears only where two relations cross, and every crossing is read. No closed knot, panel or border. A braid is short, open at both ends, and runs along one ring. A bind is a two-strand lock; three strands chain as two locks, never a three-fold rotational figure, and never interlocked triangles
Runes, Cirth, Tengwarstaves with straight branches meeting at a point; stem-and-bow lettersv1's principle, applied to all 47 new signs: bow, stagger or break. The fringe never runs along a stem-line (not Ogham)
Letters, punctuation, icons: Latin, Greek, Hebrew; ! ? ¡; emoticons; ¥; the ankh; ☽ ♀; Wi-Fi arcsone small glyph that is already somethingthe recut list. Never show one sign alone at large size out of its round v1
Circuit boards and transit mapsparallel traces with 45° jogs; orthogonal routingthe string-pulled, grain-following router, and the runner repulsion that breaks bundles
Tree-carving traditions: the Moriori rākau momori of Rēkohu (the Chatham Islands), carved in living kōpi trees; the Basque shepherds' aspen carvingsfigures cut into the bark of standing treesThe grain is cut across the end-grain of a heart, never on standing bark, and it carves no human figures in the bark. Named here with respect, so that no later sign drifts toward them
Avatar (the forest's root network that holds the ancestors)a living link between trees that holds memoryRunners are cuts inside one heart, not links between trees. "What went home through the roots" is carved: the memory ray and the file referent. Never a glowing or living network
D'ni (Myst, Riven)brush strokes, thick and thin, hooked Z- and 2-shaped; boxed base-25 numeralsunchanged v1: no pen contrast, no boxed numerals, no count above four bites and HAND

From Ogham the course-hand takes the spirit: an alphabet made to be cut, strokes set on a line, stone-honest and straight. It takes none of the system:

OghamThe course-hand
strokes on either side of a stem line, or through itletters stand on one side of a bed, never across it
letters are counts of one to five parallel scoresno letter is a count; a letter is an upright (where the sound is made) and laid stones (how)
vowels as notches on the linevowels are loose pinnings between the letters; the only marks below the bed are the mutation bites, single, never grouped
five-letter families named for their first letter; tree names; read up an edgea place-by-manner grid; no letter names; read along a course, line by line, as a wall is laid

From the reformed Egyptian of Jack’s note the dry cut takes the economy, and the idea behind it, logograms with phonetic complements, which Egyptian, Maya and Chinese writing all share. Nothing in it copies the characters of the Anthon transcript or any Egyptian sign: its signs are the First Tongue’s own marks, worn straight. The leaf-hand likewise takes only an idea, a running hand made from an inscriptional one, as Roman cursive was.

13.3 · The look-alike screen

Every new drawing of v2 (the 328 word-signs, their heads, the turned stone, the leaf-hand’s letters) was screened by machine against 1,463 characters of real scripts: Latin capitals and small letters, digits, Greek and Cyrillic capitals, the Runic block, Ogham, Tifinagh, Hebrew, the Kangxi radicals and 172 common CJK characters, katakana, hangul jamo, the Canadian syllabics, Cherokee, Old Italic, Old Turkic, Old Hungarian, Phoenician, Carian, Lycian, Gothic, and 52 symbols including the crosses, the swastikas, ⊥, ⊤, Π, ∀ and the planetary signs. Each candidate and each reference is drawn into a 64 px box, thinned to a one-pixel skeleton, and the two skeletons compared by their mean chamfer distance (0 is the same shape; a plain T scores 0.007 against Latin T). Below 0.030 against a recognisable script is a copy and must change; 0.030 to 0.045 is looked at by eye.

Every sign after the first two rows scored between 0.030 and 0.045 against a recognisable character and was looked at by eye beside it. None is a copy: each match is an artefact of the skeleton at 64 px, and the sign reads, at any size, as a head under a crown. No sign scored below 0.030 except the Fore, a Latin cross by design (“The Latin cross is fine”), and the Door, kept whole by both peoples.

  • Dropped during design because the screen or the eye found a copy: a Stem-and-cope sign (丅, T), a Bed sign (⊥, 土, 士), a Still sign (二, 王, =), a Three sign (川, Ш), a Hand sign (Ψ), a Split sign (Y), a Sprout and a Tally sign (runic ᚠ, ᛓ), two tree signs (runic ᛀ, †), a sail sign (P, ᚹ), a mouth sign (K), a wall sign (A), a gate with its capstone (开), a fire sign (a goblet), and a first leaf-hand in which every letter became an arch (it read as Armenian). The leaf-hand’s g, which read as П when its shore stood upright under the slant, was given a stronger back-lean.
  • By law, W7: no branch leaves a word-sign’s stem at a slant as a rune’s branch does. Crowns are free stones, never dots, acutes or curls, so a crowned sign never reads as a letter with a Tolkien vowel mark.
  • The leaf-hand’s near calls, looked at by eye and kept: a and A (Г, 0.037), o and O (ד, 0.036), k (0.034 to a Kangxi radical), the gate (Π, 0.034, the Door). Each is a short stroke-pair every alphabet has somewhere. The hand has angular turns, a nib and hairline joins along the line: no loops, no bowls, no stem-and-bow, no headline.
  • What the screen cannot do. It has no fonts for the invented scripts (Tengwar, Cirth, Aurebesh, Dovahzul, D’ni, Kryptonian, Sheikah, the Hylian scripts); those were checked by eye against the charts of the v0.1 pass, and nothing new resembles them. Arrival’s logograms are ink circles; nothing in the stone is round.
  • The grain’s 47 new signs were checked by eye beside their v1 neighbours and against letters, digits, runes and interface icons; twelve first drawings were recut and one withdrawn (§9.9). The first marks are proto-writing, so some are the world’s commonest strokes; none is a rune, an Ogham letter, a Cirth letter, a Tengwa or an Arrival logogram (§2.6).

13.4 · What is ours

  • One ancestor under two opposite tongues. A First Tongue whose catch became one people’s knock and the other’s long vowels; whose particles froze into one tongue’s mutations and the other’s tense suffixes; whose one word for a standing thing became one people’s stone and the other’s tree. The stone kept the sound and the wood kept the meaning.
  • The round as a sentence of time, and now relations grown as roots: runners that follow the grain, whose ends say their role, whose every crossing is read, braids for “by turns”, binds for “each only with the other”, pockets for a knowing inside a knowing, and a heart kept plain by law.
  • Real wood as the vocabulary of the marks: the fire scar that is Burn, the check that is a wound, the knot the grain flows round, the frost ring, the ring shake, included bark, the graft, the wedging year-ring, the added rays, the resin pocket.
  • A masonry alphabet, and a masonry grammar. Letters as ashlars on a mortar line; words as stones; mutations as bites cut into the mortar; the sealing lintel over a pair-name; and now the small words as mortar, left out of a dry cut as a dry-stone wall leaves out its mortar, with not the one stone laid the wrong way.
  • A history written into the hands. The Hal is the same hand, mirrored and running the other way, still spelling the endings and the three sounds the living lost, so the forgetting is visible; the Last Carver’s five tells are the same rules, broken by a carver who learned them from a cloak.
  • Two tongues built from the canon’s own names and from each people’s metaphors: to lay a tale, to cut a vow, a pair as a gate, to know as to hold; a hull as a bough, a scout as a root, sky and breath as one word.

13.5 · The v0.1 originality pass: what read as a copy, and what was done

Every v0.1 drawing was set beside the famous fictional scripts and the historical ones it could be mistaken for, and both lexicons were checked against the famous conlangs. Twelve shapes read as copies, and all twelve were recut; four words were real Tolkien words, and all four were replaced. The worst was TREE, which was the rune algiz exactly, a rune with a modern extremist use as well; the old root-foot put it, or its inversion, on every person-figure. Under note 4 all of these would still go: they were obvious.

The grain

The rule for any sign added later: runes and certhas are straight staves and branches meeting at a point, so a grain sign that is a stave with straight branches, or two straight strokes meeting, must bow, stagger or break them. The grain is grown wood, and it is allowed the curves the runes are not.

Outside the scripts: echoes in the canon itself

  • The Myst games. Myststone and Mystwood sit near two of that series’ Ages, and the Book’s Riven and Myst- already make the echo. Nothing in any hand adds to it: the D’ni letters and numerals were checked hardest, and none of the hands shares anything with them. No Orrowen word matches a published D’ni word except gor (D’ni “time”, Orrowen “every”), a form match only.
  • Avatar. “The memory that runs back through the roots” is close to that film’s forest that holds its ancestors’ memories. The grain carves memory as a ray cut into wood, and its runners are cuts inside one heart, never links between trees and never a glowing or living network.
  • Tree-carving traditions, named with respect so that no later sign drifts toward them: the Moriori rākau momori of Rēkohu, carved in living kōpi trees, and the Basque shepherds’ aspen carvings. The grain is cut across the end-grain of a heart, never on standing bark, and carves no human figures.
  • “It is known.” The canon line “what is carved in living wood is not heard. It is known” ends on a phrase a well-known television series made a catchphrase. It is ordinary English and canon, noted only because readers may smile at it.

13.8 · The audit still owed before anything ships

  • The dictionary pass (Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Breton, Cornish, Manx; the Elvish lexicons) on every reserve word: the 194 that have word-signs, the 305 the tier-3 lexicon uses, and the 26 the grain’s new signs read as. Under note 4 it is a check for obvious matches only: the same word with the same meaning. mamm “lose”, new with the I.1 pilot, looks like Welsh and Irish mam and should be looked at first.
  • An exact-string web search for the new names: Tumaʔ, ryt broc, rellor wrod, brodath lodh, Garl Flenn, and the headline Orrowen words and haven originals.
  • A fresh originality pass on the v2 grain renders by a new eye, as v0.1’s was done, including a web image search for “tree ring script”, “carved wood interlace glyph” and “dendroglyph writing”.
  • A look by eye at the leaf-hand at reading size in the Legends page’s own theme; the screen was run on skeletons.
  • Fresh blind readers: for the re-cut grain drawings, for the Hal once it has its lexicon, for the seven fixed lines of I.1, and for IV.4’s cited round.
